headline: Borno School Attack Highlights Continuing Threat to Education
summary: Suspected Boko Haram fighters attacked a community in Chibok Local Government Area of Borno State, killing one person and setting a school block containing five classrooms and an office on fire. The incident renewed concerns about the safety of schools in conflict-affected areas.
fullStory: MAIDUGURI — Suspected Boko Haram fighters attacked Kautikari Village in Chibok Local Government Area of Borno State, killing one person and setting fire to part of a secondary school, according to local authorities. The attack affected the junior secondary section of Government Day Secondary School in the community. The incident has renewed concerns about the continuing threat to education in areas affected by insurgency. According to the Education Secretary of Chibok Local Government Area, the attackers struck the community in the evening and set ablaze a block containing five classrooms and an office. Attacks on schools have consequences beyond the immediate physical damage. Students and teachers may be afraid to return to affected communities, while parents may become reluctant to send children to school. Repeated insecurity can therefore cause long-term disruption to education. Borno State has experienced years of conflict involving Boko Haram and other armed groups. Although security conditions have improved in some areas, attacks continue to pose risks to communities. Education has been among the sectors most affected because schools can become targets or be caught up in wider violence. When schools are damaged or closed, students lose valuable learning time. Children may also be displaced from their communities and forced to interrupt their education. Displacement can create additional challenges because families may move to areas where school places and learning resources are limited. The security of teachers is equally important. Teachers cannot provide effective education if they fear travelling to or working in schools. Recruitment and retention can become difficult in areas where security risks remain high. Governments therefore need to consider teacher protection as part of education planning. School security measures can include controlled access, community surveillance and stronger cooperation with security agencies. The appropriate response depends on local conditions, but schools in vulnerable areas need clear emergency plans. Communities can also contribute by reporting suspicious activity and maintaining communication with authorities. The incident demonstrates why education and security policy must be closely connected in conflict-affected regions. Rebuilding classrooms is necessary after an attack, but reconstruction alone does not solve the underlying security problem. Students need confidence that returning to school will not expose them to unacceptable risks. Government authorities also need to ensure that children affected by school closures have access to alternative learning opportunities. Temporary learning centres, accelerated programmes and catch-up classes can help students recover lost instructional time. Psychological support may also be necessary for children who experience violence. Education plays an important role in rebuilding communities affected by conflict. Schools provide children with structure, knowledge and opportunities for social development. Keeping education functioning during periods of insecurity can therefore contribute to resilience. The attack in Kautikari is a reminder that the safety of schools remains a serious issue in parts of Nigeria. Protecting children and teachers requires sustained security efforts, community cooperation and education planning that accounts for emergencies. Until schools can operate safely and consistently, children in affected communities will continue to face barriers to their education.

headline: NELFUND Expansion Plan Targets Seven Million Student Loan Beneficiaries
summary: The National Assembly and NELFUND have renewed efforts to expand Nigeria's student loan programme, with a target of reaching at least seven million beneficiaries. NELFUND said about 1.6 million students had already benefited from its interventions.
fullStory: ABUJA — The National Assembly and the Nigerian Education Loan Fund have renewed efforts to expand the country's student loan programme, with a target of increasing the number of direct beneficiaries to at least seven million. NELFUND Managing Director Akintunde Sawyerr disclosed the target during a national sensitisation programme on the student loan scheme. He said about 1.6 million Nigerian students had so far benefited directly from NELFUND interventions. The expansion plan is intended to make tertiary education more accessible to students who might otherwise struggle to meet the cost of tuition and other educational expenses. The student loan scheme forms part of the Federal Government's broader effort to improve access to higher education and reduce financial barriers for students. Rising education costs have placed pressure on many families, particularly those supporting more than one child in tertiary institutions. A functioning student financing system can provide another route for students to remain in education when household resources are limited. NELFUND's expansion will require effective identification of eligible students, reliable payment systems and clear repayment arrangements. Students need to understand the conditions attached to loans before accepting them. Transparency is therefore important to the credibility of the programme. Institutions also have a role in ensuring that students receive accurate information about the application process. Delays or uncertainty can discourage eligible applicants and create unnecessary administrative problems. Digital systems can make applications easier by allowing students to submit information electronically and track the status of requests. However, students without reliable internet access may require additional support. The programme also needs strong safeguards against fraud. Education financing schemes can attract fraudulent websites and intermediaries seeking to exploit applicants. Students should use official channels and avoid making payments to unauthorised agents. Expanding student finance could also contribute to human-capital development. Students who complete tertiary education may acquire skills needed in professional and technical fields, strengthening the country's workforce. The impact will depend on whether graduates are able to find productive employment after completing their studies. Loan recovery will therefore become important as the scheme grows. A sustainable financing system requires mechanisms that allow graduates to repay according to established rules while taking account of their ability to earn. Excessive repayment pressure could undermine the social purpose of the programme. The government and education institutions will also need to monitor whether the loans are reaching students who face genuine financial barriers. Data can help identify gaps and improve targeting. The planned expansion represents a significant increase in the scale of Nigeria's student financing system. Reaching seven million beneficiaries would require substantial administrative capacity and sustained funding. If properly managed, the scheme could reduce financial barriers and allow more young Nigerians to pursue higher education. Its long-term success, however, will depend on transparency, efficient administration, responsible lending and effective repayment systems. Expanding access to education is important, but maintaining the sustainability of the financing programme will be equally necessary.

headline: Government Denies Cyberattack on National Education Data Platform
summary: The Federal Ministry of Education has denied reports that Nigeria's Education Management Information System was hacked. The ministry said the platform remained secure and that the integrity and availability of its data had not been compromised.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Federal Ministry of Education has denied reports that the Nigeria Education Management Information System was subjected to a cyberattack, describing claims that the platform had been compromised as inaccurate and misleading. The ministry said the platform remained secure and that its data had not been breached. The denial followed reports suggesting that the education data platform had been hacked. The ministry's response was intended to reassure schools, education agencies and other users who depend on the system for education-related information. Education information systems have become increasingly important as governments move from manual records toward digital management. Such platforms can contain information used for planning, resource allocation, school administration and policy development. Protecting the integrity of that information is therefore important to the functioning of the education system. A successful cyberattack on a national education database could potentially disrupt services and undermine confidence in government information systems. The ministry's denial indicates that no such breach occurred in this case. Cybersecurity nevertheless remains an important issue for education authorities. As more schools and government agencies adopt digital systems, the amount of information stored electronically will continue to grow. Institutions need appropriate security measures, regular monitoring and procedures for responding to potential incidents. Staff training is also important. Cybersecurity weaknesses can sometimes result from human error, including poor password management, phishing and unauthorised access. Education agencies need to ensure that employees understand basic security practices. Data protection must also be considered when education systems collect information about students, teachers and schools. Personal information should only be accessed by authorised personnel and should be handled in accordance with applicable rules. Digital transformation can improve education administration by making information easier to collect and analyse. However, the benefits depend on reliable infrastructure and secure systems. Education authorities must therefore invest in both technology and cybersecurity capacity. Clear communication is also important when reports of cyber incidents emerge. Unverified claims can create unnecessary concern among users and the wider public. Authorities should provide timely information when incidents occur and distinguish between confirmed breaches and preliminary reports. The ministry's statement that the platform remains secure provides reassurance, but continued monitoring will be necessary. Cyber threats evolve rapidly and public institutions are increasingly targeted because of the volume of information they manage. Regular security assessments can help identify vulnerabilities before they are exploited. Education data can also support better policy when it is accurate and accessible to authorised users. Protecting that data is therefore part of protecting the education system itself. The incident has highlighted the need for strong cybersecurity practices as Nigeria continues its digital transformation. Secure systems, trained personnel and transparent communication can help maintain confidence in digital education administration.
img: Education officials working with a digital education management system.

headline: Students Call for Better Water, Sanitation and Security in Schools
summary: Students at King's College Lagos called for improved water, sanitation and hygiene facilities as well as stronger security for children. The demands were made during activities marking the 2026 Day of the African Child.
fullStory: LAGOS — Students at King's College Lagos have called for improved water, sanitation and hygiene facilities in schools and stronger measures to protect children from insecurity. The demands were made during activities marking the 2026 Day of the African Child, whose global theme focused on universal access to water, sanitation and hygiene. Water and sanitation are essential to children's health and ability to learn effectively. Schools without adequate toilets, clean water or handwashing facilities can expose pupils to preventable health problems and make the learning environment less comfortable. Students said access to basic facilities should be treated as an essential part of education rather than an optional addition. The condition of school infrastructure varies widely across Nigeria. Some schools have relatively good facilities, while others operate with inadequate classrooms, sanitation and water supply. Addressing those differences requires sustained investment and regular maintenance. Building new facilities without maintaining existing ones can result in resources being wasted over time. Hygiene education is also important. Students need to understand the connection between clean environments, handwashing, safe water and disease prevention. Schools can reinforce those lessons through practical activities and student-led initiatives. Security was another concern raised during the event. Insecurity has affected education in different parts of Nigeria, with incidents involving schools and students creating fear among families and disrupting academic activities. Protecting children requires cooperation between schools, communities and security agencies. Parents are more likely to keep children in school when they believe the environment is safe. School authorities can contribute by maintaining emergency procedures, monitoring access to school premises and communicating quickly with parents when security concerns arise. Government agencies also need to ensure that schools in vulnerable areas receive appropriate protection. The Day of the African Child provides an opportunity to consider children's rights beyond enrolment figures. Children require safe schools, quality teaching, adequate nutrition, healthcare and protection from violence. Improving these conditions can support both educational participation and long-term development. Students themselves can contribute to school improvement by promoting hygiene, respecting shared facilities and encouraging their peers to adopt healthy practices. Schools can also establish sanitation clubs and other activities that make pupils active participants in maintaining clean environments. The concerns raised at King's College reflect wider issues affecting children across Nigeria and Africa. Access to water and sanitation remains uneven, while insecurity continues to disrupt education in some communities. Addressing these challenges will require cooperation between governments, schools, families and development organisations. Education authorities should therefore consider infrastructure, health and security as connected parts of the learning environment. A child cannot be expected to learn effectively in an unsafe or unhealthy school. The Day of the African Child provided a platform for students to express those concerns directly. Their demands underline the importance of creating schools where children can learn in conditions that protect their health, dignity and safety.
img: Students participating in a school event marking the Day of the African Child.

headline: Businesses Seek Stronger Support for Technical and Vocational Skills
summary: NACCIMA has been recognised for supporting technical and vocational education and training through private-sector collaboration. Stakeholders said stronger industry involvement could help develop skills that match labour-market needs.
fullStory: LAGOS — The Nigerian Association of Chambers of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture has been recognised for its contribution to technical and vocational education and training through stronger collaboration between the private sector and training institutions. The association received an award recognising its support for industry-led skills development. Technical and vocational education is increasingly important as Nigeria seeks to equip young people with practical skills that can translate into employment and entrepreneurship. Employers frequently require workers who can operate machinery, maintain equipment, provide technical services and solve practical problems. Training institutions therefore need close links with industry to ensure that their programmes reflect current workplace requirements. Private-sector participation can take different forms. Companies can support training centres with equipment, provide instructors or industry experts, offer internships and help develop curricula. Such partnerships can give students exposure to real working environments before they graduate. Industry involvement can also improve the transition from school to employment. Students who acquire practical experience are more likely to understand workplace expectations and the standards required by employers. Businesses can identify promising trainees and potentially recruit them after completion of their programmes. Funding remains a challenge for technical and vocational institutions. Practical training requires workshops, equipment and consumable materials, which can be expensive to maintain. Government funding can be complemented by private-sector investment and partnerships. Training facilities must also be kept up to date because technologies used in industry change over time. Teachers and instructors require professional development as well. An instructor who has not been exposed to current industrial practices may find it difficult to prepare students for modern workplaces. Partnerships can provide opportunities for trainers to gain industry experience. Technical education can also contribute to entrepreneurship. Young people with practical skills can establish small businesses in areas such as electrical services, fabrication, construction, automotive repair and information technology. Access to finance and business training can help skilled graduates turn those abilities into sustainable enterprises. Regional differences need to be considered when developing skills programmes. Training should reflect the economic activities and employment opportunities available in different parts of Nigeria. Agriculture-related skills may be especially important in rural communities, while technology and advanced manufacturing may have greater demand in urban centres. Certification is another important issue. Employers need confidence that graduates possess the skills represented by their qualifications. National standards and credible assessment can strengthen the reputation of technical and vocational education. The recognition given to NACCIMA highlights the potential of private-sector involvement in education. Government institutions cannot meet all training needs alone, particularly as technology and labour markets continue to change. Strong partnerships can help ensure that training remains relevant. Nigeria's large youth population creates both an opportunity and a challenge. Providing young people with practical skills can support employment, productivity and economic growth. If technical and vocational education is properly funded and connected to industry, it can become an important pathway into the labour market. Stakeholders said continued collaboration between government, businesses and training institutions would be necessary to strengthen the system and ensure that graduates possess skills that employers can use.
img: Students receiving practical technical training at a Nigerian vocational institution.

headline: Kogi Begins Digital School Census to Improve Education Planning
summary: Kogi State has begun preparations for its 2025/2026 Annual School Census using the Federal Government's digital education management platform. Officials said the exercise would provide data for education planning and resource allocation.
fullStory: LOKOJA — Kogi State education authorities have begun preparations for the 2025/2026 Annual School Census as the state moves toward digital collection of information from schools. The exercise is intended to provide reliable data for education planning, policy development and resource allocation. The state Ministry of Education launched preparations through a stakeholder sensitisation meeting involving education agencies, civil society organisations, media representatives and other groups. Officials said the census would be conducted through the Federal Government's Digital Nigeria Education Management Information System portal. Moving from manual records to digital reporting could improve the speed and consistency of education data collection. School information is needed to determine how many pupils are enrolled, how many teachers are available and what infrastructure schools require. Accurate data can help government identify areas where classrooms, teachers or learning materials are insufficient. The census is also important for monitoring changes in the education system. Population growth, migration and new school construction can alter the distribution of students and teachers. Regular data collection allows authorities to respond to those changes rather than relying on outdated figures. Digital systems can make it easier to compare information across schools and local government areas. They can also help authorities identify inconsistencies that require verification. However, successful digital reporting depends on connectivity, equipment and trained personnel. Schools in remote communities may face difficulties if they lack reliable internet access. Authorities may therefore need to provide technical support and alternative arrangements where necessary. Training is also important because school administrators responsible for entering information need to understand the system and the standards expected. Data quality should remain a priority. Inaccurate entries can affect decisions about funding and infrastructure. Verification processes can help ensure that reported information reflects actual conditions. Education data should also be handled responsibly. Information about students and teachers may include personal details that require appropriate protection. Digital systems need safeguards against unauthorised access and misuse. The census could support more evidence-based planning in Kogi State if its findings are properly analysed and applied. Authorities can use the information to identify schools requiring additional support and determine where new investments are needed. Data can also help evaluate whether existing programmes are producing the intended results. Education stakeholders said cooperation from schools and communities would be important to the success of the exercise. School administrators need to provide accurate information, while government agencies must ensure that data is used responsibly. A digital school census is not an end in itself. Its value comes from what authorities do with the information after collection. If the data is translated into better planning, targeted investment and improved school services, the exercise can contribute to stronger education outcomes. Kogi's move toward digital education data therefore represents part of a wider shift toward evidence-based management of the education system.
img: Education officials preparing digital school census records in Kogi State.

headline: UBEC Digital Champions Set to Support Technology Adoption in Basic Education
summary: The Universal Basic Education Commission has inaugurated 100 digital champions to support technology adoption and improve administrative processes. UBEC said the initiative was designed to make basic education management more digital and data-driven.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Universal Basic Education Commission has inaugurated a network of 100 digital champions as part of efforts to strengthen technology adoption and improve administration across Nigeria's basic education sector. UBEC said the initiative would support digital transformation, innovation and more effective service delivery. The digital champions are expected to help promote the use of technology within education administration. Digital systems can improve how schools collect information, communicate with authorities and manage programmes. They can also make it easier for education officials to analyse data and identify areas requiring intervention. The move comes as education authorities increasingly seek to replace manual processes with digital systems. Manual records can be slow to update and difficult to analyse, particularly across a large national education system. Digital platforms can provide more timely information when schools have the necessary infrastructure and trained personnel. Technology adoption, however, requires more than providing software. Education workers need training and ongoing support to use new systems effectively. Digital champions can help bridge that gap by assisting colleagues and promoting practical use of available tools. Schools and education offices also need reliable electricity and internet access. Without those basics, digital systems may be difficult to operate consistently. This means technology programmes should be accompanied by investment in infrastructure. Digital transformation can also improve accountability. Electronic records can make it easier to track projects, monitor resources and evaluate education interventions. When information is available in a consistent format, policymakers can make better comparisons across schools and regions. Data security must also remain a priority. Digital education systems may contain information about students, teachers and schools. Appropriate safeguards are required to prevent unauthorised access and protect privacy. Staff training should therefore include basic cybersecurity awareness. Technology can support teachers as well as administrators. Digital learning resources can provide additional materials for pupils, while online professional-development programmes can help teachers improve their skills. However, digital tools should complement rather than replace classroom instruction. The success of technology programmes should ultimately be measured by their effect on education outcomes. The number of devices or digital platforms introduced does not automatically indicate improved learning. Authorities need to determine whether technology helps teachers work more effectively and whether students benefit from better access to learning resources. UBEC's digital champions initiative is part of a wider effort to modernise basic education administration. If properly supported, the network could help institutions adapt to new technologies and encourage more consistent use of digital systems. The programme will require continued training, infrastructure and monitoring. Nigeria's education system is too large to depend entirely on manual administration. Building digital capacity can make planning more efficient and improve the availability of information. The challenge will be ensuring that digital transformation reaches schools across different regions and does not widen existing inequalities. With appropriate support, the initiative could contribute to a more connected, data-driven and responsive basic education system.
img: Education officials participating in a digital training programme in Abuja.

headline: Oyo Teachers' Strike Leaves Pupils Out of Class as Parents Raise Concerns
summary: The continuing strike by public school teachers in Oyo State has kept pupils away from classrooms and raised concerns among parents and education stakeholders. The dispute followed the abduction of teachers and pupils in the state.
fullStory: IBADAN — The ongoing strike by public school teachers in Oyo State has continued to disrupt academic activities, with parents and education stakeholders expressing concern about the effect of prolonged school closures on pupils. The Nigeria Union of Teachers began the indefinite strike after the abduction of teachers and pupils in Oriire Local Government Area. The action was intended to draw attention to concerns over the safety of teachers and students. School security has become a major issue in parts of Nigeria following repeated attacks and abductions involving educational institutions. Teachers have argued that they cannot be expected to work in environments where adequate protection is not guaranteed. Parents, however, have also expressed concern about the educational consequences of prolonged closures. Children who remain out of school for extended periods can lose contact with lessons and fall behind academically. Younger pupils may be particularly affected because foundational skills require regular practice. Parents also worry about how children spend their time when schools are closed. Without structured learning activities, some pupils may become disengaged from education. Families with limited resources may also struggle to provide alternative learning arrangements at home. The strike highlights the difficult balance between protecting teachers and maintaining access to education. Safety is a basic requirement for learning, but prolonged disruption can create its own risks for children's development. Government authorities and teachers therefore face pressure to find a solution that addresses security concerns while allowing schools to reopen safely. Security measures around schools can include improved surveillance, controlled access and cooperation with local communities. In areas facing serious threats, authorities may also need broader security deployments. Teachers need confidence that such measures are genuine and sustainable rather than temporary responses to individual incidents. Communication between government and teachers is also important. Negotiations can help identify practical measures that address immediate concerns while longer-term security plans are developed. Parents should also receive clear information about school closures and reopening arrangements. The disruption in Oyo reflects a broader national challenge. Insecurity has affected education in several states, forcing some schools to close or operate under heightened security measures. Such disruptions can widen existing educational inequalities because children in vulnerable communities may lose more instructional time than those in safer areas. Education authorities therefore need strategies that allow learning to continue during periods of insecurity where possible. Alternative learning arrangements, catch-up programmes and flexible academic calendars can help reduce the effect of lost classroom time. However, such measures cannot replace safe physical schools indefinitely. The immediate priority remains the protection of teachers and pupils. At the same time, government and education stakeholders must consider the long-term educational consequences of closures. Resolving the Oyo dispute will require cooperation among the state government, teachers, security agencies and communities. The experience demonstrates that education policy and security policy cannot be treated separately. Children need both access to school and the assurance that school is a safe place to learn.
img: A closed public school classroom in Oyo State during the teachers' strike.

headline: Stakeholders Seek Stronger Inclusion for Children With Intellectual Disabilities
summary: Disability advocates have called for stronger implementation of inclusive education policies for children with intellectual disabilities. They said schools need better support systems, trained personnel and policies that protect the rights of affected children.
fullStory: ABUJA — Disability advocates and other stakeholders have called for stronger implementation of inclusive education policies for children with intellectual disabilities across Nigeria. They said more practical support was needed to ensure that children with disabilities could participate meaningfully in education and community life. Inclusive education is based on the principle that children should have opportunities to learn regardless of disability or other barriers. However, placing children in schools without providing appropriate support does not necessarily create genuine inclusion. Schools may need trained teachers, specialised learning materials and facilities that allow students with different needs to participate. Teacher training is therefore important. Educators need to understand different forms of disability and learn methods for adapting lessons to individual students. Classroom assistants and specialist professionals may also be necessary in some cases. Early identification and intervention can make a significant difference. Children who receive appropriate support at an early age may have better opportunities to develop communication, learning and social skills. Families need access to information so they can seek assistance when concerns arise. Infrastructure also matters. Schools need facilities that are accessible to children with different physical and learning needs. While intellectual disabilities may not always require physical modifications, schools must still provide appropriate learning environments and support structures. Inclusive education also benefits other students by encouraging respect, cooperation and understanding of differences. It can help reduce stigma and ensure that children grow up recognising disability as part of society rather than something that should lead to exclusion. Policy implementation remains a challenge. Nigeria has policies and legal frameworks addressing the rights of persons with disabilities, but stakeholders have repeatedly called for stronger implementation. Schools may lack resources to translate policy commitments into everyday practice. Funding is therefore an important part of inclusion. Government budgets need to provide resources for teacher training, learning materials and support services. Partnerships with disability organisations can also help schools develop appropriate programmes. Parents play a central role as well. Families should be involved in decisions about children's education and receive regular information about their progress. Schools can create stronger relationships with parents through meetings and individual support plans. Data can help authorities understand the scale of the challenge. Education systems need reliable information about children with disabilities, school attendance and the support services available. Without accurate data, planning can be difficult. Inclusive education should also extend beyond primary and secondary school. Young people with disabilities need opportunities for vocational training, higher education and employment. Developing skills can increase independence and participation in society. The call for stronger inclusion reflects the broader principle that every child should have an opportunity to learn and develop. Providing access is only the first step; education systems must also ensure that students receive the support necessary to benefit from schooling. Nigeria's progress in inclusive education will therefore depend on implementation, funding, teacher development and community awareness. Stronger support for children with intellectual disabilities can help ensure that education serves all learners rather than leaving some children behind.
img: Students participating in an inclusive learning activity in Nigeria.

headline: University Receives Approval to Launch Engineering and Management Programmes
summary: Margaret Lawrence University in Delta State has received approval from the National Universities Commission to commence engineering programmes and additional courses in management and social sciences. The approval followed a review of the institution's human and material resources.
fullStory: WARRI — Margaret Lawrence University in Delta State has received approval from the National Universities Commission to commence engineering programmes and additional courses in management and social sciences. The university said the approval followed a resource-verification exercise conducted by NUC experts. The approval allows the institution to expand its academic offerings and provide students with opportunities to study additional disciplines. Engineering programmes require adequate laboratories, equipment and qualified academic staff because students need practical as well as theoretical instruction. Resource verification is therefore an important part of the process through which universities receive approval to offer new programmes. Regulators assess whether institutions have the human and material resources necessary to provide acceptable standards of education. The expansion of programmes can give students more choices within the higher education system. It can also contribute to the development of skills needed by Nigeria's economy. Engineering graduates are needed across sectors including construction, manufacturing, energy, transportation and technology. Management and social science programmes can likewise provide skills relevant to businesses, public administration and community development. Universities expanding their programmes must maintain academic standards as enrolment grows. Recruiting sufficient qualified lecturers is important because rapid expansion without adequate staff can place pressure on existing personnel and affect teaching quality. Laboratories and libraries also require continuous investment. Equipment must be maintained and updated as technology changes. Students benefit most when academic programmes provide opportunities for practical learning. Partnerships with industry can help universities provide internships, professional exposure and access to current technologies. Such relationships can also help institutions understand the skills employers require. Accreditation and quality assurance remain important after programmes begin. Universities need to continue meeting regulatory requirements rather than treating approval as a one-time achievement. Regular review can help ensure that programmes remain relevant and properly resourced. Students and parents also need reliable information when choosing programmes. Prospective students should be able to confirm that a programme has received the appropriate regulatory approval before enrolling. This can reduce the risk of students entering unrecognised courses. The expansion at Margaret Lawrence University reflects the continuing growth of Nigeria's higher education sector. As more young Nigerians seek tertiary education, universities are under pressure to increase capacity while maintaining standards. Regulators therefore have an important role in balancing access with quality. New programmes can contribute to national development when they are properly designed and adequately supported. Engineering education in particular can help develop technical capacity for infrastructure and industrial development. Management and social science programmes can strengthen skills in areas such as administration, economics and organisational leadership. The university will now face the responsibility of maintaining the standards that supported its approval. Continued investment in staff, facilities and curriculum will be necessary. For students, the expansion provides additional opportunities to pursue professional and academic interests within the institution. For the wider education system, it demonstrates the importance of regulatory oversight as universities expand their academic offerings.
img: A Nigerian university campus where new academic programmes are being introduced.

headline: Northern Schools Need Sustained Investment in Teachers, Technology and Infrastructure
summary: Education stakeholders have called for sustained investment in schools across Northern Nigeria, with emphasis on financing, technology, teacher development and learning infrastructure. They said long-term support is needed to improve educational outcomes in the region.
fullStory: KANO — Education stakeholders have called for sustained investment in schools across Northern Nigeria, stressing that improving learning outcomes will require practical support for teachers, technology and infrastructure. The call followed discussions at the All Northern Schools Conference, where participants examined challenges facing education in the region. Stakeholders said schools needed more than temporary interventions. They argued that sustainable improvement requires financing systems that can support schools beyond individual programmes or conferences. Teacher development was identified as an important area of investment. Teachers need appropriate training, teaching materials and opportunities to improve their professional skills. In communities where schools face shortages of qualified personnel, recruitment and retention also require attention. Infrastructure remains another challenge. Schools need functional classrooms, sanitation facilities, learning materials and, increasingly, access to electricity and digital tools. Poor facilities can discourage attendance and make teaching more difficult. Investment should therefore focus on both new construction and maintenance of existing schools. Technology can support education when schools have the infrastructure required to use it. Digital learning resources can expand access to educational materials and provide teachers with additional tools. However, technology cannot substitute for basic facilities or trained educators. Programmes should therefore be designed around the actual conditions of individual schools. Financing is particularly important in underserved communities. Schools serving poor households may require additional support because families have fewer resources to contribute to education. Government and development partners can help address those inequalities through targeted investment. The private sector can also contribute through partnerships, scholarships, equipment and skills programmes. Collaboration is more effective when responsibilities and expected outcomes are clearly defined. Education data can help identify where support is most needed. Authorities can examine enrolment, attendance, teacher numbers and learning outcomes to determine which communities face the largest gaps. Reliable information can also help monitor whether interventions are producing results. Security remains a factor in some parts of Northern Nigeria. Insecurity can disrupt school attendance, force closures and make it difficult to retain teachers. Education planning therefore needs to take local security conditions into account. Communities can help schools operate safely by maintaining communication with authorities and supporting child protection measures. Girls' education also requires continued attention in areas where social and economic barriers affect participation. Keeping girls in school can improve future opportunities and contribute to household and community development. Flexible programmes and community engagement may help address some barriers. The challenges facing Northern schools are significant, but stakeholders said they are not insurmountable. Sustained investment can strengthen the education system and expand opportunities for children and young people. The focus should be on practical measures that improve classrooms, support teachers and give students access to relevant learning resources. Northern Nigeria has a large young population whose future depends heavily on the quality of education available to them. Strengthening schools can therefore contribute not only to individual opportunity but also to regional economic and social development. Stakeholders said long-term partnerships among government, communities, businesses and education organisations would be necessary to sustain progress.
img: Students and teachers at a school in Northern Nigeria.

headline: Universities Urged to Turn Research Into Practical Solutions for Industry
summary: Stakeholders at Bayero University have called for stronger links between academic research and industry. They said closer collaboration could help turn university research into practical solutions and improve opportunities for students.
fullStory: KANO — Stakeholders have called for stronger collaboration between Nigerian universities and industry to ensure that academic research produces practical solutions to economic and social challenges. The call followed discussions around the need to bridge the gap between research institutions and businesses. Universities produce research across areas including agriculture, medicine, engineering, technology and the social sciences. However, researchers often face difficulties moving their findings from academic publications into practical applications. Stronger partnerships with industry could provide a pathway for businesses and public institutions to identify problems that researchers can help solve. Such collaboration can also expose students to real-world challenges. Students who participate in industry-linked projects can gain practical experience while applying knowledge acquired in the classroom. This can improve their understanding of professional expectations and strengthen their employability after graduation. Industry also stands to benefit from access to academic expertise. Businesses may have technical or operational problems that require specialised knowledge beyond their internal capacity. Universities can provide researchers, laboratories and other facilities that can help develop solutions. Funding remains an important part of the process. Research requires sustained investment in equipment, personnel and data collection. Universities and government agencies remain important sources of research funding, while private-sector partnerships can provide additional opportunities. Such partnerships should, however, have clear rules concerning intellectual property and academic independence. Researchers need confidence that their work will be properly recognised and protected. Universities can also strengthen innovation by establishing technology-transfer offices, research hubs and incubation centres. These structures can help researchers assess whether discoveries have commercial potential and connect them with investors or companies. Students can benefit from entrepreneurship programmes linked to these initiatives. Nigeria's economic challenges provide numerous areas where university research could have practical impact. Agriculture, energy, healthcare, manufacturing and information technology all require locally relevant solutions. Research designed around local conditions may produce approaches that are more affordable and suitable for Nigerian communities. Government can encourage university-industry collaboration through competitive grants and incentives for joint projects. Public institutions can also identify national challenges that require research-based solutions. Education policy should recognise that universities have responsibilities beyond classroom teaching. They are also centres for knowledge creation and innovation. Stronger research capacity can contribute to economic development when findings are successfully transferred into practice. At the same time, universities must maintain academic standards. Commercial interests should not compromise research integrity or prevent scholars from pursuing important long-term questions. A balance between fundamental research and applied research is therefore necessary. Better collaboration could also help universities understand the skills employers require. Industry participation in curriculum development, internships and professional training can help institutions prepare students for changing labour-market conditions. The call for stronger university-industry relations reflects a broader need to make education more connected to national development. When research institutions, businesses and government agencies work together, knowledge can move more effectively from classrooms and laboratories into communities and workplaces. Sustained collaboration could therefore strengthen research, improve graduate skills and contribute to Nigeria's wider development goals.
img: Researchers at a Nigerian university laboratory working on an academic project.

headline: Tems Performs at Obama Presidential Center Opening
summary: Nigerian singer Tems performed at the opening celebration of the Obama Presidential Center in the United States. The performance placed the Grammy-winning Nigerian artist among an international lineup of major performers.
fullStory: CHICAGO — Nigerian singer Tems performed at the opening of the Obama Presidential Center, joining a major international programme celebrating the launch of the centre. The performance further highlighted the growing international profile of Nigerian and African music. Tems, whose career has expanded significantly beyond Nigeria, performed before an audience that included prominent figures from entertainment and public life. The event brought together several internationally recognised performers and provided a global platform for the Nigerian artist. Speaking about the performance, Tems acknowledged feeling nervous before taking the stage despite her growing experience performing for large audiences. Her appearance reflected the increasing presence of African artists at major international cultural events. Nigerian music has experienced significant growth in global visibility over the past several years. Afrobeats artists have built audiences across Europe, North America and other parts of the world, while collaborations with international musicians have expanded the genre's reach. Tems has been part of that wider movement. Her music has attracted international recognition, including Grammy success, and she has worked with artists from different parts of the global music industry. Performances at major international events can further strengthen the visibility of African music. They also create opportunities for artists to introduce different sounds and cultural influences to audiences who may have had limited exposure to them. The global growth of Afrobeats has created new commercial opportunities for Nigerian musicians, producers, songwriters and other professionals in the creative industry. It has also increased interest in Nigeria's wider entertainment sector. However, international recognition does not remove the challenges facing the domestic industry. Artists continue to deal with issues including intellectual-property protection, music distribution, access to finance and infrastructure. Reliable electricity, professional recording facilities and effective copyright enforcement remain important to the growth of the sector. Nigerian artists are also increasingly using digital platforms to reach audiences directly. Streaming services allow music to travel beyond geographical boundaries, while social media gives artists additional ways to promote their work. The international success of leading artists can therefore create opportunities for emerging performers. Tems' performance also demonstrated the cultural influence that Nigerian musicians can have outside the country. Music has become an important part of Nigeria's international cultural identity and can contribute to the country's creative-economy ambitions. For younger musicians, international appearances by established Nigerian artists can serve as evidence that careers built locally can achieve global recognition. The challenge for the industry will be ensuring that the benefits of international growth extend beyond a small number of stars. More investment in music education, production, management and creative entrepreneurship could help build a stronger ecosystem. As Nigerian music continues to attract global attention, performances such as Tems' appearance at the Obama Presidential Center provide another opportunity to showcase the country's creative talent. The growing international audience for African music suggests that the sector will remain an important part of Nigeria's cultural and economic influence.
img: Tems performing on stage at an international cultural event.

headline: Ekiti Governorship Election Draws Attention as Voters Head to Polls
summary: Voters in Ekiti State went to the polls in a closely watched governorship election involving the incumbent and opposition candidates. The election was regarded as an important political test ahead of Nigeria's 2027 general elections.
fullStory: ADO-EKITI — Voters across Ekiti State headed to polling units for the governorship election in a contest that attracted significant attention from political parties, observers and citizens. The election was widely viewed as an important test of party organisation and voter mobilisation ahead of Nigeria's 2027 general elections. The poll involved the incumbent All Progressives Congress and several opposition parties seeking to challenge its control of the state. Campaigns leading to election day focused on governance, development, security, employment and other issues affecting residents. Political parties invested significant resources in grassroots mobilisation, with candidates and their supporters campaigning across local government areas. Ekiti has a history of competitive politics, making the election particularly significant for parties assessing their strength in the South-West. Voter turnout, the performance of party structures and the conduct of the election were among the issues closely monitored. The Independent National Electoral Commission was responsible for organising the poll, while security agencies were deployed to maintain order. Electoral officials also worked to ensure that voters could participate without intimidation. The use of technology in voter accreditation remained an important part of the electoral process. Where technical difficulties occurred, officials were expected to follow established procedures to ensure that eligible voters were not unnecessarily prevented from voting. Political parties were encouraged to allow electoral officials to perform their duties without interference. The conduct of party agents at polling units is important because they serve as representatives of candidates and can observe the process. Any complaints arising from voting or counting are expected to be addressed through established electoral and legal procedures. The election was also significant because of its potential implications for 2027. Parties can use state-level contests to assess their campaign structures and identify weaknesses before the next general election. A strong grassroots network can be particularly important in elections where local issues and candidate relationships influence voting behaviour. For voters, however, the most important issue remains governance after the election. Citizens expect elected officials to address problems affecting education, healthcare, infrastructure, employment and public services. Campaign promises therefore become important benchmarks against which governments can later be assessed. Political competition is an essential part of democratic government, but it also requires restraint. Candidates and supporters have a responsibility to avoid violence, threats and inflammatory statements. Peaceful elections strengthen public confidence and allow citizens to express their choices freely. The Ekiti election therefore represented more than a contest between candidates. It provided an opportunity to assess the effectiveness of electoral institutions, the strength of political parties and the willingness of citizens to participate in democratic processes. Its outcome and conduct were expected to provide lessons for political actors preparing for future elections.
img: Voters queue at a polling unit during an election in Ekiti State.

headline: School Feeding Programme Faces Questions Over Implementation in Some Schools
summary: Teachers and education stakeholders have raised concerns about the implementation of Nigeria's school feeding programme in some public schools. Reports indicated that some schools had not received meals despite government commitments to the programme.
fullStory: ABUJA — Concerns have emerged over the implementation of Nigeria's school feeding programme, with teachers in some public schools reporting that meals were not being provided despite government commitments to supporting pupils through the initiative. The concerns have renewed attention on the importance of effective monitoring and accountability in social programmes connected to education. School feeding programmes are designed to provide meals to pupils while encouraging school attendance and supporting children's nutrition. For families facing financial pressure, the availability of a meal at school can provide an additional incentive to keep children enrolled. Teachers interviewed in some schools, however, said the programme was not operating consistently in their institutions. Reports cited schools in different locations where teachers said meals had not been provided for extended periods. Such gaps can reduce the programme's ability to achieve its intended objectives. The Federal Government has previously highlighted school feeding as part of broader efforts to improve education and support vulnerable children. Government officials have also reported achievements connected with teacher training, textbook distribution and other education interventions. The contrast between reported programme achievements and complaints from individual schools highlights the importance of independent monitoring. Large national programmes require reliable systems for identifying whether services actually reach their intended beneficiaries. School administrators and teachers are often in the best position to report whether meals are being delivered. Parents and community representatives can also provide information about implementation. Transparent reporting can help distinguish between temporary logistical problems and more persistent failures. Funding is another important consideration. School feeding requires regular procurement, transportation and distribution. Interruptions can occur when payment systems, suppliers or logistics arrangements fail. Authorities therefore need contingency plans to prevent long gaps in service. Procurement must also be transparent. Clear standards for food quality, supplier selection and payment can reduce opportunities for waste or abuse. Monitoring should not focus only on the number of schools enrolled in the programme. Authorities should also measure how many children actually receive meals and how frequently they are provided. Such information can reveal implementation gaps that headline statistics may not show. The programme's educational benefits also need to be assessed. If feeding improves attendance and reduces absenteeism, schools should be able to demonstrate those changes over time. Data can help policymakers determine where the programme is working and where additional support is required. Teachers have an important role in reporting problems, but they should not be expected to manage the entire programme. Education authorities, social-protection agencies and local administrations need to coordinate implementation. Communities can also help monitor delivery while ensuring that reports are based on verifiable information. School feeding is ultimately intended to support both children's welfare and education. When properly implemented, it can contribute to attendance and reduce one of the practical barriers faced by poorer families. When implementation is inconsistent, however, the programme may fail to reach the children who need it most. The concerns raised by teachers therefore underline the need for stronger monitoring, transparent procurement and regular public reporting. Government commitments can only produce meaningful results when services reach classrooms consistently.
img: Pupils seated in a Nigerian primary school during a school activity.

headline: Governors Back State Police With Conditions for Constitutional Reform
summary: Nigeria's 36 state governors have expressed support for the establishment of state police, subject to constitutional safeguards and respect for citizens' rights. The position could influence ongoing discussions about security and policing reform.
fullStory: ABUJA — Nigeria's 36 state governors have expressed support for the establishment of state police, while stressing the need for constitutional safeguards and protection of citizens' rights. The position adds momentum to a long-running national debate over whether policing should remain largely centralised or become more decentralised. Supporters of state police argue that state-level security structures could improve responses to local security challenges. They say officers operating closer to communities may have better knowledge of local conditions and could respond more quickly to incidents. Critics have historically raised concerns about possible political interference, particularly where state governments exercise substantial influence over local institutions. The governors' position indicates that any state-police system would need safeguards designed to prevent abuse. Constitutional and legislative changes would likely be necessary to establish the framework for such a system. Questions would include recruitment, training, command structures, funding and oversight. The relationship between state police and the Nigeria Police Force would also need to be clearly defined. Funding is another major issue. State governments would need sufficient resources to recruit, train, equip and pay personnel. Poorly funded security agencies could create additional problems rather than solving existing ones. Professional standards would also be necessary. Police officers at state level would need training in investigation, human rights, crowd management and community policing. Effective oversight would be required to ensure that officers operate within the law. The debate comes amid continuing security challenges across different parts of Nigeria. Communities face different combinations of banditry, terrorism, kidnapping, communal conflict and other crimes. A decentralised approach could allow security policies to reflect local conditions, but coordination between federal and state agencies would remain essential. State police would not necessarily replace federal security responsibilities. The federal government would continue to have responsibilities for national security, interstate crime and other matters. Clear jurisdictional boundaries would therefore be required. Citizens' rights must also remain central to any reform. Security agencies have powers that can affect freedom of movement, privacy and personal safety. Strong accountability mechanisms can help prevent excessive use of force and unlawful detention. The governors' support could strengthen the political case for continued reform discussions. However, reaching agreement on the details may be more difficult than agreeing on the principle. Policymakers will need to consider how state police can operate without becoming instruments of political control. Public consultation will also be important because policing affects every community. Any reform should be judged by whether it improves public safety while protecting constitutional rights. Better local intelligence, faster response and stronger community relationships could provide benefits if the system is professionally managed. Conversely, weak oversight could create new risks. The governors' position therefore represents an important development in Nigeria's policing debate, but further legislative and institutional work will be necessary before state police can become a functioning national framework.
img: Police officers conducting a community security patrol in Nigeria.

headline: AI Conference Highlights Need for Responsible Technology Use in Education
summary: Experts at an artificial intelligence conference in Nasarawa State called for responsible management of AI as the technology expands into education and other sectors. They stressed the importance of ethics, human oversight and appropriate skills.
fullStory: LAFIA — Experts at an artificial intelligence conference in Nasarawa State have called for responsible management of AI as the technology becomes increasingly important to education, business and public life. Participants said artificial intelligence could provide significant benefits but also create risks if deployed without adequate oversight. AI tools are already changing how people search for information, produce content and perform certain professional tasks. In education, they can assist teachers with lesson preparation, provide learning resources and support personalised instruction. Students can also use AI tools to explore subjects and practise skills. However, the technology raises questions about academic integrity and the reliability of information produced by automated systems. Schools and universities therefore need clear guidelines governing how students and teachers can use AI. Rather than simply banning the technology, education institutions may need to teach students how to use it responsibly. Digital literacy is becoming increasingly important because users need to understand that AI-generated information may contain errors. Students should learn to verify information and use credible sources when completing academic work. Teachers also need training so they can understand the strengths and limitations of AI tools. AI could potentially reduce some administrative workloads, but it should not replace professional judgment in areas requiring human understanding. Data privacy is another concern. AI systems may process large quantities of personal information, making it important for institutions to protect student and teacher data. Schools should understand what information is being collected and how it is used before adopting technology. Access is also an issue. Students in schools with reliable internet and digital devices may benefit more quickly from AI than students in underserved communities. This could widen existing educational inequalities if infrastructure gaps are not addressed. Governments and institutions therefore need to consider access alongside technological innovation. Teacher development will be important as AI becomes more common. Educators can learn how to use digital tools to create learning materials, analyse student performance and provide additional support. However, teachers remain essential because education involves mentorship, social interaction and judgment that technology cannot fully replace. The conference also highlighted the broader economic implications of AI. Nigerian businesses and public institutions may increasingly need workers with digital and analytical skills. Education systems will therefore need to prepare students for a labour market in which technology plays a larger role. Universities and technical institutions can contribute by developing courses and training programmes in artificial intelligence, data science and related fields. Ethical considerations should remain central to those programmes. Technology development should be guided by principles of fairness, transparency and accountability. Nigeria also needs policies that encourage innovation while protecting citizens from misuse. Strong regulation can provide safeguards without unnecessarily preventing legitimate technological development. The growing interest in AI presents opportunities for Nigerian education, but those opportunities will depend on infrastructure, skills and responsible use. Experts said the country should prepare students not only to use AI tools but also to understand how the technology works and the responsibilities that accompany it. Building that capacity can help Nigeria participate more effectively in the emerging digital economy while reducing the risks associated with poorly managed technology.
img: Students and technology experts participating in an artificial intelligence conference.

headline: Schools Need Stronger Digital Skills as Technology Changes Learning
summary: Education experts have stressed the need to strengthen digital skills among teachers and students as technology becomes more important in classrooms. They said digital access must be matched with training and responsible use.
fullStory: ABUJA — Education experts have stressed the need to strengthen digital skills among Nigerian teachers and students as technology continues to change how learning materials are created, distributed and used. They said providing devices alone would not guarantee better education unless teachers and students were trained to use them effectively. Digital tools can support learning in several ways. Students can access educational resources, practise skills and communicate with teachers through online platforms. Teachers can use technology to prepare lessons, present information and monitor student progress. However, the benefits depend on whether schools have adequate infrastructure and trained personnel. Reliable electricity and internet connectivity remain important challenges in many communities. Schools without consistent power may find it difficult to maintain computers and other devices. Internet costs can also make online learning difficult for families and institutions with limited resources. Digital programmes therefore need to consider local conditions rather than assuming that every school has the same level of access. Teacher training is particularly important. Educators need practical knowledge of how digital tools can complement classroom teaching. They also need to understand online safety, privacy and the reliability of information found on the internet. Professional development can help teachers incorporate technology without allowing it to distract from learning objectives. Students also require digital literacy. Knowing how to operate a device is different from knowing how to evaluate information or behave responsibly online. Young people need to understand issues such as misinformation, privacy, cyberbullying and intellectual property. These skills are increasingly important as more aspects of education and employment move online. Digital learning can also provide opportunities for students with different learning needs. Recorded lessons, interactive exercises and other resources can allow learners to practise at different speeds. However, technology should complement rather than replace teachers. Teachers provide guidance, motivation and social interaction that digital platforms cannot fully reproduce. Schools must also ensure that digital programmes do not create additional inequalities. Students from wealthier households may have access to personal devices and fast internet at home, while others depend entirely on school facilities. Public programmes should therefore focus on expanding access to underserved communities. Partnerships with technology companies can provide equipment and training, but institutions need clear agreements concerning data protection and long-term maintenance. Devices that are donated without plans for repairs or replacement may quickly become unusable. Curriculum development should also reflect changing technology. Students may need stronger foundations in coding, data analysis, digital communication and problem-solving as the labour market evolves. These skills should be introduced appropriately according to age and educational level. Digital transformation in education is a long-term process. It requires investment in infrastructure, teacher development, curriculum and maintenance. Policymakers should evaluate programmes based on learning outcomes rather than the number of devices distributed. If technology helps students understand concepts better, improves access to materials and supports teachers, it can make a meaningful contribution to education. Experts said Nigeria's goal should therefore be to build a digitally capable education system rather than simply a technology-filled one. The distinction is important because effective digital education depends on people, infrastructure and responsible use as much as it depends on devices.
img: Students using digital learning devices in a Nigerian classroom.

headline: INEC Says Ondo South By-Election Remains Peaceful Despite Network Challenges
summary: The Independent National Electoral Commission said voting in the Ondo South Senatorial District by-election was largely peaceful despite network-related challenges at some polling units. Officials continued efforts to ensure eligible voters could participate.
fullStory: AKURE — The Independent National Electoral Commission reported that voting in the Ondo South Senatorial District by-election was largely peaceful despite network-related challenges affecting accreditation at some polling units. The development highlighted both the growing role of election technology and the importance of contingency arrangements when technical problems occur. Electronic voter accreditation has become an important part of Nigeria's electoral process. The system is intended to help verify voters and improve the integrity of elections. However, technology can experience connectivity or equipment problems, particularly in areas with limited network coverage. Election officials therefore need clear procedures for addressing technical difficulties without unnecessarily disenfranchising eligible voters. The Ondo South election attracted attention because of its importance to representation in the National Assembly. By-elections can also provide political parties with opportunities to assess their grassroots structures and campaign strategies outside the regular general-election cycle. Political parties deployed agents to polling units to observe voting and counting. Their presence can improve transparency when agents operate within electoral rules. Parties are expected to document genuine complaints and use established legal channels rather than disrupting the process. Security agencies also have an important responsibility during elections. Their role is to protect voters and electoral officials while remaining politically neutral. A peaceful polling environment can encourage participation and reduce fear among citizens. Election officials must also communicate clearly when technical problems arise. Voters need to know whether accreditation will resume, whether alternative procedures are available and what steps they should take if difficulties persist. Poor communication can create unnecessary confusion even when the underlying technical problem is temporary. The experience also reinforces the importance of reliable digital infrastructure. As Nigeria expands the use of technology in elections, investment in equipment, maintenance and network coverage becomes increasingly important. Technical systems must be tested before election day and contingency plans should be available. Election technology is only one part of electoral integrity. Transparent procedures, trained personnel, accurate voter registers and effective dispute-resolution mechanisms remain essential. Technology can support those systems but cannot replace institutional safeguards. The Ondo South by-election was therefore another test of Nigeria's ability to conduct elections using a combination of technology and traditional administrative procedures. The reported peaceful conduct of voting was a positive development, while network difficulties provided lessons for future elections. INEC and other stakeholders can use such experiences to improve election planning. For voters, the central issue remains confidence that their votes will be properly accredited, counted and reflected in the final result. Strengthening both technical reliability and public communication can contribute to that confidence. By-elections may involve fewer voters than general elections, but they provide useful opportunities to identify weaknesses before larger national contests. The Ondo South experience could therefore contribute to preparations for future elections if the lessons are carefully documented and applied.
img: Voters and election officials at a polling unit in Ondo State.

headline: Nigeria Reviews Transition to New Tax Framework
summary: The Federal Government has issued implementation guidance for the transition to Nigeria's new tax framework. The guidelines are intended to help taxpayers and businesses understand how the revised system will operate.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Federal Government has issued implementation guidance for the transition to Nigeria's revised tax framework, providing businesses and taxpayers with information on how the new system will be applied. The transition is part of broader efforts to reform tax administration and improve revenue collection. Tax reform affects businesses, workers and consumers because changes in tax rules can influence operating costs, investment decisions and household finances. Clear implementation guidelines are therefore important to reduce uncertainty. Businesses need to understand which obligations apply to them, when they take effect and how compliance should be managed. Tax authorities also need effective communication systems to answer questions and help taxpayers adjust. Nigeria has historically faced challenges with a relatively narrow tax base and complex administrative processes. Reform efforts have sought to simplify procedures, improve compliance and increase the efficiency of revenue collection. A stronger tax system can provide government with more predictable domestic revenue for public services and infrastructure. However, tax policy must also consider the ability of households and businesses to absorb additional costs. Excessive or poorly designed taxes can discourage investment and increase pressure on consumers. Effective reform therefore requires a balance between revenue needs and economic activity. Digital systems can improve tax administration by making registration, filing and payment easier. They can also help authorities identify inconsistencies and improve compliance. Businesses may need to update accounting systems and internal procedures to comply with new requirements. Small businesses could require additional support because they often have fewer staff dedicated to tax administration. Clear guidance and simplified procedures can reduce the compliance burden. Tax professionals and business associations can also help companies understand the changes. Public awareness is important because uncertainty can lead to misinformation. Authorities should publish accessible explanations and provide channels through which taxpayers can seek clarification. The transition should also be monitored for unintended effects. If particular sectors face difficulties, policymakers may need to review implementation procedures without undermining the broader objectives of reform. Tax administration should be consistent and transparent so that taxpayers can understand how decisions are made. Improved revenue collection can support government investment in education, healthcare, infrastructure and security. However, citizens are more likely to support taxation when they can see evidence that public revenue is being used effectively.
