Accountability in public spending is therefore closely connected to tax reform. The private sector also needs predictable policies to make investment decisions. Frequent changes without adequate transition periods can create uncertainty and increase compliance costs. The government will therefore need to maintain communication with businesses and other stakeholders as implementation progresses. Nigeria's tax reform agenda is ultimately about strengthening domestic revenue and improving the relationship between taxpayers and government. A well-administered system can broaden the revenue base while reducing unnecessary administrative burdens. The success of the new framework will depend not only on the laws themselves but on how clearly they are implemented, how effectively taxpayers are supported and how transparently public revenue is managed.
img: Tax officials assisting business owners with tax documentation in Nigeria.

headline: Tinubu Praises Wike's Abuja Infrastructure Projects
summary: President Bola Tinubu praised FCT Minister Nyesom Wike for infrastructure projects in Abuja, including road networks and other developments. The remarks came during the commissioning of projects in the capital.
fullStory: ABUJA — President Bola Tinubu has praised Federal Capital Territory Minister Nyesom Wike for infrastructure projects in Abuja, citing road construction and other developments undertaken in the nation's capital. The remarks were made as the government continued to highlight infrastructure as part of its development agenda. The projects include road networks intended to improve connectivity between districts and ease movement within Abuja. Transport infrastructure is important to the capital because population growth has increased pressure on existing roads and public services. New roads can improve access to residential areas, commercial centres and government institutions when they are properly planned and maintained. The Federal Capital Territory has experienced significant expansion over the years. Development has extended beyond the original city centre into surrounding districts, creating new demands for transportation and public infrastructure. Road construction can help integrate these growing areas with established parts of the city. Infrastructure development also has economic implications. Better roads can reduce travel times and transport costs while improving access to businesses and markets. Construction projects can create temporary employment, while improved infrastructure can support longer-term economic activity. However, projects must be accompanied by maintenance plans. Roads that deteriorate quickly can impose additional costs on government and road users. Effective drainage is also important in Abuja because inadequate drainage can contribute to flooding and damage road surfaces. Urban development therefore requires coordination between roads, drainage, water supply, housing and other services. The government has continued to emphasise infrastructure as a tool for improving living conditions and supporting economic growth. Citizens, however, ultimately assess projects based on whether they make daily life easier. Reduced traffic, reliable roads and better public services are tangible indicators of infrastructure performance. Transparency in project delivery is also important. Citizens need information about project costs, contractors, timelines and expected outcomes. Such information can strengthen public confidence and allow independent observers to assess progress. The FCT administration has also faced the challenge of balancing new construction with the needs of existing communities. Rapid development can place pressure on land, housing and public services. Urban planning therefore needs to anticipate population growth rather than simply respond to congestion after it develops. The projects praised by the Presidency form part of a wider infrastructure programme in Abuja. Their long-term value will depend on construction quality, maintenance and how well they connect with broader urban planning. Infrastructure cannot solve every problem in the capital, but well-designed projects can improve mobility and support economic activity. Government officials have said continued investment will help transform Abuja into a more functional capital. Residents will ultimately judge the success of those efforts by the quality of roads and services available to them. Sustained delivery, transparent project management and proper maintenance will therefore be important as Abuja continues to expand.
img: A newly constructed road network in Abuja's expanding districts.

headline: Education Stakeholders Push Stronger Support for Basic Learning
summary: Education stakeholders have renewed calls for stronger investment in foundational learning, teacher development and school infrastructure. They said improving basic education remains essential to Nigeria's long-term human-capital development.
fullStory: ABUJA — Education stakeholders have renewed calls for stronger investment in foundational learning as Nigeria continues efforts to improve the quality of basic education. The stakeholders said greater attention to literacy, numeracy, teacher preparation and school infrastructure would be necessary to produce sustainable improvements in learning outcomes. Foundational learning provides the basis on which students build more advanced knowledge and skills. When children struggle to read, write or perform basic mathematical operations in the early years, they may face difficulties throughout their education. Stakeholders therefore argued that interventions should begin early and continue consistently through the basic education system. Teacher quality remains one of the most important factors in classroom performance. Teachers need adequate preparation, teaching materials and opportunities for continuous professional development. Training should also help educators respond to different learning needs within the same classroom. Many Nigerian classrooms contain pupils with varying levels of ability, making flexible teaching approaches increasingly important. Infrastructure is another major concern. Schools require safe classrooms, functional sanitation facilities, learning materials and, where appropriate, access to electricity and digital resources. Poor facilities can affect attendance and concentration while also making it more difficult for teachers to deliver lessons effectively. Investment in infrastructure should therefore be accompanied by proper maintenance. Education stakeholders have also stressed the importance of reliable data. Governments need accurate information about enrolment, attendance, teacher numbers and learning outcomes to determine where resources are most urgently required. Data can help identify communities where children are out of school and schools where learning conditions are particularly weak. Community participation can further strengthen education programmes. Parents and local leaders can support attendance, monitor school conditions and encourage children to remain in school. Schools that maintain strong relationships with their communities may also be better positioned to identify local challenges. Financing remains central to the issue. Education requires sustained investment rather than occasional interventions. Governments at federal, state and local levels need to coordinate spending so that programmes complement rather than duplicate one another. Development partners can provide additional support, but domestic funding remains essential for long-term sustainability. Technology can also support learning when introduced appropriately. Digital resources can provide access to educational materials and help teachers develop new instructional methods. However, technology should not be treated as a substitute for teachers or basic infrastructure. Schools without reliable electricity or connectivity may struggle to benefit from digital programmes. The quality of learning should also be measured regularly. Assessments can help identify gaps and determine whether interventions are producing results. Results should be used to improve teaching rather than simply rank schools or students. Stakeholders said that accountability must accompany increased investment. Governments and education authorities should be able to demonstrate how resources are being used and whether programmes are improving outcomes. Nigeria's large and youthful population makes education particularly important. A stronger education system can improve employment prospects, productivity and social mobility. Conversely, weak foundational learning can limit opportunities for millions of young people. Improving basic education will therefore require cooperation among governments, teachers, parents, communities and development organisations. The objective should be to ensure that every child has access not only to a school but also to meaningful learning. Sustained attention to foundational skills, teacher development and school quality can help Nigeria build an education system capable of preparing children for further study and productive participation in the economy.
img: Nigerian pupils participating in a classroom learning activity.

headline: Schools Asked to Strengthen Reading Programmes for Young Learners
summary: Education advocates have called on schools to strengthen structured reading programmes for children in the early years. They said regular reading practice and access to age-appropriate materials could improve literacy development.
fullStory: ABUJA — Education advocates have urged Nigerian schools to strengthen structured reading programmes for young learners as part of efforts to improve literacy outcomes. They said children need regular opportunities to read, discuss texts and develop vocabulary from the earliest stages of their education. Reading is a foundational skill that influences performance across almost every subject. Pupils who develop strong reading abilities are generally better positioned to understand instructions, learn new concepts and engage with written information. For this reason, literacy programmes should not be treated as the responsibility of language teachers alone. Teachers across subjects can encourage reading by incorporating age-appropriate texts into classroom activities. Schools can also establish reading clubs and regular reading periods to encourage children to practise outside normal language lessons. Access to books remains an important consideration. Many schools have limited libraries or insufficient quantities of suitable reading materials. Expanding school libraries and providing affordable books can give pupils greater opportunities to practise. Digital materials can complement physical books where reliable devices and connectivity are available. Parents also have an important role. Children who are encouraged to read at home can develop stronger habits and greater confidence. Parents do not necessarily need advanced educational resources to support reading; regular conversation, storytelling and access to simple age-appropriate texts can make a difference. Teachers require support as well. Effective literacy instruction involves more than asking pupils to memorise words. Educators need training in phonics, comprehension, vocabulary development and methods for identifying children who require additional help. Early identification is particularly important because learning difficulties can become harder to address when they are ignored for several years. Schools can use simple assessments to monitor progress. Such assessments should help teachers understand what each child can do and where additional support is required. They should not be used merely to label pupils. Children develop at different rates, and teaching strategies may need to be adjusted accordingly. Language diversity also needs to be considered in Nigeria. Many children speak indigenous languages at home while learning English at school. Teachers must therefore recognise the linguistic backgrounds of their pupils and use appropriate strategies to support comprehension. Building strong literacy skills can have long-term economic benefits. Young people who leave school with poor reading abilities may face difficulties in higher education, vocational training and employment. Improving literacy early can therefore contribute to broader human-capital development. Education authorities can support schools by providing reading materials, teacher training and clear literacy guidelines. Monitoring should focus on actual learning rather than simply the number of books distributed or programmes launched. Community organisations and libraries can also support schools through reading initiatives. A coordinated approach can help create a culture in which reading is regarded as a normal and enjoyable part of childhood. The call for stronger reading programmes reflects a wider concern about foundational learning in Nigeria. Improving literacy will require sustained effort, but practical measures in schools and homes can make a significant difference. Ensuring that children learn to read confidently at an early age should remain a central priority for the education system.
img: Young Nigerian pupils reading books in a classroom.

headline: Political Parties Review Strategy After Ekiti Governorship Poll
summary: Major political parties have begun reviewing their strategies following the Ekiti State governorship election. The outcome is expected to influence preparations for future elections and grassroots mobilisation.
fullStory: ADO-EKITI — Political parties have begun reviewing their strategies following the Ekiti State governorship election as attention gradually shifts toward future electoral contests. The poll provided parties with an opportunity to assess their grassroots structures, campaign strategies and ability to mobilise voters. The All Progressives Congress retained control of the state with the re-election of Governor Biodun Oyebanji. The result gives the party another opportunity to consolidate its political structure in Ekiti while opposition parties consider how to strengthen their positions. Elections in Ekiti are closely watched because of the state's history of competitive politics and high levels of political participation. Parties seeking to challenge the ruling party will need to study the factors that influenced the result. These include candidate selection, campaign organisation, local alliances and voter mobilisation. Grassroots organisation is particularly important in state elections. Political parties need active structures at ward and local-government levels to communicate with voters and monitor polling activities. Campaigns conducted primarily through major cities may fail to reach communities where local issues have a strong influence on voting decisions. Candidate credibility is another important consideration. Voters often assess candidates based on their records, personalities and ability to address local concerns. Parties therefore need transparent selection processes that can produce candidates with broad appeal. The election also highlighted the continuing importance of electoral integrity. Allegations of irregularities must be handled through established legal and institutional channels, while electoral authorities need to maintain public confidence in the process. Political parties have a responsibility to provide evidence when making serious allegations and to respect lawful dispute-resolution mechanisms. The Independent National Electoral Commission will also be expected to review lessons from the election. Election management improves when authorities identify operational weaknesses and address them before subsequent polls. Voter education, logistics, technology and communication all affect the experience of voters. The Ekiti election may also influence preparations for the 2027 general elections. Parties are likely to use the result to evaluate their strength in the South-West and consider how to build wider coalitions. Emerging parties will need to establish credible structures if they intend to compete effectively against the established political organisations. For voters, however, elections are ultimately about governance. Political campaigns may end after results are declared, but citizens continue to judge elected officials based on performance. Infrastructure, education, healthcare, employment and public services remain important measures of government effectiveness. The ruling party therefore faces the responsibility of translating its electoral mandate into tangible improvements. Opposition parties, meanwhile, must demonstrate that they can provide credible alternatives rather than simply criticising the government. The period after an election is also an opportunity for political reconciliation. Parties can reduce tensions by encouraging supporters to respect democratic institutions and avoid inflammatory rhetoric. Such an environment benefits citizens and strengthens democratic culture. The Ekiti result has therefore provided lessons for all major political actors. Parties will study the outcome, electoral authorities will review the process and voters will observe how the new mandate is used. The next stage of Nigerian politics will depend not only on campaign strategies but also on the ability of elected officials and political organisations to maintain public trust.

headline: Manufacturers Seek Lower Production Costs to Sustain Industrial Growth
summary: Manufacturers have called for measures to reduce production costs and improve the operating environment for businesses. They said reliable electricity, transport infrastructure and access to affordable finance remain important to industrial expansion.
fullStory: LAGOS — Manufacturers have renewed calls for policies that can reduce production costs and improve the operating environment as Nigerian businesses seek to expand industrial activity. Industry operators said high energy expenses, logistics challenges and financing constraints continue to affect competitiveness. Manufacturing plays an important role in economic diversification because factories create jobs, develop supply chains and produce goods that might otherwise be imported. Expanding domestic production can also support exports when local companies become competitive in regional and international markets. However, manufacturers face several structural challenges. Electricity costs remain a major concern for businesses that require continuous power for machinery and production lines. Companies that rely heavily on alternative energy sources may incur significantly higher operating expenses. Improving electricity reliability can therefore reduce costs and increase productivity. Transport infrastructure is another issue. Poor roads, congestion and inefficient logistics can increase the cost of moving raw materials and finished products. Manufacturers may pass those costs to consumers, contributing to higher prices. Better transport networks can improve connections between factories, suppliers and markets. Access to finance is also important. Manufacturing often requires significant investment in machinery and facilities, but long-term credit can be difficult or expensive to obtain. Financial institutions can support industrial growth by developing financing products suited to businesses with longer investment cycles. Government incentives may also help strategic industries expand, provided such incentives are transparent and carefully targeted. Local production can contribute to employment and reduce pressure on foreign exchange by lowering dependence on imported goods. However, local manufacturers also need access to imported machinery and raw materials that are not readily available domestically. Stable foreign-exchange policies can therefore help businesses plan their operations. Skills development is another requirement. Modern manufacturing increasingly relies on technical knowledge, automation and quality-control systems. Companies need workers who can operate equipment, maintain machinery and meet production standards. Partnerships between industry and educational institutions can help develop those skills. Small and medium-sized manufacturers require particular attention because they often have fewer financial resources than large corporations. Support in areas such as access to credit, training and market information can help smaller businesses grow into larger enterprises. Industrial policy must also take consumer interests into account. Measures designed to support local production should encourage efficiency rather than permanently protecting inefficient businesses from competition. Companies need incentives to improve quality and reduce costs. Regional trade opportunities provide another avenue for growth. Nigerian manufacturers can potentially access larger markets through the African Continental Free Trade Area if they can meet required standards and compete on price. This makes improvements in productivity increasingly important. Manufacturers said cooperation between government and industry would be necessary to address the challenges facing the sector. Regular consultation can help policymakers understand how regulations affect businesses and identify practical solutions. Industrial growth is ultimately linked to the wider economy. Stronger manufacturing can increase employment, generate tax revenue and reduce dependence on imported products. Achieving those benefits will require sustained investment in infrastructure, energy, skills and finance. Lowering production costs would therefore not only help individual businesses but could also support Nigeria's broader economic diversification agenda.
img: Workers operating machinery at a Nigerian manufacturing facility.

headline: Education Authorities Highlight Teacher Training as Key to Better Outcomes
summary: Education authorities have emphasised continuous teacher training as an important part of efforts to improve learning outcomes. They said professional development should equip teachers with practical classroom skills and modern teaching methods.
fullStory: ABUJA — Education authorities and stakeholders have emphasised the importance of continuous teacher training in efforts to improve learning outcomes across Nigeria. They said teachers need regular professional development to keep pace with changes in curricula, classroom needs and educational technology. Teacher preparation does not end when an educator receives an initial qualification. Classrooms change as new technologies, teaching approaches and student needs emerge. Continuous professional development can help teachers respond to those changes while strengthening skills they already possess. Training programmes are most effective when they address practical classroom challenges. Teachers may benefit from support in areas such as literacy instruction, mathematics teaching, classroom management, assessment and the use of digital resources. Professional development can also help teachers identify students who are struggling and provide appropriate support. Rural and underserved schools require particular attention. Teachers working in remote communities may have fewer opportunities to attend training programmes because of distance and limited resources. Online learning can provide an alternative where internet access is available, but face-to-face support remains valuable for practical training. School leadership also has a role in professional development. Head teachers and principals can create environments where teachers share ideas and discuss classroom experiences. Peer learning can complement formal training and help educators adapt successful approaches to their own schools. Assessment should be connected to teacher development. When learning assessments identify areas where students are performing poorly, education authorities can examine whether teachers need additional support in those subjects. This creates a link between evidence about student performance and interventions aimed at improving teaching. Teacher welfare is also important. Professional development programmes are unlikely to have lasting impact if teachers work under difficult conditions without adequate support. Salaries, working environments, teaching materials and career progression can all affect motivation. Governments therefore need a broad approach that combines training with better working conditions. Technology is increasingly part of education policy. Teachers need digital skills to use learning-management systems, online resources and educational applications effectively. However, technology training should reflect the realities of individual schools. A teacher in a school without reliable electricity may require different support from one working in a well-connected urban institution. Education authorities also need to evaluate training programmes. Attendance at workshops does not necessarily mean that classroom practices have improved. Follow-up assessments, classroom observation and feedback can help determine whether teachers are applying what they have learned. Strong teacher development can have effects beyond individual classrooms. Well-prepared teachers can become mentors for colleagues and contribute to a stronger professional culture within schools. Over time, this can improve institutional capacity. Nigeria's growing school-age population makes teacher preparation increasingly important. More children entering school will require enough qualified teachers to provide effective instruction. Recruitment must therefore be accompanied by training and retention strategies. Strengthening teacher development is not a quick solution to all education challenges, but it is a necessary part of improving learning. When teachers have the knowledge, resources and support required to do their jobs effectively, students are more likely to benefit. Sustained investment in teacher development should therefore remain central to Nigeria's education agenda.
img: Nigerian teachers participating in a professional development workshop.

headline: African Film Makers Seek Wider Global Audience Through Streaming
summary: African filmmakers are increasingly looking to streaming platforms to reach audiences beyond their traditional markets. Industry participants say wider distribution could create new opportunities for producers, actors and other creative professionals.
fullStory: LAGOS — African filmmakers are increasingly exploring digital streaming platforms as a way to reach audiences beyond their traditional markets. The growth of online distribution has created new opportunities for producers, actors, directors and other professionals in the continent's creative industries. Historically, African films have often faced distribution challenges outside their home countries. Limited cinema networks and high distribution costs could make it difficult for productions to reach international audiences. Streaming platforms have changed that equation by allowing films to be made available to viewers in multiple countries through digital services. Nigerian filmmakers in particular have benefited from the international interest generated by the country's large film industry. Nollywood produces a substantial volume of content and has developed audiences across Africa and among the African diaspora. Streaming can help producers reach those audiences more efficiently. However, wider distribution also increases competition. African productions now compete for viewers' attention with films and television programmes from Hollywood, Europe, Asia and other regions. Producers therefore face pressure to improve storytelling, production quality and marketing. Financing remains one of the industry's challenges. High-quality productions require investment in equipment, skilled personnel, locations, post-production and promotion. Independent filmmakers may struggle to raise sufficient capital, particularly when revenues are uncertain. New financing models and partnerships could help address the gap. Intellectual-property protection is another concern. Unauthorised copying and distribution can reduce the income available to creators. Stronger enforcement of copyright laws and greater public awareness can help protect creative work. Streaming companies also need to work with creators to develop fair commercial arrangements. African stories can have strong cultural value as well as entertainment appeal. Films can introduce international audiences to local languages, traditions, social issues and historical experiences. This can contribute to cultural exchange while creating economic opportunities for the creative sector. Training is equally important. The industry requires cinematographers, editors, sound engineers, writers, animators and other specialists in addition to actors and directors. Developing these skills can create employment for young people and strengthen the quality of local productions. Governments can support the sector by improving access to finance, protecting intellectual property and creating policies that encourage creative investment. Reliable electricity and internet infrastructure are also essential because production and digital distribution depend heavily on technology. Local cinemas remain important even as streaming grows. The two distribution channels can complement each other, allowing films to reach different audiences. A successful theatrical release can also generate publicity that supports later digital distribution. For filmmakers, the challenge will be balancing artistic goals with commercial realities. International audiences may be interested in authentic African stories, but producers must still meet professional standards of storytelling and production. The growth of streaming provides an opportunity rather than a guarantee of success. African creative professionals will need strong content, effective business models and reliable distribution partnerships to take advantage of the changing market. If these conditions develop, the continent's film industry could expand its international presence and create more opportunities for the next generation of filmmakers.
img: African filmmakers working on a film production set.

headline: Universities Encouraged to Link Research More Closely to Industry Needs
summary: Higher education stakeholders have called for stronger collaboration between Nigerian universities and industry. They said research partnerships could help turn academic discoveries into practical solutions and improve graduate employability.
fullStory: ABUJA — Higher education stakeholders have called for stronger collaboration between Nigerian universities and industry to ensure that academic research contributes more directly to economic development. They said partnerships could help universities address practical problems while giving students greater exposure to the needs of employers. Universities are major centres of research and innovation, but academic discoveries do not always move easily from laboratories into commercial or public applications. Stronger links with businesses and government agencies could help close that gap. Industry can identify practical challenges that researchers can investigate, while universities can provide expertise and specialised facilities. Such cooperation can benefit students as well. Internships, industrial placements and joint research projects can expose students to real workplace conditions. This experience can improve their understanding of professional expectations and help employers identify promising graduates. Skills development is increasingly important as industries adopt new technologies. Employers need graduates with both theoretical knowledge and practical abilities. Universities can respond by updating curricula and working with companies to identify emerging skills requirements. Research funding is another consideration. Universities need resources to conduct meaningful research, but public funding alone may be insufficient. Private-sector partnerships can provide additional support while giving companies access to academic expertise. Such partnerships require clear rules to protect academic independence and intellectual property. Intellectual-property arrangements should be agreed before research projects begin so that universities, researchers and companies understand their respective rights. Commercialisation can also generate additional revenue that universities can reinvest in research and teaching. Agriculture, healthcare, engineering, information technology and renewable energy are among the sectors where stronger university-industry partnerships could have significant benefits. Research into local challenges can produce solutions better suited to Nigeria's conditions than technologies developed elsewhere. Universities can also support small businesses and startups through innovation hubs and incubation programmes. Young entrepreneurs can gain access to technical expertise, research facilities and mentorship. This can help transform ideas into viable businesses. Government policy can encourage collaboration through competitive grants and incentives for joint research. Public agencies can also identify national problems that require academic expertise. The goal should be to build an ecosystem in which research, education and economic activity reinforce one another. Academic institutions must nevertheless preserve the quality and independence of their research. Partnerships should not result in lower standards or research driven solely by short-term commercial interests. A balance between fundamental research and applied research is necessary. Stronger collaboration can also improve the reputation of Nigerian universities. Institutions that produce useful research and successful innovations can attract students, researchers and investment. International partnerships may develop from domestic collaborations that demonstrate institutional capacity. Nigeria's large population and diverse economic challenges provide numerous areas where university research can contribute. What is required is a stronger mechanism for connecting researchers with organisations that can use their findings. Universities and industry therefore have an opportunity to move beyond occasional partnerships toward more structured and sustained cooperation. Such relationships can improve education, strengthen research and contribute to economic development.
img: Nigerian university researchers working in a laboratory.

headline: Community Groups Renew Calls for Better Support for Out-of-School Children
summary: Community organisations have renewed calls for stronger interventions targeting children who remain outside the formal education system. They said poverty, insecurity and limited access to schools continue to affect attendance in some communities.
fullStory: ABUJA — Community organisations have renewed calls for stronger interventions to bring out-of-school children into education, saying several factors continue to prevent children from attending school regularly. They identified poverty, insecurity, distance to schools and inadequate facilities among the challenges affecting access in different communities. Nigeria has a large population of children and young people, making education access a major national development issue. Children who remain outside school may face limited opportunities later in life, particularly when they lack basic literacy and numeracy skills. Community organisations said interventions need to address both access and the reasons children leave school. Household poverty can make education difficult even when tuition is not charged. Families may struggle to provide uniforms, books, transport and other necessities. Children may also be expected to assist with household or economic activities. Social-support programmes can help reduce some of these pressures. Security is another factor in areas affected by violence or criminal activity. Parents may be reluctant to send children to school when they fear attacks or abductions. Protecting schools and improving security around vulnerable communities is therefore essential. Distance can also be a barrier, particularly in rural areas. Children who have to travel long distances may be less likely to attend consistently. Building schools closer to communities and providing safe transportation can improve access. The quality of education matters as much as physical access. Families may be less motivated to keep children in school if classrooms are overcrowded, teachers are unavailable or learning materials are inadequate. Improving school quality can therefore support retention. Girls may face additional barriers in some communities, including early marriage, household responsibilities and concerns about safety. Programmes designed to keep girls in school need to consider these social and economic factors. Community leaders can help by encouraging parents to support education and discouraging practices that prevent children from attending. Flexible learning programmes can also help children who have fallen behind. Remedial classes and accelerated education can provide pathways back into formal schooling. Such programmes need qualified teachers and appropriate materials to be effective. Accurate data is important for identifying children who are out of school. Local authorities can work with schools and community organisations to determine where children are located and why they are not attending. This information can guide targeted interventions rather than broad programmes that may not address local conditions. Government agencies, charities and community organisations all have roles to play. However, programmes need coordination to prevent duplication and ensure that resources reach the communities most in need. Monitoring should also determine whether children who return to school remain enrolled. Bringing children into classrooms is only the first step. They need safe learning environments and adequate support to stay and succeed. Education can provide long-term benefits for individuals and communities by improving skills, employment prospects and civic participation. Addressing Nigeria's out-of-school population will therefore require sustained commitment rather than short-term campaigns. Community groups said continued investment in schools, social protection, security and teacher development would be necessary to make progress. Ensuring that children can enter, remain in and benefit from education should remain a national priority.
img: Children attending a community education programme in Nigeria.

headline: Small Businesses Seek Easier Access to Affordable Credit
summary: Small-business operators have called for greater access to affordable and longer-term financing. They said high borrowing costs and limited credit options continue to restrict expansion and job creation.
fullStory: LAGOS — Small and medium-sized businesses have called for improved access to affordable credit, saying financing constraints continue to limit their ability to expand operations and create jobs. SMEs make up a significant part of economic activity and provide employment for millions of Nigerians, but many businesses struggle to secure suitable financing. Banks and other financial institutions often require documentation, collateral or repayment conditions that smaller businesses may find difficult to meet. Even when loans are available, high interest costs can discourage borrowing for expansion. Businesses need different types of finance depending on their stage of development. New enterprises may require working capital, while established companies may need longer-term funding to purchase equipment or expand facilities. Financing products should therefore reflect the different needs of businesses. Government-backed programmes can help reduce some barriers, but such schemes require transparent eligibility criteria and efficient administration. Entrepreneurs need clear information about how to apply and what obligations they will have. Digital lending platforms have expanded access to finance for some businesses, although borrowers also need protection from unfair terms and excessive charges. Financial literacy is important because business owners need to understand the costs and risks associated with different forms of credit. Better record-keeping can also improve access to formal finance. Businesses that maintain reliable accounts and transaction records are better positioned to demonstrate their financial performance to lenders. Training programmes can help entrepreneurs develop these skills. Access to markets is another part of the financing problem. A business with reliable customers and predictable revenue may be better able to repay loans. Government procurement programmes can provide opportunities for local businesses, while larger companies can develop supply-chain relationships with smaller suppliers. Infrastructure also affects SME performance. Poor electricity supply, transportation difficulties and high communication costs can reduce the amount of money available for investment. Lowering operating costs can therefore improve the ability of businesses to use financing productively. Small businesses are important to employment because they can create jobs in communities where large companies may not operate. Supporting them can therefore contribute to broader economic inclusion. However, financial support should be accompanied by measures that improve productivity and competitiveness. Businesses need training, technology and market access as well as money. Women and young entrepreneurs may face additional barriers to finance and can benefit from targeted programmes where evidence shows that such barriers exist. Financial institutions can also develop products based on the needs of specific sectors. Agriculture, retail, manufacturing and services often have different cash-flow patterns and financing requirements. A more flexible financial system could therefore serve SMEs better. Stronger credit information systems can also help lenders assess borrowers without relying excessively on physical collateral. This can expand access while allowing lenders to manage risk. The government and financial sector have a shared interest in strengthening small businesses. When SMEs grow, they can create employment, expand the tax base and increase demand for local goods and services. Improving access to appropriate finance is therefore part of the wider effort to support economic growth. Business owners say that predictable policies, lower operating costs and accessible financing would provide a stronger foundation for expansion. Addressing these issues could help more Nigerian businesses move from survival to sustainable growth.
img: A small business owner serving customers at a Nigerian market.

headline: Education Researchers Call for Better Use of School Data
summary: Education researchers have called for stronger use of reliable school data in planning and policy decisions. They said accurate information on enrolment, attendance and learning outcomes can help authorities direct resources to areas of greatest need.
fullStory: ABUJA — Education researchers have called for greater use of reliable school data in planning and policy decisions, saying evidence can help authorities identify weaknesses and direct resources more effectively. They said information on enrolment, attendance, teachers, infrastructure and learning outcomes should form part of routine education management. Data is particularly important in a large and diverse education system such as Nigeria's. Schools in different regions can face very different challenges, meaning a single intervention may not produce the same results everywhere. Reliable information allows authorities to identify those differences and design more targeted programmes. Enrolment figures can show how many children are entering school, but attendance data provides additional information about whether pupils are regularly participating. A child who is formally enrolled but frequently absent may still be at risk of falling behind. Monitoring attendance can therefore help schools identify problems early. Learning assessments provide another layer of information. They can show whether pupils are acquiring expected skills and which subjects require additional attention. When assessment data is combined with information about teachers and infrastructure, policymakers can better understand possible causes of poor performance. Data quality is essential. Inaccurate or outdated information can lead governments to allocate resources based on a false picture of conditions. Education authorities need systems that allow schools to update information regularly and verify records. Training school administrators in data management can improve reliability. Technology can make data collection easier, but digital systems require investment. Schools need appropriate devices, connectivity and technical support. Where digital access is limited, authorities may need transitional systems that combine electronic and manual processes. Data protection is also important because school records can contain personal information about children, teachers and families. Authorities must ensure that information is stored securely and used for legitimate educational purposes. Schools should also receive feedback from the data they provide. If teachers and administrators submit information but never see how it influences decisions, reporting can become a routine administrative burden. Sharing useful findings can encourage better participation. Education data can also support accountability. Governments can compare planned targets with actual outcomes and identify programmes that are not producing expected results. Public reporting can help citizens understand whether education investments are improving schools. However, data should not be used simply to rank institutions without considering their different circumstances. A school serving a remote community with limited resources may face challenges that require additional support rather than punishment. Researchers also stressed the importance of combining quantitative information with local knowledge. Statistics can show where a problem exists, while teachers and communities can often explain why it exists. Both forms of evidence are valuable. Better use of education data can improve planning at federal, state and local levels. It can help authorities identify teacher shortages, infrastructure gaps, attendance problems and learning difficulties. It can also support evaluation of reforms by showing whether outcomes improve over time. Nigeria's education system requires significant resources, making efficient allocation particularly important. Reliable data can help ensure that available funds are directed toward areas with the greatest potential need. Strengthening education information systems should therefore remain part of broader efforts to improve learning. Evidence cannot replace good policy or effective implementation, but it can make both more informed. When authorities know what is happening in schools, they are better positioned to decide what should happen next.
img: Education officials reviewing school data and records in Nigeria.

headline: NCCE Turns to Digital Tools to Strengthen Teacher Education
summary: The National Commission for Colleges of Education has begun using digital learning and analytics platforms to improve teacher education and institutional oversight. Officials say the technology will provide real-time information for better decision-making across colleges of education.
fullStory: ABUJA — The National Commission for Colleges of Education has intensified its use of digital technology to improve teacher education, institutional governance and quality assurance across Nigeria's colleges of education. The commission said digital platforms would provide better access to information about activities within institutions and support evidence-based decisions. The initiative includes training staff on Blackboard Learning Management System and Illuminate Analytics. According to the commission, the platforms can provide real-time visibility into institutional activities and help administrators monitor teaching and learning more effectively. Technology is increasingly becoming an important part of education management. Colleges of education require reliable systems for managing students, academic programmes, staff information and institutional performance. Digital platforms can bring these functions together and make information easier to analyse. For teacher education, better data can help institutions identify areas requiring attention and improve the quality of training provided to future teachers. Nigeria's education system depends heavily on the quality of its teachers. Teachers influence learning outcomes at every level, making their preparation and professional development central to education reform. Colleges of education therefore have an important responsibility to ensure that students receive appropriate academic and practical training before entering classrooms. Digital tools can support that process by giving institutions access to learning materials and performance information. They can also make it easier for education authorities to monitor institutions without relying entirely on physical inspections. However, technology cannot replace qualified educators or adequate infrastructure. Colleges still require trained lecturers, functioning classrooms, libraries, laboratories and other resources. Internet connectivity and electricity are also necessary for digital systems to operate consistently. The NCCE will therefore need to ensure that technology adoption is accompanied by investment in basic infrastructure. Digital learning can nevertheless expand opportunities for professional development. Teachers and lecturers can access courses, training materials and other resources without travelling long distances. This can be especially useful for institutions in underserved areas. Analytics can also help administrators identify patterns in student participation and performance. If used properly, such information can support early intervention for students who may be struggling. Data management must also be handled responsibly. Educational institutions collect personal information about students and staff, meaning digital systems require appropriate security and privacy safeguards. Users need confidence that their information will not be misused or exposed. The commission's initiative reflects a broader effort to modernise teacher education in Nigeria. As schools increasingly incorporate technology into teaching, teachers themselves need to understand digital tools and how to use them effectively. Teacher-training institutions must therefore prepare graduates for classrooms where technology is becoming more common. The programme also creates an opportunity for the NCCE to strengthen accountability. Reliable institutional data can help regulators identify differences in performance and determine where support is required. Rather than relying only on periodic reports, authorities can potentially monitor developments more continuously. The long-term success of the initiative will depend on implementation across institutions. Staff need adequate training and technical support, while colleges must maintain the infrastructure required to keep the platforms functioning. If these conditions are met, digitalisation could improve the management and quality assurance of teacher education. The broader objective is to produce better-prepared teachers who can contribute to improved learning outcomes across Nigeria.

headline: JAMB Ends Degree Admissions Through Affiliated Colleges of Education
summary: The Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board has discontinued admissions into degree programmes run through university-affiliated colleges of education from the 2026/2027 academic session. The board also directed that new entrants into colleges of education must follow the approved admission route.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board has announced the discontinuation of admissions into degree programmes operated by colleges of education through affiliations with universities, effective from the 2026/2027 academic session. The decision represents a significant change in the structure through which prospective teachers and other students enter degree-level programmes in colleges of education. The board's decision was contained in its 2026 registration guidelines and is intended to clarify the admission pathway for students seeking places in colleges of education. Under the new arrangement, colleges of education will continue to admit students into approved programmes such as the Nigeria Certificate in Education, while the previous route into affiliated university degree programmes will no longer be available. The change is likely to affect students who had considered colleges of education as an alternative route to university degrees. JAMB plays a central role in coordinating admissions into tertiary institutions in Nigeria, and its admission guidelines are designed to ensure that institutions operate within approved procedures. The decision also reflects continuing efforts to streamline tertiary education and clarify the roles of different institutions. Colleges of education have traditionally focused strongly on teacher preparation, particularly through the NCE qualification. The NCE remains an important route into the teaching profession, especially for those preparing to teach at basic and junior secondary levels. Supporters of the policy may argue that clearer institutional roles can improve quality control and prevent confusion about qualifications. When students enrol in affiliated programmes, they may sometimes be uncertain about which institution is responsible for academic standards and certification. A clearer structure can make accreditation and oversight easier. However, students affected by the change will need adequate information about alternative routes into higher education. Prospective teachers may still seek degree qualifications through universities or other approved institutions. Education authorities will need to ensure that students understand the available pathways before making application decisions. The policy also places greater responsibility on colleges of education to strengthen their core programmes. Institutions will need to maintain strong NCE curricula, teaching practice and professional preparation. Teacher education quality remains important because graduates eventually become responsible for teaching millions of Nigerian children. The decision therefore has implications beyond admissions. It raises broader questions about how Nigeria should organise teacher education and the relationship between colleges of education and universities. Effective coordination can help ensure that students receive training appropriate to the level at which they will teach. Colleges may also need to expand professional development opportunities for graduates seeking further qualifications. Universities and colleges can potentially work together through other approved arrangements without relying on the discontinued affiliated degree pathway. JAMB's announcement provides institutions and prospective students with time to adjust before the 2026/2027 academic session begins. Clear communication will be important to prevent students from applying for programmes that are no longer approved. The board and education institutions will also need to monitor implementation and address questions from applicants. The change is part of the continuing effort to strengthen Nigeria's tertiary education system through clearer regulation and quality assurance. Its success will depend on whether students are provided with reliable alternatives and whether colleges of education receive the support necessary to improve their principal teacher-training programmes.

headline: INEC Declares Oyebanji Winner of Ekiti Governorship Election
summary: The Independent National Electoral Commission declared Governor Biodun Oyebanji the winner of the Ekiti State governorship election after he secured the highest number of votes across the state's 16 local government areas. The result secured another term for the All Progressives Congress candidate.
fullStory: ADO-EKITI — The Independent National Electoral Commission has declared Ekiti State Governor Biodun Oyebanji the winner of the state's governorship election after he secured the highest number of votes in the poll. The declaration followed the collation of results from the state's 16 local government areas. Oyebanji, the candidate of the All Progressives Congress, won a second term after defeating his major challengers. The election attracted significant attention because of its importance to the political balance in the state and the wider preparations for Nigeria's 2027 general elections. Ekiti is one of Nigeria's smaller states but has historically been politically competitive, making governorship elections closely watched by the major parties. The result gives the APC another four years in control of the state. Oyebanji's campaign focused heavily on continuity and his administration's development record. Supporters argued that his first term had produced progress in infrastructure and other areas and should be followed by another term. Opposition candidates, however, raised concerns about the conduct of the election and the political environment. The African Democratic Congress candidate, Dare Bejide, rejected the result and alleged irregularities including vote buying and intimidation. Such allegations are common after closely contested elections, but they must be established through the appropriate legal and electoral processes. The Independent National Electoral Commission is responsible for conducting and declaring the election, while election petitions provide a legal mechanism for candidates who believe the process was compromised. The Ekiti election is therefore not necessarily the end of the political dispute. Candidates dissatisfied with the result can challenge it before the appropriate tribunal within the time permitted by law. The election also provides lessons for Nigeria's wider electoral system. The use of technology, including the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System and electronic result processes, remains an important part of efforts to improve electoral transparency. Technical difficulties or concerns about result management can nevertheless affect public confidence. Political parties and civil society organisations have called for stronger safeguards against vote buying and other forms of electoral malpractice. Voter participation is also important. Citizens who vote help determine who governs their communities, while electoral observers can contribute to accountability by documenting the process. For Oyebanji, the victory gives his administration another opportunity to implement its development programme. A second term can provide greater continuity because the government does not need to prepare for another immediate governorship contest. The administration will nevertheless face expectations from voters who want improvements in employment, infrastructure, education, healthcare and the local economy. The opposition parties will now assess their performance and consider how to strengthen their organisations ahead of future elections. The outcome may also influence political calculations ahead of the 2027 presidential and legislative elections. While state elections have their own local dynamics, the performance of political parties provides indications of their organisational strength. The Ekiti result therefore has significance beyond the state. The immediate priority, however, remains the transition into the new administration and the resolution of any legal challenges. Oyebanji's victory has given the APC another mandate in Ekiti, but the quality of governance during the next term will ultimately determine how voters assess the result.

headline: ADC Candidate Rejects Ekiti Election Result, Cites Alleged Irregularities
summary: African Democratic Congress candidate Dare Bejide has rejected the result of the Ekiti governorship election won by incumbent Governor Biodun Oyebanji. Bejide alleged vote buying, intimidation and other irregularities and indicated that the result would be challenged.
fullStory: ADO-EKITI — The African Democratic Congress candidate in the Ekiti State governorship election, Dare Bejide, has rejected the result declared by the Independent National Electoral Commission and raised allegations about the conduct of the poll. Bejide described the election as lacking credibility and cited alleged vote buying, intimidation and other irregularities. The APC's Biodun Oyebanji was declared winner after securing the highest number of votes across the state's 16 local government areas. The rejection by an opposition candidate means that the political contest could move from the polling stations to the courts. Nigerian electoral law provides mechanisms through which candidates and political parties can challenge results they believe were affected by substantial irregularities. Such challenges require evidence and are determined through the election petition process. Allegations of vote buying have remained a persistent concern in Nigerian elections. Political parties and civil society groups have repeatedly called for stronger enforcement against the practice because it can influence voters and undermine confidence in democratic competition. Intimidation and other forms of electoral violence are similarly serious because voters must be able to participate freely. The use of technology has also become an important part of election management. Accreditation systems and electronic result transmission are intended to reduce manipulation and improve transparency, but technical failures can generate disputes when voters or candidates believe the process has not worked as intended. The Ekiti election will therefore be closely examined by observers and political parties. The final result was based on the official collation conducted by INEC, but dissatisfied candidates have the right to pursue legal remedies. Courts will consider evidence presented by petitioners and respondents before determining whether any alleged irregularities were substantial enough to affect the outcome. For the APC and Oyebanji, the declaration provides a clear electoral mandate. The administration will be expected to begin preparations for its second term and address the development priorities raised during the campaign. For the ADC, the immediate challenge will be demonstrating its allegations through the appropriate legal process if it chooses to file a petition. Electoral disputes can be lengthy, so the final judicial outcome may take time. The dispute also highlights the importance of transparency in election administration. INEC must communicate clearly with parties and voters and ensure that electoral procedures are applied consistently. Political parties have a responsibility to respect legal processes while presenting evidence when they believe their rights have been violated. Citizens, meanwhile, need access to accurate information rather than competing claims that cannot be independently verified. The Ekiti contest will therefore continue to attract attention even after the declaration of the winner. Whatever happens in the courts, the election offers another opportunity to examine the strengths and weaknesses of Nigeria's electoral system. Reducing vote buying, improving security and strengthening result management will remain important if future elections are to command broad public confidence.

headline: Experts Urge Nigeria to Convert Short-Term Capital Into Long-Term Investment
summary: Economic experts have called for policies that would convert short-term capital inflows into productive long-term investment. They said Nigeria needs to use improved macroeconomic stability to attract capital into sectors that can support sustainable growth.
fullStory: ABUJA — Economic experts have urged Nigeria to develop stronger policies for converting short-term capital inflows into long-term productive investment. The call comes amid efforts by the Federal Government to improve economic stability and attract investment into the country. Short-term capital can provide liquidity and support financial markets, but it can also leave quickly when economic conditions change. Long-term investment, by contrast, can support factories, infrastructure, agriculture, technology and other productive sectors. Experts therefore argue that Nigeria needs policies that encourage investors to commit resources for longer periods. Macroeconomic stability is an important part of that process. Investors generally consider inflation, exchange-rate conditions, interest rates, fiscal policy and political stability when deciding where to place capital. Reforms that improve predictability can make Nigeria more attractive to investors seeking long-term opportunities. The country has significant economic potential because of its large population, natural resources and growing consumer market. However, challenges including infrastructure deficits, high operating costs and financing constraints can make investment more difficult. Addressing these issues could increase the productivity of existing businesses and encourage new investment. Infrastructure is particularly important. Reliable electricity, efficient transport networks and telecommunications reduce the cost of doing business. Businesses that spend heavily on generators, logistics and other basic requirements may have less money available for expansion and employment. Public and private investment in infrastructure can therefore improve the wider investment environment. Financial markets also have a role to play. Pension funds, insurance companies and other institutional investors can provide long-term capital when appropriate investment opportunities exist. Strong regulatory frameworks are necessary to protect investors while directing capital toward productive assets. The government can also use incentives carefully to encourage investment in sectors considered strategically important. Agriculture, manufacturing, technology and renewable energy are among the areas with potential to create jobs and diversify the economy. Nigeria's dependence on oil revenue makes diversification particularly important. A stronger non-oil economy can provide more stable sources of employment and government revenue. Small and medium-sized enterprises also need access to long-term financing. Many Nigerian businesses rely on short-term and relatively expensive credit, making it difficult to invest in machinery, research or expansion. Financial institutions can help by developing products suited to the needs of growing businesses. Policy consistency is another requirement. Investors need confidence that rules governing taxation, foreign exchange, licensing and other areas will not change unpredictably. Frequent policy changes can discourage long-term commitments even when the underlying market opportunity is attractive. The government therefore faces the challenge of balancing reforms with predictability. Attracting capital is not enough on its own. The quality of investment matters because capital directed into speculative activities may produce less lasting economic benefit than investment in productive capacity. Policymakers will therefore need to focus on the sectors and projects capable of generating employment, exports and productivity gains. Nigeria's large domestic market gives it an advantage if investment barriers can be reduced. Long-term investment can also help develop local supply chains and transfer technology. If businesses expand, demand for skilled workers and supporting services can increase. Converting short-term capital into long-term investment will require cooperation among government, financial institutions and private investors. Economic reforms can create the conditions, but businesses ultimately determine whether opportunities are converted into productive activity. The broader objective is to build an economy in which capital supports sustained growth rather than temporary financial movements.

headline: NANS Calls for Probe Into Alleged NELFUND Funds Mismanagement
summary: The National Association of Nigerian Students has called for an investigation into alleged irregularities involving student-loan funds at an Ogun State polytechnic. The students' body said transparent handling of education financing was necessary to protect beneficiaries.
fullStory: ABEOKUTA — The National Association of Nigerian Students has called for an investigation into alleged financial irregularities involving funds associated with the Nigeria Education Loan Fund at a polytechnic in Ogun State. The students' organisation urged relevant authorities to examine the allegations and establish whether public education financing had been properly managed. The development highlights the importance of transparency as Nigeria expands student financing programmes. NELFUND was established to provide financial support to eligible students and reduce the burden of tertiary education costs on families. Student loans can help qualified young people remain in school when tuition and other expenses would otherwise make higher education difficult to afford. Because the programme involves public funds, effective oversight is essential. Students need confidence that approved funds reach their intended beneficiaries and that institutions handle related financial processes properly. Any allegation of mismanagement can therefore create concern among students and parents. Investigations are important because allegations should be established through evidence rather than public claims alone. Relevant agencies can examine financial records, payment information and institutional procedures to determine whether wrongdoing occurred. If irregularities are found, those responsible should be held accountable according to the law. If allegations are not substantiated, transparent findings can also help protect institutions and individuals from unfounded accusations. The student-loan programme is part of broader efforts to expand access to higher education. Nigeria has millions of young people seeking tertiary education, while many families face significant financial pressure. Tuition is only one part of the cost. Accommodation, transportation, textbooks, food and other expenses can also create barriers. A functioning student-financing system can help reduce some of these pressures. However, financing must be accompanied by effective administration. Students need clear information about eligibility, application procedures, disbursement schedules and repayment obligations. Institutions also need systems for accurately identifying eligible students and processing payments. Technology can improve transparency by allowing beneficiaries to track applications and disbursements. Public reporting can also help demonstrate how much money has been allocated and how many students have benefited. Strong oversight is especially important as the programme expands. Larger numbers of beneficiaries mean more transactions and greater administrative complexity. Independent monitoring can help identify weaknesses before they become systemic. Students' organisations can contribute by reporting problems and representing beneficiaries, but their claims should also be supported by evidence. The NELFUND initiative has the potential to make higher education more accessible, particularly for students from lower-income households. Its credibility, however, depends on trust. Students must believe that the system is fair and that funds are distributed according to established criteria. Institutions must also understand that financial support intended for students cannot be diverted or improperly handled. The call for investigation in Ogun therefore raises a wider issue about accountability in education financing. As government invests more resources in student support, strong financial controls will be necessary. Authorities should publish clear information about programme performance and investigate credible complaints promptly. The ultimate objective should be to ensure that financial assistance reaches students and helps them complete their education. A transparent and accountable student-loan system can become an important tool for expanding access to tertiary education and reducing financial barriers for Nigerian students.
