headline: Women in Arts Push for Greater Role in Nigeria's Creative Economy
summary: Stakeholders in Nigeria's creative industry have called for greater investment in women and improved access to funding, leadership opportunities and markets. They said stronger inclusion could help unlock more value from the country's creative economy.
fullStory: LAGOS — Stakeholders in Nigeria's creative industry have called for increased investment in women, saying greater access to funding, leadership opportunities and market platforms could help unlock more value from the country's expanding creative economy. The call was made at a Women in the Arts: Power, Voice and Economic Impact gathering organised by the National Delphic Council Nigeria in partnership with stakeholders in the creative sector. Nigeria's creative economy covers a wide range of activities, including music, film, visual arts, fashion, literature, theatre and digital content. Women participate extensively across these fields, but stakeholders say barriers to financing, leadership and market access can limit the ability of female creatives to build sustainable careers. Access to capital is particularly important for creative entrepreneurs. Artists and other creative professionals often need funding for equipment, production, promotion and distribution. Without adequate financing, talented professionals may struggle to develop projects or reach larger audiences. Women may face additional barriers when seeking investment or entering leadership positions. Improving access to funding can therefore contribute to both individual careers and broader economic growth. The creative economy has become an important source of employment and cultural influence for Nigeria. Nigerian music and film have attracted international audiences, while fashion and visual arts have developed growing markets at home and abroad. Supporting women within these sectors can broaden the range of voices represented in Nigerian creative output. Leadership opportunities are another important issue. Women who occupy decision-making positions can influence how projects are funded, produced and distributed. Greater representation in creative organisations can also provide mentorship and professional networks for younger women entering the sector. Education and skills development are equally important. Creative professionals increasingly need digital skills in addition to artistic ability. Social media, streaming services and online marketplaces have changed how artists reach audiences. Women who understand these tools can promote their work independently and access customers beyond their immediate communities. However, digital access itself can be limited by the cost of equipment and internet services. Public and private initiatives can help reduce some of these barriers. Training programmes, grants, exhibitions and mentorship schemes can provide practical support. Partnerships between government agencies, private companies and cultural organisations can expand the scale of such programmes. Market access is another major consideration. Producing creative work is only part of the challenge; artists also need opportunities to sell, exhibit or distribute what they create. International festivals and digital platforms can provide new markets, but Nigerian creatives need support to meet professional standards and navigate commercial arrangements. Intellectual property protection is also important. Artists need confidence that their work will not be used without permission or fair compensation. Stronger enforcement of copyright and related rights can encourage investment in creative projects. The economic value of women's participation in the creative sector extends beyond individual income. Successful creative businesses can employ designers, technicians, marketers, assistants and other professionals. They can also contribute to tourism and Nigeria's cultural reputation abroad. Greater inclusion can therefore have wider economic effects. The call for stronger investment in women comes as Nigeria seeks to expand its creative economy as a source of jobs and foreign exchange. Sustainable growth will require more than international recognition for a few successful artists. It will require systems that allow a wider range of creative professionals to build viable careers. Supporting women through funding, skills development, leadership opportunities and market access can help achieve that goal. For Nigeria's creative sector, greater inclusion is therefore not only a question of representation but also an economic opportunity.

headline: NDC Appeals Court Decision Setting Aside Order for INEC Registration
summary: The Nigeria Democratic Congress has appealed a Federal High Court decision that set aside an earlier order directing INEC to register the party. The NDC says it remains legally recognised and plans to challenge the ruling at the Court of Appeal.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Nigeria Democratic Congress has announced plans to challenge a Federal High Court decision that set aside an earlier judgment directing the Independent National Electoral Commission to register the party. The NDC said it had instructed its legal team to file an appeal after Justice Isah Dashen of the Federal High Court in Lokoja vacated the earlier judgment. The court's decision followed an argument by the Peace Movement Party, which claimed that its rights had been affected because it was not joined in the original case. The party also claimed ownership of the logo relied upon in the process that led to the earlier judgment directing INEC to register the NDC. The NDC has rejected the latest ruling and insists that it remains legally recognised. The dispute illustrates the importance of court decisions in Nigeria's political party system. Political parties must meet legal requirements before participating in elections, while disputes over registration, symbols and party status can ultimately be determined through the courts. INEC plays a central role in administering the registration process. However, when parties or other interested organisations challenge decisions, the courts provide a mechanism for resolving legal questions. The NDC's decision to appeal means that the dispute is not necessarily settled by the Federal High Court ruling. An appeal allows a higher court to examine whether the lower court correctly interpreted and applied the law. Until the appeal process is resolved, political actors involved in the case will continue to operate under legal uncertainty. The timing of the dispute is significant because political activity is increasing ahead of the 2027 general elections. Parties are beginning to consider candidates, alliances, campaign structures and mobilisation strategies. Questions over registration can therefore affect political planning. The NDC has said it intends to participate in the 2027 elections, while the court decision has raised questions about the party's status. The legal dispute also involves broader questions about procedural fairness. Courts are expected to ensure that parties whose legal interests may be affected by a judgment have an opportunity to participate in proceedings. The Peace Movement Party's complaint centred on that issue. The Federal High Court found that its rights had been adversely affected because it was not joined in the earlier case. The NDC disagrees with the effect of that decision and plans to seek review by the Court of Appeal. The case demonstrates why political organisations must pay close attention to legal procedures when seeking registration or challenging electoral decisions. Party registration disputes can involve complex questions relating to constitutional requirements, ownership of symbols and procedural rights. The courts may need to examine documents and previous judgments before determining the matter. INEC's role will also remain important. The commission has said it will review the certified court ruling before deciding what action to take. That approach allows the electoral body to act on the actual judgment rather than media interpretations of it. For the NDC, the immediate priority is the appeal. For INEC, the priority is compliance with valid legal directives. For other political parties, the case is another reminder that the legal status of political organisations can become an important issue well before elections. The eventual decision by the appellate courts could clarify the position of the NDC and determine whether the earlier registration order remains effective. Until then, the dispute remains part of Nigeria's expanding pre-2027 political and legal contest.

headline: National Assembly Develops Funding Framework for Proposed State Police
summary: Deputy Speaker Benjamin Kalu says the National Assembly is developing a funding framework for the proposed establishment of state police. He said financing should not prevent the constitutional reform if the proposal is approved.
fullStory: ABUJA — The National Assembly is developing a funding framework for the proposed establishment of state police, Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives Benjamin Kalu has said. Kalu said financing should not become an obstacle to implementing the proposed constitutional amendment if it is approved. The discussion comes amid growing debate over whether state governments would have the financial capacity to establish and sustain independent police services. State police has become one of the major issues in Nigeria's security and constitutional reform discussions. Supporters argue that state-based policing could improve local intelligence and allow security agencies to respond more quickly to threats. Critics have raised concerns about political interference, accountability and the possibility that state police could be used against political opponents or vulnerable communities. Funding is another major question. Establishing police services requires substantial resources for personnel, training, equipment, vehicles, communications and operational facilities. State governments have different levels of revenue and financial capacity, meaning a uniform funding model could be difficult to implement. The National Assembly's work on a funding framework is therefore important to the feasibility of the proposal. A workable system would need to address who pays for personnel and equipment, how funds are distributed and how financial oversight is maintained. It would also need safeguards to ensure that police officers can perform their duties professionally. The debate over state police is connected to Nigeria's wider security challenges. The country faces different forms of insecurity across its regions, including terrorism, banditry, kidnapping, communal violence and other criminal activity. Local authorities often argue that security agencies based outside a community may not have sufficient knowledge of local conditions. State police could potentially improve access to local information and community relationships. However, the success of such a system would depend heavily on training and accountability. Police officers would need clear rules governing their conduct and mechanisms for citizens to report abuse. Independent oversight would also be important. Funding arrangements could influence the independence of state police. If state police forces depend entirely on state governors for operational resources, concerns about political control could increase. A funding framework would therefore need to balance state responsibility with institutional safeguards. Recruitment is another issue. States would need qualified personnel who understand policing standards and community relations. Training institutions would have to prepare officers for modern law enforcement, including investigation, evidence handling, digital crime and human rights. Coordination with the Nigeria Police Force and other national security agencies would also be necessary. Criminal networks do not stop at state borders, so state police forces would need systems for sharing intelligence and coordinating operations. The National Assembly's constitutional reform process will determine the legal structure under which state police could operate. Public consultation and careful drafting will be important because policing affects fundamental rights and public safety. The funding question cannot be separated from these broader institutional issues. If states are given responsibility without sufficient resources, the system may become ineffective. If states receive resources without strong oversight, accountability concerns may increase. A successful model must therefore combine adequate funding with professional standards and independent safeguards. Kalu's comments indicate that lawmakers recognise financing as one of the central questions surrounding the proposal. As constitutional reform discussions continue, Nigerians will need clarity about how state police would be established, financed and supervised. The final framework will determine whether the proposal can strengthen local security while protecting citizens from political abuse.

headline: Finance Minister Calls for Wider Tax Base Rather Than Higher Rates
summary: Finance Minister Taiwo Oyedele says Nigeria's revenue challenge should be addressed by bringing more people into the tax system rather than increasing tax rates. He said expanding the tax base would improve government revenue while reducing pressure on compliant taxpayers.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, has said Nigeria's revenue challenge should be addressed primarily by expanding the tax base rather than increasing tax rates. Oyedele made the remarks during a meeting with the leadership of the Chartered Institute of Taxation of Nigeria in Abuja. The discussion came as Nigeria marked one year since President Bola Tinubu signed the country's tax reform laws. The minister's position reflects the government's broader effort to increase public revenue while limiting the burden on individuals and businesses that already comply with tax requirements. Nigeria's tax system has historically faced challenges involving a relatively narrow formal tax base, informal economic activity and uneven compliance. When a limited number of taxpayers provide a large proportion of revenue, compliant individuals and businesses can face greater pressure. Expanding the number of people and businesses participating in the tax system can potentially improve revenue without relying solely on higher rates. Increasing the tax base requires better identification of taxpayers, clearer rules and more efficient collection systems. Digital tools can help tax authorities identify economic activity and reduce opportunities for evasion. However, expanding the tax system must also consider the capacity of small businesses and low-income households. Tax policies that are difficult to understand or administer can discourage compliance. Public trust is therefore important. Taxpayers are more likely to comply when they believe that the system is fair and that government revenue is used responsibly. Tax awareness campaigns can help people understand their obligations. The Chartered Institute of Taxation of Nigeria has also played a role in public education about taxation. The National Tax Awareness Day activities included public sensitisation efforts designed to improve understanding of the tax system. For businesses, predictable tax administration is important for planning. Companies need to know what they owe and when payments are due. Complicated procedures can increase compliance costs, particularly for smaller enterprises. Simplifying processes can therefore support both businesses and government revenue. The informal sector presents another challenge. Many Nigerians earn income through small businesses and self-employment outside traditional payroll systems. Bringing more informal businesses into the tax net requires careful policy because excessive enforcement can harm vulnerable entrepreneurs. Authorities need systems that distinguish between businesses capable of contributing and individuals whose incomes are below taxable thresholds. Better data can help make that distinction. Nigeria's tax reforms are also connected to the government's broader fiscal strategy. Higher revenue can provide resources for infrastructure, education, healthcare and other public services. However, increased revenue alone does not guarantee better outcomes. Public spending must be transparent and efficient for taxpayers to see tangible benefits. The minister's emphasis on more taxpayers rather than higher rates therefore raises questions about both collection and accountability. If more Nigerians are brought into the tax system, they will expect government services to improve. Tax compliance can become more sustainable when citizens see a connection between what they pay and the services they receive. The government also needs to maintain clear communication about tax reforms. Confusion can create resistance and encourage misinformation. Businesses and individuals need accessible information about their obligations. Expanding the tax base is likely to remain a major part of Nigeria's fiscal policy as the government seeks more stable domestic revenue. The challenge will be to increase compliance without placing excessive pressure on households and businesses. A fair, transparent and efficient system could improve revenue collection while strengthening confidence in public finance.

headline: JAMB Explains New Colleges of Education Policy as Enrolment Strategy
summary: JAMB says its new policy for colleges of education is designed to increase enrolment and strengthen teacher training. Candidates seeking National Certificate in Education programmes will still register with JAMB, although some may not need to sit the UTME.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board has explained that its new policy affecting colleges of education is intended to increase student enrolment and strengthen teacher training across Nigeria. JAMB Public Communication Advisor Fabian Benjamin said many colleges of education had recorded low enrolment, with some institutions filling less than 20 percent of their available places. Under the new arrangement, candidates seeking admission into National Certificate in Education programmes will continue to register through JAMB but may not be required to sit the Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination where demand for the programmes is low. The policy is intended to make entry into teacher education more accessible while maintaining an organised admission system. Colleges of education play an important role in Nigeria's teacher-training structure. They provide programmes that prepare students for teaching, particularly at basic and secondary education levels. The quality and availability of teacher training have direct consequences for classroom learning. Nigeria has a large school-age population and requires a substantial number of qualified teachers. Low enrolment in teacher-training institutions can therefore create concerns about the future supply of educators. JAMB said the new arrangement is part of a longer-term effort agreed upon by education stakeholders to improve the attractiveness of the teaching profession. Under the policy, students will begin with NCE studies and may progress directly to degree programmes within the same institution once the institution has the required facilities and approvals. Colleges of education that want to award degrees independently will need to improve infrastructure, staffing and other requirements. The approach could encourage institutions to strengthen their academic programmes rather than depending entirely on affiliate universities. However, improving teacher education requires more than changes to admission procedures. Colleges need qualified lecturers, laboratories, libraries, teaching practice opportunities and adequate learning materials. Students also need confidence that the qualifications they obtain will provide meaningful career opportunities. The policy therefore places responsibility on institutions to improve their standards. Teacher education is particularly important because teachers influence learning outcomes at every stage of the education system. A well-trained teacher can help students develop literacy, numeracy, critical thinking and subject-specific knowledge. Poor preparation can have the opposite effect. Strengthening teacher-training institutions can therefore have benefits that extend across the education system. Increasing enrolment alone should not become the main objective. Institutions must ensure that students admitted under the new system receive quality education and adequate practical training. Teaching practice should remain an important part of teacher preparation because students need experience working in real classrooms. The policy also raises questions about the future of the teaching profession. If teaching is to attract more capable young people, graduates need clear career pathways and professional recognition. Better working conditions and opportunities for advancement can complement reforms in teacher education. The government and education authorities therefore have roles beyond admission policy. JAMB's explanation indicates that the new policy is intended to address both enrolment and teacher supply. The success of the approach will depend on how institutions use the opportunity to improve facilities and academic standards. If colleges can attract more students while maintaining quality, the policy could contribute to strengthening Nigeria's teacher workforce. If enrolment rises without corresponding investment, however, institutions could face additional pressure. The reform therefore needs to be monitored carefully. Increasing access to teacher education is important, but the ultimate goal should be producing competent educators who can improve learning in Nigerian classrooms.

headline: Sanwo-Olu Moves to Strengthen Waste Management Operations Across Lagos
summary: Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu has acknowledged challenges facing private waste operators and announced measures aimed at improving their capacity. The state says the steps are intended to strengthen waste evacuation and improve sanitation.
fullStory: LAGOS — Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu has acknowledged operational and logistical challenges facing Private Sector Participation waste operators in Lagos State and announced measures aimed at improving their capacity. The governor's intervention comes amid continuing efforts by the state government to improve waste evacuation and maintain cleaner communities across Lagos. Private waste operators play a major role in the state's waste management system. They collect refuse from homes, businesses and other locations before it is transferred through the wider waste management chain. When operators experience difficulties involving equipment, finance, routes or logistics, delays in collection can quickly become visible in communities. Lagos is one of Africa's largest urban centres and generates large volumes of waste every day. Effective waste management therefore requires coordination among households, businesses, private operators and government agencies. The state government has responsibility for regulation and overall management, while private operators provide important collection services. Improving their capacity can help reduce the amount of refuse left on roads and in public spaces. Waste management is also connected to public health and environmental protection. Poorly managed waste can block drainage channels, contribute to flooding and create conditions that encourage pests. During periods of heavy rainfall, accumulated refuse can be washed into drainage systems and worsen flooding risks. Proper collection and disposal are therefore important parts of urban planning. The governor's acknowledgment of operational difficulties indicates that improving the system requires attention to the practical conditions faced by waste operators. Trucks need maintenance and replacement, while workers require appropriate equipment and safety measures. Operators also need efficient routes and access to disposal facilities. Government can support the system by addressing regulatory bottlenecks and improving infrastructure. Public participation is equally important. Residents need to dispose of waste properly and comply with collection arrangements. Illegal dumping can undermine the work of operators and increase costs. Public education can help communities understand the relationship between responsible disposal and cleaner neighbourhoods. The state may also need stronger enforcement against indiscriminate dumping. Enforcement works best when residents have access to reliable collection services. If collection is inconsistent or unaffordable, some households may resort to illegal disposal. Improving service delivery and enforcement should therefore proceed together. Waste management also has an economic dimension. The sector provides employment for drivers, collectors, mechanics, recycling businesses and other workers. Better organised waste systems can create opportunities for recycling and resource recovery. Materials such as plastics, metals and paper can be collected and processed rather than sent directly to landfills. Lagos has significant potential to develop a circular economy around waste, although such systems require investment and reliable markets for recovered materials. The state's relationship with private operators is therefore important to long-term waste policy. Clear contracts, fair regulation and effective monitoring can help ensure that operators deliver services while remaining financially sustainable. The government must also be able to respond when operators fail to meet agreed standards. Sanwo-Olu's announcement provides an indication that the state intends to address operational weaknesses rather than leaving them unresolved. The success of the measures will depend on implementation and sustained monitoring. Lagos residents will ultimately judge the programme by whether waste is collected more reliably and whether neighbourhoods become cleaner. For a rapidly growing city, effective waste management is not simply a sanitation issue. It is an essential part of public health, environmental protection and urban development. Strengthening the capacity of private operators could therefore contribute significantly to the state's broader effort to improve living conditions.

headline: University of Ilorin Student Leads African Union Simulation Summit
summary: A student leader at the University of Ilorin organised the 2026 African Union Simulation Summit, bringing together 78 delegates to debate governance, diplomacy and African integration. The programme exposed students to practical discussions around the African Union's Agenda 2063.
fullStory: ILORIN — A student leader at the University of Ilorin has convened the 2026 African Union Simulation Summit, bringing together 78 delegates to debate governance, diplomacy and continental integration. The summit, held at the university's Faculty of Law Auditorium, was designed to give students an opportunity to examine African policy questions through a simulated diplomatic process. The programme reflects a growing interest among Nigerian students in practical forms of education that extend beyond conventional classroom instruction. Participants representing different positions within the simulated African Union were expected to discuss issues connected to governance, development and continental cooperation. Such exercises can help students develop communication, negotiation and research skills while giving them a better understanding of how international institutions operate. The African Union's Agenda 2063 provides a framework for long-term continental development, covering areas including economic integration, peace and security, democratic governance and human development. Introducing students to those themes can encourage them to consider how national policies fit into wider African priorities. Universities play an important role in preparing young people for participation in public life. Academic programmes provide foundational knowledge, but practical activities such as debates, simulations and conferences can help students apply that knowledge. For law students and others interested in governance, a diplomatic simulation can also provide experience in presenting arguments and responding to competing positions. The involvement of 78 delegates demonstrates the potential for student-led academic initiatives to create wider engagement. Such programmes can bring together students from different backgrounds and disciplines. They can also encourage participants to develop confidence in public speaking and collaborative problem-solving. Student organisations frequently provide opportunities that complement formal university programmes. When properly supported, they can contribute to leadership development and civic education. The summit also highlights the importance of African-focused scholarship. Young Nigerians are often exposed to international political developments through global media, but understanding African institutions and regional challenges requires attention to the continent's own policy frameworks. Discussions about the African Union can help students examine issues such as free movement, regional trade, peacebuilding and development. The success of such programmes depends partly on the quality of preparation. Participants need access to reliable information and should understand the distinction between simulated positions and actual government policy. Organisers also have a responsibility to create an environment in which participants can disagree respectfully. Universities can strengthen these initiatives by providing venues, academic advisers and access to research resources. Student-led conferences can also create networks that continue beyond a single event. Participants may remain connected through academic collaborations, professional associations or future policy initiatives. For Nigeria, developing young people with knowledge of diplomacy and public policy is important as the country continues to participate in regional and international affairs. Graduates who understand negotiation and multilateral institutions can contribute in government, international organisations, law, academia and civil society. The University of Ilorin summit therefore represents more than a student gathering. It demonstrates how universities can create practical learning opportunities around issues affecting Africa's future. Continued investment in student-led academic programmes could help develop a generation of graduates who are better prepared to engage with governance, diplomacy and continental development.
img: University of Ilorin students participating in an African Union simulation programme.

headline: MSMEs Drive Majority of Nigerian Businesses and Millions of Jobs, Shettima Says
summary: Vice President Kashim Shettima says micro, small and medium enterprises account for about 90 percent of businesses in Nigeria and provide roughly 60 million jobs. He said government policies were being directed toward creating a stronger environment for enterprise-led growth.
fullStory: ABUJA — Vice President Kashim Shettima has said micro, small and medium enterprises account for about 90 percent of businesses in Nigeria and provide roughly 60 million jobs, highlighting their importance to the country's economic development. Shettima made the remarks during the 8th National MSME Awards in Abuja, where he said the Federal Government was working to build a sustainable, enterprise-led economy. The vice president said government efforts were focused on creating an ecosystem that supports innovation, improves infrastructure and removes barriers facing small businesses. MSMEs are central to economic activity in Nigeria because they operate across almost every sector. Small businesses are involved in agriculture, manufacturing, retail, transportation, hospitality, technology and professional services. Their widespread presence makes them an important source of employment and income, particularly outside large corporate organisations. For many Nigerians, small businesses provide the first opportunity to enter the labour market or become self-employed. However, entrepreneurs continue to face significant challenges. Access to finance remains a major issue, particularly for businesses without substantial collateral or long operating histories. High operating costs, unreliable electricity, transportation expenses and changing market conditions can also limit the ability of small businesses to expand. Government support programmes can help address some of these constraints, but their effectiveness depends on transparency and accessibility. Business owners need to know how to apply for support and should not be excluded by complicated procedures. Infrastructure is another important part of the MSME environment. Reliable electricity can reduce production costs for businesses that would otherwise depend on generators. Better roads and transport systems can make it easier for enterprises to move goods between markets. Digital infrastructure can also allow small businesses to reach customers beyond their immediate communities. The growth of digital commerce has created new opportunities for Nigerian entrepreneurs. Businesses can advertise, receive payments and communicate with customers through online platforms. However, digital expansion requires affordable internet access and basic digital skills. Training can therefore complement financial and infrastructure support. The government's enterprise-focused approach also reflects the importance of creating opportunities outside public-sector employment. Nigeria's growing population means the formal economy must generate large numbers of new jobs. Government alone cannot employ everyone entering the workforce. A strong private sector, including MSMEs, is necessary to absorb new workers and stimulate economic activity. Business awards can provide recognition for successful entrepreneurs, but long-term growth requires consistent policies. Small businesses need predictable taxation, clear regulations and access to markets. They also need protection from unfair practices and unnecessary administrative obstacles. Entrepreneurs who succeed can create additional jobs and contribute to their communities. The government therefore has an interest in ensuring that businesses can survive beyond their early years. Shettima's remarks underline the scale of the MSME sector and its importance to Nigeria's employment challenge. If policies aimed at supporting small enterprises are implemented effectively, they can contribute to broader economic inclusion. The objective should not simply be to increase the number of businesses registered, but to help viable enterprises become more productive, create jobs and remain sustainable. For millions of Nigerians already working in small businesses, improvements in infrastructure, finance and regulation could have a direct effect on their livelihoods.

headline: Rema Takes Global Spotlight to Mawazine Festival in Morocco
summary: Nigerian Afrobeats star Rema performed at Morocco's Mawazine Festival after appearing at the FIFA World Cup opening ceremony. The performance added to the singer's growing international profile and highlighted the expanding global reach of Nigerian music.
fullStory: RABAT — Nigerian Afrobeats star Rema continued his international run with a headline performance at the Mawazine Festival in Rabat, Morocco, days after appearing at the opening ceremony of the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The performance placed the Nigerian singer before another large international audience and added to a period of increased visibility for African music. Rema has become one of the Nigerian artists whose work has achieved substantial recognition outside the country. His international profile reflects the wider growth of Afrobeats, which has developed from a predominantly regional sound into a major part of the global music industry. Nigerian artists now perform at major festivals and events in different parts of the world, reaching audiences who may have had little exposure to African music in previous years. The Mawazine Festival is one of Morocco's major music events and attracts performers and audiences from different countries. Rema's appearance there provided an opportunity to connect Nigerian popular music with North African audiences. International performances also contribute to the commercial growth of the Nigerian entertainment industry. Musicians, producers, dancers, managers and other professionals can benefit when Nigerian music gains wider international demand. The success of individual artists can therefore have effects beyond the performers themselves. Global streaming has played an important role in the expansion of African music. Digital platforms allow songs to reach listeners without depending entirely on traditional radio or physical distribution. Artists can build international audiences through streaming, social media and live performances. This has changed how musicians promote their work and organise tours. However, international success also creates greater expectations. Artists must maintain high production standards and adapt to different markets while retaining the cultural identity that makes their music distinctive. Nigerian musicians have increasingly collaborated with artists from other countries, creating opportunities for cross-cultural exchange. Such collaborations can introduce African sounds to new audiences while giving Nigerian artists access to different creative networks. Rema's recent international appearances demonstrate how quickly the profile of an Afrobeats performer can expand when music connects with global audiences. The development also contributes to Nigeria's cultural influence. Popular music has become one of the country's most recognisable cultural exports, alongside film, fashion and literature. Nigerian artists can therefore play an informal role in shaping perceptions of the country abroad. The growth of the entertainment industry also presents opportunities for young people seeking careers in creative fields. Beyond performers, the industry needs sound engineers, photographers, videographers, choreographers, event organisers, publicists and digital specialists. Strong international demand can create additional work across these areas. At the same time, the industry needs better structures for protecting artists' rights and ensuring that creative professionals receive fair compensation. International visibility is valuable, but sustainable careers require effective management and commercial systems. Rema's Mawazine performance is another milestone in the continuing international expansion of Nigerian popular music. For the broader industry, each successful global appearance strengthens the argument that creative talent can become an important part of Nigeria's economic and cultural influence. The challenge now is to convert global attention into sustainable opportunities for a wider generation of Nigerian artists.
img: Rema performing at the Mawazine Festival in Rabat, Morocco.

headline: INEC Reviews Court Ruling Before Taking Action on NDC Registration
summary: The Independent National Electoral Commission says it will review the certified court ruling affecting the registration of the Nigeria Democratic Congress before deciding its next steps. The commission said its legal department would study the judgment and act in accordance with the court's directives.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Independent National Electoral Commission has said it will review a certified copy of a Federal High Court judgment affecting the registration of the Nigeria Democratic Congress before deciding on its next course of action. INEC said it had seen reports about the ruling but had not yet received the Certified True Copy required for its legal department to conduct a detailed review. The position followed a Federal High Court judgment in Lokoja, Kogi State, which set aside an earlier decision directing INEC to register the NDC as a political party. The court's decision has become part of a wider legal and political dispute over the party's registration and the use of its identifying symbols. INEC is responsible for registering political parties that meet the requirements established by Nigerian law. Its decisions can have significant consequences for political organisations, particularly as parties prepare for future elections. The commission must therefore ensure that its actions are supported by the applicable law and court decisions. Waiting for the certified ruling before acting allows INEC to understand the precise orders made by the court. Court judgments can contain specific directions that differ from summaries circulated in the media. Legal institutions and public bodies generally rely on certified documents when implementing judicial decisions. The NDC has rejected the ruling and said it intends to appeal. The party maintains that it remains legally recognised and plans to challenge the decision at the Court of Appeal. The dispute illustrates the role that the courts can play in Nigeria's electoral process. Political parties operate within a legal framework that includes registration requirements, internal rules and electoral regulations. When disagreements arise, judicial review provides a mechanism for resolving questions of law. The matter also comes as political activity increases ahead of the 2027 general elections. New and existing political organisations are seeking to position themselves for the next electoral cycle. Questions about party registration can therefore become politically significant. For INEC, however, the immediate responsibility is to follow the law and comply with valid judicial orders. The commission's legal review is expected to determine the practical implications of the judgment. Political parties and candidates need certainty about their legal status before beginning formal electoral activities. Uncertainty can affect planning, fundraising, candidate selection and mobilisation. The case also highlights the importance of clear judicial processes in electoral matters. Parties need access to the courts when they believe their rights have been affected, while electoral authorities need clear instructions when court decisions alter existing arrangements. The Appeal Court may ultimately have to determine the dispute if the NDC proceeds with its challenge. Until then, INEC's decision to review the certified judgment before acting reflects the procedural steps expected of an electoral management body. The development demonstrates how legal decisions can influence political competition well before an election takes place. It also reinforces the importance of allowing electoral institutions to make decisions based on official documents rather than competing political interpretations. As Nigeria approaches another electoral cycle, the handling of party registration disputes will remain an important test of confidence in the country's electoral institutions.
img: INEC officials during an electoral briefing in Abuja.

headline: JAMB Training Programme Offers Free Preparation to 500 Lagos Students
summary: The Adeboruwa of Igbogbo Kingdom has unveiled a free JAMB preparation programme for 500 Senior Secondary School Three students in Lagos. The initiative is intended to help candidates prepare for tertiary admission examinations and improve their chances of gaining admission.
fullStory: LAGOS — A free preparation programme for 500 Senior Secondary School Three students has been unveiled in Lagos to help candidates prepare for the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board examination and improve their chances of gaining admission to tertiary institutions. The initiative was announced by the Adeboruwa of Igbogbo Kingdom, Oba Semiudeen Kasali, as part of activities marking his 10th coronation anniversary. The programme is aimed at students preparing to make the transition from secondary education to tertiary institutions. Admission examinations can be a major challenge for students, particularly those from households that cannot easily afford additional coaching. Free preparation programmes can reduce some of that financial pressure while giving students access to structured academic support. The Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination is an important part of Nigeria's tertiary admission system. Candidates compete for places based on their performance and must also meet the requirements of their chosen institutions and programmes. Strong preparation can therefore be valuable, particularly for students targeting competitive courses. The initiative also highlights the role of community institutions in supporting education. Traditional leaders, religious organisations, foundations and private groups can complement government programmes by helping students access learning opportunities. Such support is especially useful where public schools have limited resources for additional examination preparation. Effective JAMB preparation involves more than memorising answers. Students need a good understanding of the subjects they will be tested on and should develop the ability to manage time during computer-based examinations. Practice tests can help candidates become familiar with the examination format and identify areas where they need improvement. Teachers and tutors participating in such programmes can also help students understand common examination mistakes. However, preparation programmes need qualified instructors and appropriate learning materials to be effective. Students should be encouraged to use official JAMB information when preparing for examinations. Unofficial claims about examination questions or shortcuts can expose candidates to malpractice and fraud. The programme therefore has an opportunity to combine academic preparation with guidance on examination integrity. Access to tertiary education remains an important concern for Nigerian families. The cost of university education, accommodation, transportation and learning materials can create significant financial pressure. While a free JAMB programme does not remove all those challenges, it can help students reach the admission stage. Community-based educational support can also build confidence among young people. Students who receive encouragement and structured preparation may become more motivated to pursue their academic goals. The programme's focus on 500 students provides a measurable target and could serve as a model for similar initiatives in other communities. Scaling such efforts would require additional funding, qualified teachers and suitable facilities. Community leaders can work with schools and education authorities to identify students who would benefit most. The initiative also demonstrates that educational development can involve multiple actors. Government remains responsible for the broader education system, but communities and individuals can make meaningful contributions. For the participating students, the immediate objective is to prepare effectively for tertiary admission. For the wider community, the programme represents an investment in young people. If the students use the opportunity successfully, the initiative could produce benefits that extend beyond the examination itself by helping more young Nigerians gain access to higher education and professional training.
img: Secondary school students participating in a JAMB preparation programme in Lagos.

headline: Education Minister Says 24 Nigerian Universities Enter 2026 Global Rankings
summary: Education Minister Tunji Alausa says 24 Nigerian universities have been listed in the 2026 Times Higher Education World University Rankings. He described the result as the country's strongest performance so far in the ranking.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Minister of Education, Tunji Alausa, has said 24 Nigerian universities were listed in the 2026 Times Higher Education World University Rankings, describing the result as the country's strongest performance so far in the ranking. The development has drawn attention to the performance of Nigerian universities in international assessments and to the broader question of improving the quality and visibility of higher education in the country. International university rankings use different methodologies to assess institutions. Depending on the ranking system, factors can include teaching, research, citations, international collaboration and other indicators. A university's position in a ranking does not capture every aspect of educational quality, but participation can provide institutions with an additional benchmark against which to assess their performance. The appearance of more Nigerian universities in an international ranking could indicate growing visibility of the country's higher education sector. Nigerian universities have a large student population and a significant academic community, but they continue to face challenges involving infrastructure, research funding, staff capacity and international competitiveness. Improving rankings therefore requires sustained investment rather than short-term campaigns. Research is particularly important because universities are expected not only to teach students but also to generate knowledge. Researchers need laboratories, libraries, data, grants and opportunities for collaboration. Universities also need systems that encourage academics to publish high-quality work and engage with international research networks. Teaching quality remains equally important. Students should have access to qualified lecturers, functional facilities and programmes that reflect current academic and professional requirements. A stronger international profile can be useful if it is accompanied by improvements in the student experience. The ranking announcement also provides an opportunity to examine the performance of individual institutions. Universities can study the indicators used by ranking organisations and identify areas where they need to improve. However, institutions should avoid treating rankings as the sole measure of success. A university can make important contributions to its community even if it is not highly placed in a global table. Local research, professional training and community engagement remain significant measures of educational value. The Federal Government has continued to promote reforms intended to strengthen tertiary education. Funding, accreditation, digital learning, research development and staff training are all connected to the quality of universities. State governments and university governing bodies also have roles to play. The increase in ranked institutions may encourage universities to pursue stronger international partnerships. Collaboration with universities abroad can provide opportunities for joint research, staff development and student exchanges. Such partnerships can also increase the visibility of Nigerian research. International recognition may benefit graduates as well. Employers and institutions outside Nigeria can find it easier to identify Nigerian universities when their programmes and research are visible internationally. Nevertheless, the ultimate test of university performance remains the quality of education and research provided to students and society. Rankings should therefore be viewed as one source of evidence rather than the final judgment on an institution. The reported performance of 24 Nigerian universities offers encouragement to the sector, but sustaining progress will require continued investment. Universities must strengthen research, teaching, infrastructure and governance while ensuring that improvements reach students. If that happens, increased international visibility can become part of a broader improvement in Nigerian higher education rather than an isolated ranking achievement.
img: Nigerian university students attending a lecture on campus.

headline: Telecom Subscriptions Rise as Nigeria's Broadband Penetration Reaches 55.67%
summary: Nigeria's telecommunications subscriptions have risen to about 188 million while broadband penetration reached 55.67 percent. The growth reflects continued expansion of mobile connectivity and demand for digital services across the country.
fullStory: LAGOS — Nigeria's telecommunications sector has recorded further growth, with total subscriptions rising to about 188 million while broadband penetration reached 55.67 percent. The figures highlight the continuing expansion of digital connectivity and the importance of telecommunications to economic and social activity across the country. Mobile communications have become an essential part of everyday life in Nigeria. Individuals use phones not only for voice calls but also for banking, education, commerce, entertainment and access to public services. The expansion of broadband connectivity can therefore have effects across several parts of the economy. Higher broadband penetration can give more people access to digital opportunities. Businesses can reach customers through online platforms, workers can participate in remote services and students can access educational materials. Government agencies can also use digital channels to deliver information and services. However, the number of subscriptions does not necessarily mean that every Nigerian has reliable internet access. Some people own more than one SIM card, while others may have limited access because of affordability or poor network coverage. Quality and affordability are therefore important alongside overall subscription figures. Infrastructure investment remains essential to improving connectivity. Mobile networks require base stations, fibre infrastructure, data centres and reliable electricity. Rural communities can be particularly difficult and expensive to serve because of distance and lower commercial returns. Government and telecom operators need to find sustainable ways to extend coverage to underserved areas. Broadband expansion also depends on the cost of data. Even where networks are available, high data prices can limit usage among low-income households. Affordable access can help more people benefit from digital services. Digital skills are another consideration. Connectivity becomes more valuable when people know how to use it productively. Schools, businesses and community organisations can help users develop digital literacy. The telecommunications industry also supports employment and entrepreneurship. Mobile technology has created opportunities for software developers, online merchants, content creators and digital service providers. Small businesses increasingly rely on social media and messaging platforms to market products and communicate with customers. Financial technology has also benefited from widespread mobile connectivity. Mobile banking and payment services allow people to conduct transactions without travelling long distances to bank branches. This can be particularly useful for small businesses and people in areas with limited banking infrastructure. At the same time, the growth of digital services increases the importance of cybersecurity and consumer protection. Users need protection from fraud, identity theft and misuse of personal information. Regulators and service providers must therefore strengthen security while expanding access. The latest telecommunications figures suggest that Nigeria's digital economy continues to grow. For the country to capture the full economic benefits, expansion must be accompanied by reliable service, affordability and wider digital skills. Broadband access can support education, business and public services, but the benefits depend on whether people can actually use the connections consistently. Continued investment in telecommunications infrastructure will therefore remain important as Nigeria seeks to build a more digitally connected economy.
img: A Nigerian telecom user accessing mobile broadband services.

headline: Nigeria Plans Digital Curriculum to Strengthen Teacher Training
summary: The Federal Government is planning a competency-based digital curriculum for teacher training as part of efforts to prepare educators for a changing learning environment. The initiative is intended to strengthen digital skills and improve the quality of teacher preparation.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Federal Government is planning a competency-based digital curriculum for teacher training as part of efforts to improve the preparation of educators in Nigeria. The proposed approach is intended to equip teachers with skills that can support effective teaching in increasingly digital learning environments. Technology has become an important part of education, particularly as schools and universities adopt digital learning resources. Teachers are expected to understand how to use technology not simply for presenting information but also for assessment, communication, research and classroom management. A digital curriculum for teacher education can provide a structured way of developing those competencies. Nigeria's education system faces significant differences in access to technology. Some urban schools have computers and internet connectivity, while many rural schools continue to operate with limited electricity and digital infrastructure. Teacher training must therefore recognise the realities teachers will encounter in different environments. Digital competence should complement, rather than replace, strong teaching fundamentals. Teachers still need knowledge of their subjects, classroom management skills and the ability to understand individual learners. Technology can become useful when it supports those core responsibilities. Training programmes can teach educators how to use digital resources to explain difficult concepts, provide additional learning materials and monitor student progress. Digital tools can also help teachers collaborate with colleagues and access professional-development materials. Continuous training is important because technology changes quickly. A one-time course may not be enough to keep teachers up to date with new platforms and methods. Education authorities and institutions will need systems for ongoing professional development. Teacher education institutions will also need appropriate infrastructure to deliver the new curriculum. Colleges and universities require computers, internet access, software and qualified instructors. Without those resources, a digital curriculum could remain largely theoretical. The government will also need to consider teachers working in schools where technology is limited. Training should include practical strategies for using available resources rather than assuming that every classroom has advanced equipment. Mobile devices and offline digital resources may provide alternatives in locations with weak connectivity. The proposed curriculum comes amid broader efforts to improve learning outcomes. Nigeria continues to face concerns about literacy, numeracy and the quality of basic education. Better teacher preparation can contribute to addressing those challenges because teachers have a direct influence on classroom learning. Digital skills may also become increasingly important to students preparing for the labour market. Schools need teachers who can introduce learners to responsible technology use and basic digital problem-solving. The initiative could therefore have benefits beyond the immediate teacher-training system. However, implementation will determine its impact. Curriculum design must be followed by adequate funding, training materials and monitoring. Teachers should also have opportunities to provide feedback on what works in real classrooms. Education policies are more likely to succeed when teachers are involved in their implementation. A competency-based digital curriculum can help modernise teacher education if it is properly supported. Nigeria's large education system makes implementation challenging, but the need for digitally capable educators is clear. As schools increasingly interact with technology, teacher training must evolve accordingly. The proposed curriculum represents an attempt to ensure that teachers are prepared not only to teach traditional subjects but also to help students navigate a digital economy.
img: Nigerian teachers participating in digital education training.

headline: BIGI and Soundcity Combine Music Event With Student Scholarships
summary: BIGI and Soundcity hosted a music and youth engagement event at the University of Lagos while supporting students through scholarship opportunities. The initiative combined entertainment with education-focused support.
fullStory: LAGOS — A youth-focused entertainment event at the University of Lagos combined live music with scholarship opportunities, bringing together entertainment and education in a programme involving BIGI and Soundcity. The event formed part of efforts to engage young Nigerians through popular culture while providing practical support for students. Music and entertainment have become important channels for reaching young audiences in Nigeria. Brands increasingly use concerts, campus events and creative partnerships to connect with students and young consumers. When such programmes include education initiatives, they can also provide benefits beyond entertainment. Scholarships can help students facing financial difficulties continue their studies. The cost of tertiary education extends beyond tuition and includes accommodation, transportation, textbooks, digital devices and other learning materials. Support programmes can therefore make a meaningful difference, particularly for students from lower-income households. Universities are also important spaces for youth engagement because they bring together large communities of young people from different parts of the country. Campus-based initiatives can create opportunities for students to interact with artists, media professionals and businesses. Such interactions can expose students to possible careers within the wider creative economy. Nigeria's entertainment sector employs people across many disciplines. Music requires performers, producers, sound engineers, event organisers, marketers, photographers, videographers and digital specialists. Students interested in creative careers can benefit from understanding the professional opportunities available beyond becoming performers. Partnerships between brands and universities can also provide platforms for talent discovery. Young musicians and other creatives may use campus events to develop their skills and build audiences. However, educational components remain important because not every student will pursue entertainment as a career. Scholarship programmes can help ensure that the benefits of sponsorship reach students with academic needs. Corporate support for education can complement government funding and university welfare programmes. Such initiatives are most effective when scholarship selection is transparent and based on clearly communicated criteria. Students should understand who is eligible, how applications are assessed and what support is provided. The combination of music and education also reflects a broader trend in youth-oriented programmes. Young people often engage strongly with entertainment, sport and digital culture. Using those channels to promote educational opportunities can make support programmes more visible. Universities can work with private organisations to develop initiatives that connect entertainment with skills development, entrepreneurship and academic support. Such partnerships need to be managed carefully so that commercial interests do not overshadow educational objectives. The University of Lagos event illustrates how entertainment can serve as a platform for wider engagement. Music provided the attraction, while scholarships provided a direct educational benefit. Similar programmes could be developed around technology, entrepreneurship and creative skills. For students, the most important outcome is whether opportunities created through such initiatives produce lasting benefits. A scholarship can help a student complete a programme, while exposure to industry professionals can open doors to future employment. As Nigeria's creative economy grows, partnerships between brands, media organisations and educational institutions are likely to remain important. Combining cultural engagement with practical educational support can provide young people with both inspiration and tangible opportunities.
img: Students and performers at the BIGI and Soundcity campus event at UNILAG.

headline: Education Experts Urge Universities to Lead Sustainability and ESG Innovation
summary: Education experts have called on Nigerian universities to take a stronger role in environmental, social and governance innovation. They said universities can help develop research, skills and solutions for sustainable development.
fullStory: LAGOS — Education experts have called on Nigerian universities to play a stronger role in environmental, social and governance innovation, arguing that higher institutions can contribute significantly to sustainable development. The call reflects growing attention to the relationship between education, research and the environmental and social challenges facing businesses and communities. Universities traditionally serve as centres for teaching and research, but their role in addressing sustainability issues is expanding. Students and researchers can develop solutions related to energy, waste management, agriculture, transportation and other areas that affect environmental performance. The private sector is also increasingly interested in environmental, social and governance principles as investors, consumers and regulators pay greater attention to sustainability. Universities can help businesses develop the knowledge and skills required to respond to those expectations. Research partnerships between universities and companies can provide practical opportunities for students. Instead of studying sustainability only as a theoretical subject, students can work on projects involving real organisations and community challenges. Such experience can improve employability while giving companies access to new ideas. Nigeria faces several environmental challenges that require local research. Waste management, flooding, erosion, energy access and climate-related pressures affect communities across the country. Universities can contribute by conducting research that takes local conditions into account. International solutions may not always be directly applicable to Nigerian communities. Local research can therefore help identify approaches that are affordable and practical. Sustainability also has a social dimension. Education institutions need to consider issues such as inclusion, accessibility, community development and ethical governance. Students who understand these principles can carry them into future careers in business, government and civil society. University governance itself can benefit from stronger ESG thinking. Institutions manage large campuses, employ significant numbers of people and interact with surrounding communities. Energy efficiency, responsible procurement and waste reduction can lower costs while improving environmental performance. Student participation can also strengthen sustainability programmes. Campus projects can provide practical learning while improving university facilities. However, sustainability initiatives require funding and institutional commitment. Universities may need to invest in laboratories, data systems and staff training. Government agencies and private organisations can support research through grants and partnerships. The development of relevant academic programmes is another important step. Universities can integrate sustainability concepts into existing disciplines rather than treating them only as specialised subjects. Engineering students, for example, can study energy efficiency, while business students can examine responsible corporate practices. Law students can explore environmental regulation and public policy. This interdisciplinary approach reflects the fact that sustainability problems rarely belong to one field alone. Nigeria's young population also creates an opportunity. Students entering the workforce will influence how businesses and public institutions operate in the coming decades. Giving them strong knowledge of sustainability can help shape future decision-making. Universities can therefore become laboratories for ideas that later spread into society. The call for stronger university involvement in ESG innovation is part of a wider conversation about the purpose of higher education. Institutions are expected not only to award qualifications but also to generate solutions to national problems. If universities strengthen research partnerships, practical training and campus sustainability, they can contribute meaningfully to Nigeria's development. The challenge will be converting broad commitments into measurable projects and useful research. With sustained support, higher education can become an important driver of environmental and social innovation.
img: University students working on a sustainability research project.

headline: ASUU Warns of Possible Strike in State Universities Over Unimplemented Agreement
summary: The Academic Staff Union of Universities has warned that academic activities could be disrupted in several state universities if governments fail to implement the 2025 agreement on lecturers' remuneration and allowances.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Academic Staff Union of Universities has warned of possible industrial action in several state-owned universities over the failure of some state governments to implement provisions of the 2025 Federal Government-ASUU agreement. The union said continued delays in the payment of agreed allowances and other entitlements were creating tension within the university system. The warning followed separate statements from ASUU zones covering universities in different parts of the country. In the Benin Zone, the union said seven state-owned universities in Edo, Delta and Ondo states could face an indefinite strike if the agreement was not implemented in the July salary payments. The affected institutions include Ambrose Alli University, Adekunle Ajasin University, Olusegun Agagu University of Science and Technology, Delta State University, University of Delta, Dennis Osadebay University and Southern Delta University. Similar concerns were raised by ASUU zones in other parts of the country. The union has argued that state universities should not be excluded from arrangements negotiated with the Federal Government when their academic staff are affected by the same national issues. Among the issues raised are salary arrears and allowances intended to support academic staff. University lecturers' welfare has remained a recurring issue in Nigeria's higher education system. Previous disputes over remuneration, working conditions and funding have contributed to prolonged disruptions of academic calendars. ASUU has repeatedly warned that failure to address outstanding agreements could undermine stability in public universities. The union's latest position places pressure on state governments to resolve the issues before the proposed deadlines. Students are among those most affected when universities shut down. Industrial action can interrupt lectures, examinations, research and graduation schedules. It can also increase the financial burden on students who may have to remain away from their institutions for extended periods. University authorities therefore have an interest in resolving disputes before they escalate. Funding is central to the broader debate. State-owned universities depend heavily on government support, while institutions also face increasing demands for infrastructure, staff recruitment and research. Without predictable funding, universities can struggle to retain experienced academics and maintain facilities. ASUU has also argued that proper implementation of agreements is important for staff morale. Lecturers who believe that negotiated commitments are not being honoured may become less motivated, while institutions may find it difficult to attract qualified personnel. The union has therefore called on the affected governments to act before the situation develops into another nationwide disruption. Government officials have an opportunity to use dialogue to resolve the disagreements. Negotiations can help establish realistic payment schedules and clarify which obligations have already been fulfilled. Preventing a strike would also protect students from another interruption to their academic programmes. The situation highlights the importance of maintaining credible agreements between governments and university staff. When commitments are negotiated and signed, implementation becomes essential to maintaining trust. The coming weeks will determine whether the affected state governments can settle the outstanding issues before ASUU's deadlines. For students and parents, the preferred outcome remains uninterrupted academic activity. For universities, stable industrial relations are essential to maintaining teaching, research and institutional development.
img: Academic Staff Union of Universities officials during a briefing.

headline: Nigeria Begins Training Programme to Strengthen Technical and Vocational Education
summary: Nigeria has begun a capacity-building programme for technical and vocational education instructors in partnership with Singapore's Institute of Education. The programme focuses on modern teaching methods and assessment skills.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Federal Government has commenced a capacity-building programme designed to strengthen teaching and assessment in Nigeria's technical and vocational education and training system. The initiative is being implemented in collaboration with the Institute of Education in Singapore and involves instructors from federal and state institutions. The programme, known as the Train the Trainers Pedagogy and Assessment Programme, is intended to improve the ability of TVET instructors to deliver practical and industry-relevant education. The first cohort consists of 60 teachers undergoing training in Abuja, while another 60 instructors are expected to participate in a second cohort in Lagos. Technical and vocational education has become increasingly important in Nigeria as policymakers seek to expand opportunities for young people beyond conventional academic pathways. TVET can equip students with practical skills in areas such as construction, manufacturing, information technology, agriculture, electrical work and other technical occupations. The quality of instruction is central to the success of vocational education. Teachers need both technical knowledge and effective methods for transferring that knowledge to students. Modern assessment techniques can also help institutions determine whether learners have acquired the practical competencies expected of them. The training programme therefore focuses not only on subject knowledge but also on pedagogy and assessment. Industry relevance is another important consideration. Employers require workers who can use equipment safely, solve problems and adapt to changing technologies. TVET institutions must therefore keep their programmes aligned with workplace requirements. Partnerships with industry can provide opportunities for instructors and students to gain exposure to modern practices. Nigeria's growing population makes skills development a major policy issue. Large numbers of young people enter the labour market every year, while businesses continue to report shortages of workers with specialised technical skills. Strengthening vocational education can help close part of that gap. It can also support entrepreneurship. Skilled graduates can establish small businesses and provide services within their communities rather than depending entirely on formal employment. However, effective TVET requires more than teacher training. Institutions need functioning workshops, laboratories, tools and equipment. Students must have opportunities to practise the skills they are taught. Reliable electricity and other infrastructure are also important for technical programmes. The government's training initiative can therefore be viewed as one component of a wider reform agenda. The partnership with Singapore provides Nigerian instructors with exposure to approaches used in another education system. Knowledge gained through the programme can then be adapted to Nigerian conditions. Assessment is particularly important because employers need confidence that graduates possess the skills indicated by their qualifications. Competency-based approaches can help institutions measure practical abilities more accurately. The programme also demonstrates the importance of continuous professional development for teachers. Education systems change as technology and labour-market needs evolve. Instructors must therefore have opportunities to update their knowledge throughout their careers. If sustained, capacity-building programmes can improve the quality of instruction and strengthen the reputation of vocational education. Nigeria needs a system in which technical skills are valued alongside university degrees. Such an approach can expand opportunities for young people and support industrial development. The latest training programme is therefore part of a broader effort to improve the country's human capital. Its long-term impact will depend on how the participating instructors apply the knowledge gained and whether institutions receive the facilities required to support effective practical education.
img: TVET instructors during a capacity-building programme in Nigeria.

headline: Government Set to Launch Digital Education Data Platform
summary: The Federal Government announced plans to launch a digital platform designed to consolidate information on schools, learners and education services across Nigeria. Officials said the system would improve education planning and make key data more accessible.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Federal Government has announced plans to launch a Digital National Education Management Information System designed to bring education data from across Nigeria onto a unified platform. The system is intended to improve the way information about schools, teachers and learners is collected, managed and used for policy decisions. Education data is essential for planning. Governments need reliable information about enrolment, teachers, infrastructure and learning resources to determine where investment is required. Without accurate data, resources can be distributed inefficiently and some communities may remain underserved. The planned digital system is expected to consolidate information currently held by different institutions and levels of government. Officials said more than 32 million students were already enrolled on the existing data platform.
