headline: Nigerian Students Protest South African Xenophobia, Shut MTN Abuja Headquarters
summary: Nigerian students protested alleged xenophobic attacks against Nigerians in South Africa and shut access to MTN Nigeria's headquarters in Abuja. The National Association of Nigerian Students demanded stronger action to protect Nigerians and other Africans facing anti-foreigner violence.
fullStory: ABUJA — Nigerian university students staged a protest at the headquarters of MTN Nigeria in Abuja over alleged xenophobic attacks against Nigerians and other Africans in South Africa. The demonstration was organised by the National Association of Nigerian Students as part of a wider response to anti-foreigner protests and violence reported in South Africa. The students blocked access around the telecommunications company's premises and confronted police officers who attempted to control the demonstration. The protesters argued that South African businesses operating in Nigeria should not continue to benefit from the Nigerian market while Nigerians living in South Africa face threats and attacks. The demonstration formed part of growing anger in Nigeria following reports of xenophobic violence and campaigns calling for the removal of foreign nationals from South Africa. Nigerian authorities have been evacuating citizens who requested assistance amid the unrest. The federal government has maintained that the safety of Nigerians abroad remains a priority and has engaged South African authorities over the situation. The student protesters demanded stronger diplomatic action and greater protection for Nigerians living and working in South Africa. They also threatened further action against South African-linked businesses in Nigeria if the situation did not improve. MTN and other South African companies have significant commercial operations in Nigeria, making the issue economically sensitive. Nigeria and South Africa maintain extensive political, commercial and people-to-people ties, but relations have periodically been strained by xenophobic attacks against African migrants in South Africa. Nigerians are among the African nationals who have frequently been targeted during such episodes. The latest tensions have also raised concerns about retaliation in Nigeria. Officials and community leaders have urged Nigerians not to attack South African citizens or businesses and have stressed the importance of resolving the dispute through diplomatic channels. Retaliatory attacks could harm bilateral relations and expose innocent people to danger. The protests nevertheless reflect the strength of public anger in Nigeria. Students argued that Nigerians living abroad should be able to work and study without fear of violence because they contribute to the economies and communities in which they live. The issue has also generated debate about the responsibility of African governments to protect citizens across borders. Nigeria has historically played a major diplomatic role on the continent and has frequently advocated for African unity and regional cooperation. At the same time, the government faces pressure from citizens to respond decisively when Nigerians abroad are threatened. The evacuation of Nigerians from South Africa has provided immediate assistance to people who felt unsafe or stranded, but it does not resolve the underlying problem. Long-term improvement will require cooperation between Nigerian and South African authorities, stronger enforcement against perpetrators of xenophobic violence and efforts to reduce anti-immigrant sentiment. Economic relations could also be affected if protests against South African businesses escalate. Companies such as MTN and MultiChoice employ Nigerians and contribute taxes and investment to the Nigerian economy. Disrupting their operations could therefore have consequences for workers and consumers in Nigeria. The student protest has brought the xenophobia issue back into national attention and demonstrated the emotional response it has generated among young Nigerians. The government is expected to continue diplomatic engagement while supporting citizens who want to return home. For Nigeria and South Africa, the challenge is to protect citizens, prevent retaliatory violence and preserve important bilateral relations. The protests underline the need for African countries to confront xenophobia while maintaining peaceful channels for resolving disputes.
img: Nigerian university students protesting against alleged xenophobic attacks on Nigerians in South Africa.
source: National Association of Nigerian Students; Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs

headline: University of Abuja Appoints Substantive Registrar and University Librarian
summary: The Governing Council of the University of Abuja approved the appointment of Alkasim Musa Umar as substantive Registrar and Rose Lade Mommoh as substantive University Librarian. Both officials will serve five-year terms under the university's governing regulations.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Governing Council of the University of Abuja has approved the appointment of Malam Alkasim Musa Umar as the university's substantive Registrar and Dr Rose Lade Mommoh as substantive University Librarian. The appointments were approved during the council's 101st regular meeting held on July 10 and 11. The two officials will serve five-year terms in accordance with the relevant provisions governing Nigerian universities and the institution's regulations. The appointments fill key administrative positions at the university and are expected to strengthen the institution's management structure. The Registrar is responsible for a wide range of administrative functions, including maintaining institutional records, supporting academic and administrative processes and coordinating the implementation of decisions of the university's governing bodies. The University Librarian, meanwhile, oversees the institution's library system and plays an important role in supporting teaching, research and learning. University libraries have changed significantly as Nigerian higher education institutions increase their use of digital resources. Students and researchers increasingly depend on electronic journals, online databases, digital repositories and other technology-based academic materials. A modern university library therefore requires both physical resources and effective digital services. The appointment of substantive officers can provide greater continuity in the administration of these responsibilities. The University of Abuja has continued to pursue efforts to strengthen its academic and administrative systems. Like other Nigerian universities, it faces challenges related to funding, infrastructure, technology, student enrolment and the changing demands of higher education. Effective administration is essential to addressing these challenges. The Registrar's office also plays a role in student administration and institutional coordination. Accurate records, efficient communication and transparent administrative procedures can improve students' experiences and reduce delays in academic processes. The library is equally important to students and academic staff. Access to current books, journals and research databases can influence the quality of teaching and research conducted at a university. Investment in digital library systems can expand access beyond physical opening hours and allow researchers to use resources from different locations. The new University Librarian will therefore have an important responsibility in maintaining and expanding the institution's information resources. The five-year tenure provides the appointed officials with time to develop and implement long-term plans. University administrators must balance institutional policies with the needs of students, academic staff, non-teaching employees and external stakeholders. Good governance requires consultation, accountability and adherence to university regulations. The Governing Council's approval of the appointments was welcomed by the university management. The Vice-Chancellor congratulated the new officials and described the appointments as significant to the institution's continuing development. The university is expected to work with the new officers to strengthen administrative efficiency and support its academic mission. Nigerian universities are under increasing pressure to produce graduates with skills relevant to a changing economy. This requires strong academic programmes as well as effective administrative and support systems. Registrars and librarians contribute to that environment by ensuring that students and researchers can access essential institutional and academic resources. The appointments therefore have implications beyond the two offices themselves. Efficient administration can improve the delivery of services across the university, while a strong library system can support research and academic excellence. The new officers are expected to begin their substantive responsibilities as the institution prepares for another academic cycle. Their performance will be assessed over the course of their tenure as they work with the university's leadership, governing council and wider community. The appointments represent another step in the university's effort to maintain stable leadership and improve its institutional capacity.

headline: Venezuela Earthquake Death Toll Rises to 4,333 as Search and Recovery Continue
summary: The death toll from Venezuela's June 24 earthquakes rose to 4,333, while 16,740 people were reported injured and about 17,000 left homeless. Authorities said search operations were continuing as preparations began for housing reconstruction.
fullStory: CARACAS — The death toll from the devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela on June 24 has risen to 4,333, according to National Assembly President Jorge Rodriguez. The authorities also reported that 16,740 people had been injured and about 17,000 people were left homeless following the disaster. The earthquakes, which struck Caracas and the coastal state of La Guaira, caused widespread destruction and brought down buildings and homes in several communities. Emergency teams from Venezuela and other countries have been involved in search, rescue and recovery operations since the disaster. Authorities said 6,462 people had been rescued during the response. Search operations were still continuing at several sites where rescuers believed there could be survivors. The government also reported that hundreds of buildings had been affected, with some suffering complete or partial structural collapse. The scale of the destruction has created a major humanitarian challenge. Thousands of people have been forced to live in temporary camps established in stadiums, public spaces and other areas. Families living in these camps require food, water, medical assistance and shelter while authorities assess damaged communities. The government has begun planning for longer-term reconstruction. Officials said the first housing units for affected families were expected to be allocated as reconstruction efforts progressed. Authorities estimated that tens of thousands of homes would ultimately be needed to accommodate people who lost their houses in the earthquakes. Rebuilding after a major earthquake is a complex process because damaged structures must first be assessed to determine whether they can be repaired or need to be demolished. Infrastructure such as roads, water systems, electricity networks and hospitals may also require extensive repairs. The disaster has placed significant pressure on emergency services. Hospitals have treated large numbers of injured people while medical teams have worked in temporary facilities. Volunteers and international rescue teams have also contributed to the response. Earthquakes can produce secondary risks after the initial shock, including aftershocks, damaged buildings and landslides. Authorities have therefore had to balance the need to continue searching for survivors with the safety of rescuers and displaced residents. Officials reported that more than a thousand aftershocks had occurred since the main earthquakes. The continuing seismic activity has complicated rescue and recovery operations. The disaster has also created a major economic burden for Venezuela. Thousands of homes and commercial buildings have been damaged, while families have lost property and livelihoods. Rebuilding will require significant public resources and assistance from international partners. The government has identified areas where new housing could be constructed for displaced families. The challenge will be to ensure that reconstruction meets safety standards and provides residents with access to essential services. For families still searching for missing relatives, the recovery process remains deeply uncertain. Authorities have said that search operations will continue while there is still a possibility of finding survivors. The death toll could change as rescue teams examine damaged structures and identify victims. The Venezuelan government has also appealed for support as it manages the humanitarian consequences of the disaster. International assistance can provide medical supplies, rescue equipment, temporary shelter and technical expertise. The earthquake response demonstrates the importance of disaster preparedness and resilient infrastructure, particularly in areas vulnerable to seismic activity. Building codes, emergency planning and public awareness can reduce casualties during future disasters. For Venezuela, however, the immediate priority remains saving lives, treating the injured and providing shelter for people who lost their homes. The rising death toll has made the June 24 earthquakes one of the country's most devastating recent disasters. As search operations continue, authorities face the difficult task of responding to immediate humanitarian needs while beginning the long process of rebuilding communities destroyed by the earthquakes.
img: Rescue workers search through rubble after the devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela.

headline: One Killed, Seven Injured in Gombe Judiciary Complex Building Collapse
summary: A building under construction at the new Judiciary Complex in Gombe State collapsed, killing one person and injuring seven others. Emergency responders conducted search and rescue operations while authorities assessed the site.
fullStory: GOMBE — A building at the new Judiciary Complex in Gombe State collapsed, killing one person and injuring seven others, according to the National Emergency Management Agency. Emergency responders were deployed to the scene to conduct search and rescue operations and provide assistance to victims. NEMA's Gombe Operations Office led the response alongside other emergency agencies and relevant stakeholders. Preliminary assessments indicated that one person lost their life in the incident while seven injured victims were receiving medical treatment at hospitals in the state. The collapse occurred at a major public construction site, raising questions about building safety, construction standards and compliance with approved specifications. Building collapses remain a serious concern in Nigeria, particularly when structures are constructed without adequate supervision or when materials and engineering standards are compromised. Construction projects require proper design, quality materials, competent professionals and regular inspection. Failure at any stage can increase the risk of structural collapse and put workers and members of the public in danger. The Gombe incident also highlights the importance of emergency preparedness at construction sites. When a structure collapses, rescue teams must quickly determine whether additional people are trapped beneath debris while ensuring that rescuers themselves are not exposed to further danger. Search and rescue operations can be complicated by unstable sections of a damaged building. NEMA advised members of the public to avoid the affected area and rely on verified information from relevant authorities while emergency operations continued. The agency also said it would continue monitoring the situation and providing humanitarian assistance where necessary. Building collapses can have consequences beyond the immediate injuries and deaths. Workers may lose colleagues, families can lose breadwinners and construction projects can be delayed while investigations are conducted. The incident can also affect public confidence in the safety of government infrastructure projects. Authorities are expected to investigate the circumstances surrounding the collapse. Such investigations can examine the building's design, construction materials, foundation, structural calculations and supervision arrangements. Determining the cause is important not only for accountability but also for preventing similar incidents in other projects. Construction safety is particularly important on large public projects because workers may spend long periods on sites while members of the public may eventually use the completed facilities. Contractors and government agencies responsible for supervision therefore have a duty to ensure that safety standards are maintained throughout the construction process. Nigeria has experienced numerous building collapses over the years, prompting repeated calls for stronger enforcement of building regulations. Experts have often pointed to weak supervision, poor-quality materials, unauthorised modifications and failure to follow approved designs as possible contributors in different cases. Each incident, however, requires its own investigation before a cause can be established. The Gombe collapse therefore underscores the need for caution against speculation while investigations are ongoing. For the families of the victims, the immediate priority is medical care for those injured and support for the family of the person who died. Emergency agencies, hospitals and state authorities must coordinate to ensure that affected people receive the assistance they need. The incident is a reminder that construction safety should remain a priority throughout Nigeria. Public infrastructure projects must meet engineering and safety standards before workers and members of the public are exposed to them. Transparent investigations and enforcement can help ensure that lessons from the Gombe incident are applied to future projects. As rescue and assessment operations continued, authorities were expected to establish the circumstances that led to the collapse and determine whether any further action was necessary. The incident has once again highlighted the human cost of failures in construction safety and the importance of effective oversight.
img: Emergency responders at the new Judiciary Complex in Gombe following the collapse of a building under construction.

headline: Oyo Schoolchildren and Teachers Regain Freedom After 56 Days in Captivity
summary: Schoolchildren and teachers abducted from schools in Oriire Local Government Area of Oyo State have regained their freedom after 56 days in captivity. The rescue followed a joint security operation involving Nigerian security agencies.
fullStory: IBADAN — Schoolchildren and teachers abducted from schools in Oriire Local Government Area of Oyo State have regained their freedom after spending 56 days in captivity. The victims were taken from their schools on May 15 and were eventually rescued during a joint security operation involving Nigerian security agencies. Their release brought relief to families and communities that had spent weeks waiting for their return. The abduction had generated widespread concern because the victims were taken from educational institutions, highlighting the continuing threat faced by schools in parts of Nigeria. Parents of the rescued children expressed relief while waiting to be reunited with their children. The authorities said the victims would undergo medical examinations and receive necessary support following their release. The rescue was the result of intelligence gathering and coordinated efforts by security agencies. The operation involved the military, police and other security institutions working together to locate the abducted students and teachers. The successful recovery demonstrates the importance of inter-agency cooperation in responding to mass abductions. Kidnapping has become a major security concern in Nigeria, with schools sometimes targeted because children can be used to generate ransom demands or create widespread public pressure. The attacks have forced some schools to strengthen security arrangements and have caused parents to reconsider sending children to schools in vulnerable areas. The psychological effects of captivity can also be significant. Children who experience prolonged abduction may require counselling and other forms of support after returning home. Teachers who were held alongside the students may also need assistance in dealing with the trauma of captivity. Families can face emotional and financial consequences during prolonged abductions. Parents may spend weeks searching for information about their children while communities organise support and pressure authorities to secure their release. The uncertainty can be particularly difficult when communication with kidnappers is limited. The successful rescue has therefore been welcomed as a major relief, but officials and community leaders have stressed the need to prevent similar incidents. Protecting schools requires more than security personnel at school gates. Authorities may need to improve intelligence gathering, monitor vulnerable routes and strengthen communication between schools and security agencies. Community involvement can also help. Local residents often have information about unusual movements or criminal activity in their areas. Creating trusted channels through which such information can be shared may help authorities identify threats before they develop into attacks. The incident has also renewed debate about the safety of schools in Nigeria. Education can be severely disrupted when parents fear that children could be kidnapped. Some families may keep children at home, while teachers may refuse postings to insecure areas. Such disruptions can deepen Nigeria's already significant education challenges. The government has a responsibility to ensure that children can attend school safely. This requires cooperation between education authorities and security agencies, as well as investment in safe school infrastructure. The rescue also demonstrates the importance of providing assistance after victims are released. Medical examinations can identify physical injuries or other health problems, while psychological support can help children and teachers process their experiences. Returning to school may itself require careful planning so that victims do not face unnecessary pressure. The successful operation is an important development for the affected families and communities. However, it also serves as a reminder of the continuing risks faced by schools and communities in parts of Nigeria. Security agencies will need to maintain pressure on kidnapping networks and strengthen intelligence operations to prevent future abductions. For the rescued children and teachers, the priority is now recovery and reunion with their families. Their return ends 56 days of uncertainty but also begins the longer process of healing from the experience.
img: Rescued Oyo schoolchildren and teachers after their release following 56 days in captivity.
source: Federal Government of Nigeria; Nigerian Army

headline: Nigeria Records 882 Security Incidents in June as Violence Remains Widespread
summary: A security report recorded 882 security incidents and 792 deaths across Nigeria in June 2026. Borno recorded the highest number of fatalities, while armed groups remained responsible for a large share of deaths linked to violence.
fullStory: ABUJA — Nigeria recorded hundreds of security incidents and hundreds of deaths across the country in June, according to a monthly security assessment that highlighted the continuing economic and social consequences of violence. The report recorded 882 security incidents and 792 deaths across Nigeria's 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory during the month. Borno State recorded the highest number of fatalities, reflecting the continued security challenges associated with insurgency in the North-East. The report also recorded significant levels of violence in Zamfara, Plateau, Katsina, Lagos and the Federal Capital Territory. Non-state armed groups were responsible for a substantial proportion of the reported fatalities, while security forces also carried out hundreds of operations against armed groups. The figures demonstrate that insecurity remains a major national challenge despite ongoing military and law-enforcement operations. Nigeria's security problems vary considerably from region to region. The North-East continues to face threats from insurgent groups, while parts of the North-West have experienced banditry and mass kidnapping. The North-Central region has also suffered attacks linked to communal and farmer-herder tensions. In the South, security concerns include criminal violence, cult-related activity and other forms of organised crime. The economic consequences of insecurity are significant. Farmers may avoid cultivating land in areas considered dangerous, reducing agricultural output and affecting food supplies. Traders and transport operators can also face disruptions when roads become unsafe. Businesses operating in affected communities may reduce their activities or relocate, resulting in lost jobs and lower local investment. Rural communities are particularly vulnerable because agriculture is often their main source of income. When residents are forced to flee because of violence, they may lose access to farms, livestock and other productive assets. Displacement can therefore create long-term economic hardship even after the immediate security threat has declined. Education is also affected. Schools may close temporarily or permanently when communities become unsafe. Parents may keep children at home because they fear abduction or attacks while travelling to school. Prolonged disruption can contribute to learning losses and increase the number of children who are out of school. Health services can also suffer. Clinics and hospitals in insecure areas may struggle to retain staff or maintain supplies. Pregnant women, children and elderly people can face particular difficulties when movement becomes restricted. The report's findings highlight the need for a comprehensive approach to security. Military operations remain necessary against armed groups, but security responses also need to address the conditions that allow violence to continue. Intelligence gathering, community engagement, border security and effective policing can complement military action. Economic opportunities are another part of the solution. Young people without stable employment can become vulnerable to recruitment by criminal groups, particularly in communities where legitimate opportunities are limited. Investment in education, skills training and local businesses can help reduce those vulnerabilities. Strong institutions are also important. Effective investigation and prosecution can deter criminal activity by increasing the likelihood that perpetrators will be held accountable. Communities that lose confidence in the justice system may become less willing to cooperate with authorities. Security spending itself has economic implications. Government resources must be allocated to personnel, equipment, intelligence, infrastructure and welfare for security agencies. At the same time, large security expenditures can reduce the resources available for other public services if national revenues are limited. Policymakers therefore face the challenge of maintaining adequate security while also investing in the social and economic development needed to reduce the causes of instability. The June figures provide another indication of the scale of Nigeria's security problem. The number of incidents recorded across the country demonstrates that insecurity is not confined to a single region or type of threat. Different communities require different responses based on their circumstances. For citizens, the most important measure of success will be whether violence declines and communities become safe enough for people to work, farm, trade and send their children to school without fear. Sustained improvements in security could support economic activity and strengthen public confidence. Until then, the continuing incidence of violence will remain a major obstacle to Nigeria's broader development.
img: Nigerian security personnel conducting an operation as the country continues to confront widespread insecurity.

headline: Eight Killed in Suspected Terrorist Attack in Benue Community
summary: Eight people were killed and five others injured after armed assailants attacked a community in Otukpo Local Government Area of Benue State. Police described the incident as a suspected terrorist attack and said investigations were continuing.
fullStory: MAKURDI — Eight people have been killed and five others injured in a suspected terrorist attack on a community in Otukpo Local Government Area of Benue State. The Benue State Police Command confirmed the deaths and said security personnel had been deployed to the affected area to restore calm and prevent further violence. The victims were reported to include five adults and three children. The attack has renewed concerns over insecurity in rural communities across Benue, where residents have repeatedly faced deadly attacks, displacement and destruction of property. According to the police, the attackers used guerrilla-style tactics, striking the community before retreating into surrounding forest areas. Such tactics have made it difficult for security agencies to apprehend perpetrators immediately after attacks. The police commissioner visited the affected communities with other security personnel to assess the situation and coordinate efforts to restore order. Local residents also protested after the attack, with roads reportedly blocked as anger and frustration grew over the continuing violence. Security authorities worked with community members to reopen the affected routes and prevent the situation from escalating. Benue has experienced repeated episodes of violence involving armed groups and communal tensions. Rural communities are particularly vulnerable because they may have limited security presence and difficult terrain can make rapid intervention challenging. Attacks can also have consequences beyond the immediate loss of life. Farmers may abandon their fields, families may flee their homes and local markets can be disrupted. These effects can contribute to food insecurity and deepen economic hardship in affected communities. The latest incident also highlights the vulnerability of children during attacks on rural settlements. The deaths of three children in the Benue attack underline the need for stronger protection of civilians, particularly in communities where security threats have become persistent. The police said investigations were ongoing to determine the motive for the attack and whether it was connected to previous incidents in the area. Establishing the identity and motivation of the attackers will be important for preventing further violence and holding those responsible accountable. Security agencies face significant challenges when responding to attacks in remote communities. Poor roads, limited communication networks and difficult terrain can delay emergency responses. Intelligence gathering from local communities is therefore important, but residents may be reluctant to provide information when they fear retaliation. Building trust between communities and security agencies can improve the flow of information and help authorities identify threats before attacks occur. The continuing violence also raises questions about the protection of displaced people and the restoration of livelihoods after attacks. Families forced to leave their homes may require shelter, food, healthcare and other forms of assistance. Children who are displaced may also lose access to education. Government authorities and humanitarian organisations therefore need to consider both immediate relief and longer-term recovery. Preventing further attacks will require more than military operations. Community engagement, improved intelligence, economic opportunities and measures to address local disputes can all contribute to reducing insecurity. At the same time, security forces must be able to respond quickly to armed groups and protect civilians. The Benue attack adds to a wider pattern of insecurity affecting several parts of Nigeria. Continued violence can undermine confidence in government institutions and discourage economic activity. Farmers may reduce cultivation, businesses may close temporarily and families may relocate to safer areas. For residents of the affected community, the immediate concern is mourning the victims and ensuring that those injured receive treatment. The police have assured residents that efforts are being made to track the attackers and restore security. The incident nevertheless demonstrates the urgent need for stronger protection of vulnerable communities and effective action against armed groups operating in Nigeria's rural areas.
img: Security personnel at a community in Benue State following a deadly attack that claimed eight lives.

headline: FG Suspends Proposed WAEC, NECO Fee Increase After Public Concerns
summary: The Federal Government suspended its proposed increase in registration fees for the 2027 WAEC and NECO senior secondary examinations. The decision followed public concerns and will allow wider consultations with education stakeholders before a final decision is made.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Federal Government has suspended its proposed review of registration fees for the 2027 West African Senior School Certificate Examination and the National Examinations Council Senior School Certificate Examination. The Federal Ministry of Education announced the decision after concerns were raised by parents, students, education organisations and other members of the public over the proposed increase. The ministry said the letter communicating the fee adjustment, dated June 18, had been withdrawn to allow for a comprehensive review and broader consultations with relevant stakeholders. The proposed adjustment would have raised the registration fee to N50,000 per candidate, representing a substantial increase from the existing charge. The government said the review had initially been prompted by the rising cost of conducting credible national examinations. Examination bodies face increasing expenses in areas including logistics, security, printing, technology, quality assurance and the movement of examination materials across the country. Despite these challenges, the proposed increase generated considerable public concern because many Nigerian families are already struggling with the rising cost of education and household necessities. Parents and education stakeholders argued that a sharp increase in examination fees could place additional pressure on families and make secondary school certification more difficult for students from low-income households. The Federal Ministry of Education acknowledged the concerns and said the decision to suspend the proposal was intended to provide an opportunity for broader consultation. The ministry stressed that no adjustment would take effect until the consultation process had been completed and a final decision reached. The consultations are expected to involve examination bodies, state ministries of education, school proprietors and administrators, parents' associations, organised labour and other education stakeholders. The review highlights the continuing challenge of financing public examinations in Nigeria. WAEC and NECO examinations require extensive logistical arrangements because candidates are distributed across thousands of schools and examination centres. Security is also an important consideration, particularly in areas affected by insecurity. Examination materials must be transported and protected, while officials need to be deployed to centres throughout the country. Technology has also become increasingly important in the administration of examinations. Digital systems can improve registration, monitoring and examination management, but they require investment and maintenance. The cost of these services has increased alongside wider economic pressures. However, examination fees cannot be considered separately from the broader question of access to education. Secondary school students depend on WAEC and NECO certificates for admission to tertiary institutions, vocational training and employment opportunities. Making the examinations significantly more expensive could therefore have consequences beyond the immediate financial burden on families. The suspension gives the government an opportunity to examine alternatives. One possibility is to review the structure of examination financing and determine whether some costs can be reduced through improved efficiency or government support. Another is to consider targeted assistance for students from particularly vulnerable households. The government will also need to balance the financial needs of examination bodies with the principle of affordable access to education. The controversy demonstrates the importance of consultation before policies affecting millions of students and families are introduced. Education policies can have long-term consequences, particularly when they involve essential examinations. A transparent review process could help ensure that the eventual fee structure is financially sustainable while remaining accessible to students. For parents, the immediate suspension provides temporary relief and removes uncertainty over whether the higher fee would take effect as originally proposed. For WAEC and NECO, however, the financial pressures that prompted the review remain. The examination bodies will continue to face rising operational costs and will need to work with government and stakeholders to find sustainable solutions. The Federal Government's decision therefore represents a pause rather than the end of the debate. Further consultations will determine whether the proposed increase is revised, reduced or abandoned. The outcome will be closely watched by students, parents, teachers and education administrators across Nigeria.

headline: Nigeria Takes Greater Role in Humanitarian Response as UN Support Model Changes
summary: Nigeria is preparing to assume a greater role in coordinating its humanitarian response as the United Nations and international donors adjust their support model. The transition comes amid major needs linked to conflict, displacement, food insecurity and climate-related emergencies.
fullStory: ABUJA — Nigeria is preparing to take a greater leadership role in coordinating its humanitarian response as international donors and United Nations agencies adjust their approach to supporting the country's humanitarian needs. The development was discussed during a joint transition workshop involving the Nigerian government and the United Nations in Abuja. Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Alleviation Minister Bernard Doro said the transition should not be interpreted as an end to international assistance. Instead, he described it as a move toward greater government leadership supported by technical assistance from the United Nations system. Nigeria faces humanitarian challenges arising from conflict, displacement, food insecurity, climate shocks and health emergencies. Millions of people across the country require some form of humanitarian or social assistance, while several regions continue to experience insecurity and displacement. The humanitarian system has historically relied heavily on international donors and UN agencies to provide funding, coordination and technical support. Changes in global aid budgets and increasing donor fatigue have created pressure for countries to take greater responsibility for financing and coordinating their own humanitarian responses. The Nigerian government is therefore seeking to strengthen domestic institutions and increase the role of local and private-sector funding. One of the major concerns is food insecurity. Humanitarian officials estimate that tens of millions of Nigerians face significant risks related to hunger as international assistance becomes more constrained. Conflict and displacement have disrupted agriculture and livelihoods in parts of the country, while high food prices have increased pressure on vulnerable households. Climate-related disasters are another growing concern. Flooding and other extreme weather events can destroy homes, farmland and infrastructure, forcing communities to seek temporary assistance. Effective humanitarian planning requires coordination between federal agencies, state governments, local authorities, aid organisations and affected communities. The proposed transition is intended to strengthen that coordination and place the Nigerian government at the centre of the response. International agencies will continue to provide technical assistance, data and expertise where needed. Developing the country's 2027 humanitarian plan is expected to be an important part of the transition. A national plan can help identify priority areas, estimate funding requirements and coordinate the activities of government agencies and humanitarian organisations. Reliable data will be essential because humanitarian needs can change rapidly when conflict, flooding or disease outbreaks occur. Local organisations are also expected to play a larger role. Community-based groups often have direct knowledge of affected populations and can reach areas that larger organisations may find difficult to access. Strengthening local capacity could therefore improve the speed and effectiveness of humanitarian assistance. Private-sector participation could provide another source of funding. Nigerian businesses and philanthropic organisations can contribute resources, logistics and technical expertise to emergency responses. However, humanitarian assistance must remain focused on need and should not become dependent on commercial interests. The transition also places greater responsibility on government institutions. Effective coordination requires clear leadership, transparent funding and mechanisms for monitoring how assistance is distributed. Public confidence can be strengthened when affected communities can see how resources are allocated and when complaints can be addressed. The changing international funding environment makes this particularly important. Reduced donor contributions can create gaps in humanitarian programmes if domestic resources are not increased quickly enough. Nigeria will need to balance its ambition for greater ownership with the continuing need for international support. The UN has indicated that it will remain involved through technical assistance and coordination. The organisation's experience in humanitarian planning, food security, health and protection can help Nigeria strengthen its own systems. The transition therefore represents a change in roles rather than a complete withdrawal of international partners. For communities affected by conflict and displacement, the most important issue is whether assistance continues to arrive when it is needed. Humanitarian systems must be capable of responding quickly to emergencies while also addressing longer-term recovery and resilience. Nigeria's move toward greater government leadership could strengthen national ownership if it is supported by adequate resources and effective institutions. The coming period will test the country's ability to coordinate federal and state responses, mobilise domestic funding and work effectively with international partners. With millions of people facing humanitarian risks, strengthening the national response will remain an important priority.

headline: UNESCO Backs Nigeria's Zero-Rated Educational Content Initiative
summary: UNESCO has commended the Nigerian Communications Commission's initiative to provide zero-rated access to educational platforms and content. The programme is designed to reduce the digital learning gap by making online educational resources more accessible to students.
fullStory: ABUJA — UNESCO has welcomed an initiative by the Nigerian Communications Commission to provide zero-rated access to selected educational platforms and digital content, describing the programme as a potentially important step toward reducing the country's digital literacy gap. The endorsement came during a public consultation on the proposed framework in Abuja. The initiative seeks to allow students to access approved educational platforms without paying normal data charges. Supporters believe the approach could make online learning more affordable, particularly for students whose families struggle with the cost of internet data. Digital education has become an increasingly important part of Nigeria's education system. Universities, secondary schools and training institutions use online platforms to distribute learning materials, conduct research and provide supplementary instruction. Yet unequal access to the internet means that many students cannot take full advantage of these opportunities. The cost of data is one barrier, while poor network coverage and inadequate electricity supply create additional challenges. The zero-rated access programme is intended to address at least part of the affordability problem. By removing data charges for selected educational resources, students could spend more time accessing lessons, digital libraries, research materials and other academic content. UNESCO's support reflects the importance of digital inclusion to educational development. Digital tools can help students access information beyond the physical resources available in their schools. They can also provide opportunities for self-directed learning and skills development. However, digital education works best when students have appropriate devices and teachers are able to guide them. Smartphones can provide basic access to online resources, but computers and larger screens may be more suitable for extended study and specialised applications. The programme therefore needs to be supported by broader investments in digital infrastructure and literacy. The consultation involved representatives of government agencies, education stakeholders and technology organisations. Such consultations are important because the success of zero-rating depends on technical and regulatory arrangements. Telecommunications operators need to identify eligible traffic while ensuring that the system cannot easily be abused for unrelated purposes. Educational platforms also need to provide reliable and relevant content. The initiative is part of Nigeria's broader efforts to use technology to improve education. The country has a large youth population and an expanding digital economy, creating strong demand for digital skills. Students who gain access to quality online resources can improve their knowledge in science, technology, mathematics, languages and other subjects. Digital education can also support vocational and entrepreneurial training. For students in remote communities, online content can supplement the limited educational resources available locally. But connectivity remains uneven. Rural and underserved areas often have weaker telecommunications infrastructure, meaning that zero-rated services may have limited impact unless network coverage improves. Government and telecommunications companies will therefore need to continue investing in infrastructure. Teachers are another important part of the digital education equation. Professional development can help teachers use online resources effectively and integrate technology into classroom instruction. Without appropriate training, digital platforms may remain underused even when students can access them for free. The experience of the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated both the possibilities and limitations of digital education. School closures forced institutions to adopt remote-learning methods, but millions of students were unable to participate because they lacked internet access, devices or electricity. Reducing data costs could help address one of those barriers during future disruptions. The initiative also raises questions about the quality of educational content. Free access is valuable only when students can reach reliable and age-appropriate resources. Education authorities may therefore need to establish standards for platforms that qualify for zero-rated access. Monitoring will also be important to determine whether students are actually using the services and whether their learning outcomes improve. UNESCO's support gives the initiative international visibility, but implementation will ultimately determine its effectiveness. Nigeria will need cooperation among telecommunications companies, education authorities, technology providers, schools and development partners. The programme should also be accompanied by efforts to improve electricity, device availability and teacher training. If these challenges are addressed, zero-rated educational content could become a useful tool for expanding access to learning resources. For students from low-income households, removing data costs could make a meaningful difference. The initiative therefore represents an important step in Nigeria's effort to close the digital divide and ensure that technology contributes to better educational opportunities rather than creating another source of inequality.

headline: Nigeria's Economy Returns to Expansion as June PMI Rises Above 50 Points
summary: Nigeria's Purchasing Managers' Index rose to 50.1 points in June from 49.6 in May, indicating a return to expansion. The improvement was driven largely by agriculture, although households remained cautious about current economic conditions.
fullStory: ABUJA — Nigeria's economy returned to expansion in June as the Purchasing Managers' Index rose above the 50-point threshold, according to the Central Bank of Nigeria. The PMI increased to 50.1 points from 49.6 in May, indicating a modest improvement in business activity. A PMI reading above 50 generally indicates expansion, while a reading below 50 signals contraction. The June improvement was supported largely by activity in the agricultural sector, although weakness remained in some other parts of the economy. The figures provided a positive signal after the previous month's contraction, but they also highlighted the uneven nature of Nigeria's economic recovery. The CBN's report was accompanied by its Household Expectations Survey, which showed that many Nigerians remained pessimistic about prevailing economic conditions despite having a more positive outlook for the medium term. The difference between business activity and household sentiment illustrates the difficulty of translating macroeconomic improvements into immediate improvements in living standards. For households, food prices, transportation costs, housing expenses and other essential expenditures remain major concerns. Economic growth does not automatically mean that families experience higher purchasing power, particularly when inflation continues to affect consumer prices. Agriculture's contribution to the June expansion is significant because the sector remains a major source of employment and income in Nigeria. Increased agricultural activity can support food supply and rural incomes, although farmers continue to face challenges including insecurity, inadequate infrastructure, high input costs and limited access to finance. Industry and services showed weaker conditions, demonstrating that growth remains uneven across sectors. Manufacturing businesses continue to face difficulties related to energy costs, foreign exchange, financing and logistics. Service providers also remain sensitive to household purchasing power because weaker consumer demand can reduce spending on discretionary goods and services. The PMI is closely watched because it provides an early indication of economic activity before some broader national statistics become available. It captures information from businesses about production, orders and other operating conditions. A sustained increase in the index would provide stronger evidence of a broad-based recovery, while a decline could signal renewed pressure. The Household Expectations Survey provides another perspective by measuring how consumers view current and future economic conditions. Household confidence can influence spending and investment decisions. When consumers are uncertain about their incomes or future expenses, they may postpone major purchases and increase savings where possible. This can affect businesses that depend on consumer demand. Nigeria's economic reforms have sought to improve fiscal stability, foreign exchange conditions and investor confidence. The government has argued that reforms such as the removal of the petrol subsidy and changes to the foreign exchange system are necessary to create conditions for long-term growth. However, the reforms have also produced significant short-term adjustments for households and businesses. Fuel costs and transportation expenses remain important drivers of economic pressure. The government has therefore faced the challenge of maintaining reform momentum while introducing measures intended to protect vulnerable households. Social programmes, infrastructure investment and employment initiatives can help reduce the impact of economic adjustment if they are effectively targeted. The June PMI result suggests that some sectors are beginning to recover, but policymakers will need to watch the data closely. A single month of expansion does not establish a long-term trend. Continued growth would require improvements across agriculture, manufacturing and services as well as stronger consumer confidence. For businesses, greater certainty in the foreign exchange market and improved infrastructure could support investment. Reliable electricity and transportation networks can reduce operating costs and improve productivity. Access to affordable financing is also important for companies seeking to expand production and create jobs. For households, the key measure of recovery will be whether incomes rise faster than the cost of living. Stronger employment opportunities and lower inflation would provide more tangible benefits than improvements in economic indicators alone. The CBN's June data therefore present a mixed picture. The return to expansion is encouraging, but household pessimism demonstrates that many Nigerians have yet to feel a substantial improvement in their daily economic circumstances. Sustaining growth while improving living standards will remain a major challenge for policymakers in the months ahead.

headline: Nigeria Pushes Free Educational Internet Access to Bridge Digital Learning Gap
summary: The Nigerian Communications Commission continued consultations on a framework to provide students with free access to selected educational platforms and content. The initiative is intended to reduce the cost of digital learning and expand access to online educational resources.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Nigerian Communications Commission is consulting education and technology stakeholders on a framework designed to provide students with free access to selected educational platforms and digital learning content. The initiative is aimed at reducing the cost of internet access for students and helping more Nigerians benefit from online educational resources. Access to reliable internet has become increasingly important to education as schools, universities and training institutions incorporate digital materials into teaching and learning. However, the cost of data remains a barrier for many students, particularly those from low-income households. The proposed zero-rated access initiative would allow users to reach approved educational platforms without paying normal data charges. The approach is intended to encourage students to make greater use of online resources while reducing one of the financial barriers to digital education. The consultation involves stakeholders from the telecommunications, education and technology sectors. Participants are expected to examine how educational platforms can be identified, how access can be provided and how the system can be implemented without compromising network security or user privacy. Digital education can provide students with access to materials that may not be readily available in their schools. Online libraries, recorded lessons, examination preparation resources and interactive learning platforms can supplement classroom teaching. For students in areas where educational facilities are limited, digital resources can provide additional opportunities for learning. However, internet access alone cannot solve all of Nigeria's education challenges. Many communities continue to experience unreliable electricity, weak telecommunications coverage and shortages of digital devices. Students who do not have smartphones, computers or other suitable devices may still be unable to benefit fully from online education. The government and private-sector partners therefore face the broader challenge of improving digital infrastructure alongside affordability. Teachers also require training to use digital resources effectively. Providing free access to educational platforms is more useful when teachers can guide students toward reliable materials and incorporate them into lessons. Digital literacy programmes can help teachers and students develop the skills required to search for information, evaluate sources and use online tools responsibly. The initiative is also linked to broader efforts to improve learning outcomes through technology. Nigeria has a large young population and an expanding technology sector, making digital skills increasingly important for employment and economic participation. Students who gain access to online educational resources can develop skills in areas such as computing, science, mathematics, languages and entrepreneurship. The consultation process is important because telecommunications operators and education authorities must coordinate the technical requirements of the programme. Zero-rating educational services requires agreements on which platforms qualify and how traffic will be identified. The system must also prevent misuse while ensuring that legitimate educational content remains accessible. The initiative could also support students during periods when physical access to schools is disrupted. Online learning became particularly important during the COVID-19 pandemic, when school closures forced education systems to seek alternative ways of teaching. The experience demonstrated both the potential of digital education and the inequalities created when students lack reliable internet access. By reducing data costs, the proposed programme could make digital learning more accessible to a larger number of Nigerian students. Its success will depend on the range and quality of educational content available, the reliability of telecommunications networks and the ability of students to access suitable devices. Stakeholders will also need to monitor the programme to ensure that it achieves its educational objectives. Providing affordable digital access is an important part of modernising education, but it should complement rather than replace investment in teachers, classrooms, textbooks and other essential resources. Nigeria's effort to expand free access to educational platforms therefore represents one component of a broader digital education strategy. If effectively implemented, the initiative could help reduce the cost of online learning and give more students access to educational opportunities beyond the classroom.

headline: House of Representatives Moves to Consider Executive Proposal for State Police
summary: The House of Representatives withdrew its earlier constitutional amendment bill on state police and adopted an Executive-sponsored proposal for further consideration. The proposal is expected to undergo detailed scrutiny as lawmakers examine the structure, funding and operation of state police.
fullStory: ABUJA — The House of Representatives has withdrawn its earlier constitutional amendment bill seeking to establish state police and resolved to consider a similar proposal transmitted by the Executive. The decision marks a new stage in the long-running debate over whether Nigeria's security architecture should be decentralised to allow states to establish and operate their own police forces. The House considered the Executive-sponsored proposal during plenary and approved it for further legislative consideration. The bill was subsequently referred to the relevant committee responsible for constitutional review. Supporters of state police argue that the existing centralised policing structure makes it difficult to respond effectively to security threats that vary considerably from one part of Nigeria to another. Nigeria faces different security challenges across its regions, including kidnapping, banditry, communal violence, terrorism and attacks on rural communities. Proponents believe that police forces closer to communities could improve intelligence gathering and response times. The proposal has also generated debate about funding. Establishing state police would require substantial resources for recruitment, training, salaries, equipment, communications and infrastructure. Lawmakers will therefore need to examine how states would finance the proposed institutions and how their operations would be coordinated with the Nigeria Police Force and other federal security agencies. Concerns have also been raised about political interference. Critics of state police have argued that governors or other powerful political actors could attempt to use state-controlled security agencies against political opponents. Any constitutional framework would therefore need strong safeguards to protect the independence and professionalism of state police officers. Recruitment and training would also be important. A state police system would need officers who understand local communities while still meeting national professional standards. Clear rules would be required for investigations, arrests, use of force and cooperation with federal agencies. The proposal comes as security remains one of the most important concerns among Nigerians. Kidnapping and attacks on communities have continued to affect economic activity, education and movement in several parts of the country. Schools have also become targets for criminals, increasing pressure on authorities to improve security around educational institutions. Supporters of decentralised policing believe local authorities may be better positioned to identify emerging threats because they are closer to residents and community leaders. They argue that local knowledge could improve the ability of security agencies to identify criminal networks and prevent attacks. Opponents, however, remain concerned that multiple police structures could create confusion and competition between federal and state agencies. They also question whether poorer states would have sufficient resources to maintain effective police forces. The constitutional review process provides lawmakers with an opportunity to examine these concerns. Any amendment would require support through the constitutional procedure involving the National Assembly and state Houses of Assembly. Public debate is also expected to continue as the proposal moves through the legislative process. The discussion over state police has been ongoing in Nigeria for years, with successive governments and political leaders offering different positions on the issue. Recent security challenges have renewed demands for a new approach to policing and community protection. The effectiveness of any state police system would ultimately depend on its design and implementation. Proper funding, professional recruitment, accountability and cooperation with existing security agencies would be essential. Strong oversight would also be needed to prevent abuse of power. For communities facing insecurity, the debate is not simply constitutional or political. It concerns the ability of government to protect lives and property and allow people to conduct their daily activities without fear. The House's decision to consider the Executive proposal therefore represents an important development in Nigeria's continuing search for a more effective security system. Further legislative scrutiny will determine whether the proposal can address the country's security needs while maintaining professional standards and protecting citizens' rights.

headline: G7 Calls for Halt to Attacks in Sudan's El-Obeid and Wider Arms Embargo
summary: The G7 and the European Union called for an immediate end to attacks in El-Obeid, Sudan, amid the country's continuing war. They urged all sides to stop hostilities, allow humanitarian access and support efforts to expand the arms embargo beyond Darfur.
fullStory: BERLIN — The Group of Seven and the European Union called for an end to attacks in El-Obeid, Sudan, as international concern over the country's prolonged war and its impact on civilians continued to grow. In a joint statement, G7 foreign ministers and the European Union's foreign policy chief urged the Rapid Support Forces and allied armed groups to stop actions that could lead to further atrocities or endanger civilians in the city. They also called on all parties to the conflict, including the Sudanese army, to cease hostilities, allow humanitarian assistance to reach affected communities and engage in meaningful negotiations. Sudan's war has created one of the world's most serious humanitarian crises. Fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces has displaced millions of people and severely damaged infrastructure, food systems and public services. Communities have faced shortages of food, medicine and clean water, while humanitarian organisations have struggled to reach people trapped in conflict zones. El-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, has strategic importance because of its location and its links between different parts of Sudan. Fighting around the city has raised concerns about the safety of civilians and the possibility of further displacement. The G7 and EU urged the United Nations Security Council to consider expanding the existing arms embargo on Darfur to cover all of Sudan. The call reflects international concern that the continued flow of weapons and financial support is helping sustain the conflict. The statement also urged external actors to stop providing military and financial assistance to the warring parties. Sudan's conflict has attracted involvement from regional and international actors, making the search for a political settlement more complicated. External support can provide the resources required for combatants to continue fighting even when civilians face severe humanitarian consequences. The G7 and EU also backed United Nations efforts to reduce tensions and promote dialogue. International diplomacy has repeatedly sought to establish ceasefires and create conditions for negotiations, but previous agreements have frequently broken down. The continued fighting demonstrates the difficulty of reaching a lasting political settlement when the opposing forces remain committed to military objectives. Humanitarian access is one of the most urgent concerns. Aid organisations require safe routes to deliver food, medicine and other supplies to civilians affected by the war. Restrictions, insecurity and attacks on humanitarian personnel can prevent assistance from reaching communities at the time it is most needed. The international community has repeatedly called on all parties to respect international humanitarian law and protect civilians. The conflict has also created severe food insecurity. Displacement disrupts agriculture and trade, while damaged infrastructure makes it harder to move food between regions. Families forced to flee their homes may lose access to farms, livestock and other sources of income. Children are particularly vulnerable because prolonged displacement can interrupt education and increase exposure to disease and malnutrition. Health services have also been badly affected. Hospitals and clinics in conflict areas may lack medicines, electricity and medical staff. Disease outbreaks can become more difficult to control when communities are displaced and sanitation systems are damaged. International aid organisations have warned that continued fighting could deepen these problems. The G7 and EU said they supported accountability for violations and the protection of Sudan's unity and democratic aspirations. Accountability is a significant issue because allegations of atrocities and abuses have emerged throughout the conflict. Establishing responsibility for crimes can be difficult during an active war, but international officials have argued that perpetrators should not be allowed to act with impunity. Sudan's political future also remains uncertain. The conflict began in April 2023 after tensions between the army and the RSF escalated into open warfare. Efforts to establish a civilian-led political transition were derailed, and millions of Sudanese have since been displaced. A sustainable solution will ultimately require political negotiations as well as security arrangements. For civilians in El-Obeid and other conflict-affected areas, however, the immediate priority remains survival. Ending attacks, opening humanitarian corridors and restoring access to basic services are essential steps toward reducing suffering. The G7 and EU statement placed additional international pressure on the warring parties and their external supporters. Whether that pressure produces concrete changes will depend on the willingness of combatants and foreign actors to cooperate. The continuing crisis in Sudan remains one of Africa's most urgent humanitarian and security challenges, making international efforts to stop the fighting increasingly important.

headline: Nigeria Plans Poverty and Income Scorecard to Measure Impact of Economic Reforms
summary: The Federal Government plans to introduce a scorecard tracking poverty, income and inequality as it seeks clearer evidence of how economic reforms are affecting Nigerians. The proposed system will focus on multidimensional poverty, real income per capita and inequality.
fullStory: LAGOS — The Federal Government plans to introduce a new scorecard to track poverty, household income and inequality as it seeks to measure whether its economic reforms are improving living standards across Nigeria. The proposed system was announced by Finance Minister Taiwo Oyedele as the government attempts to demonstrate that reforms are translating into measurable benefits for citizens. The scorecard is expected to focus on three major indicators: reductions in multidimensional poverty, growth in real income per person and a reduction in inequality. The initiative reflects growing pressure on policymakers to demonstrate that improvements in government revenue, foreign-exchange liquidity and investor confidence are reaching ordinary households. Nigeria has undergone major economic reforms since 2023, including the removal of the petrol subsidy and changes to the foreign-exchange system. The government has argued that the reforms were necessary to improve public finances, attract investment and create a stronger foundation for long-term economic growth. However, the reforms also created significant short-term pressures. Fuel prices increased sharply following the removal of the subsidy, while changes in the foreign-exchange market contributed to periods of substantial naira depreciation. Higher transportation and import costs affected businesses and consumers, contributing to increased pressure on household budgets. For many Nigerians, the success of economic reforms is therefore judged less by financial-market indicators than by the cost of food, transportation, housing and other necessities. A formal scorecard could provide government and the public with a clearer way to track whether conditions are improving. Multidimensional poverty is broader than income alone because it can include access to education, healthcare, housing, sanitation, electricity and other essential services. Tracking these indicators can provide a more complete picture of living standards. Real income is another important measure because nominal increases in wages do not necessarily mean that households are better off if prices are rising faster. Measuring income after accounting for inflation can therefore provide a better indication of purchasing power. Inequality is also significant because economic growth can occur without benefiting all groups equally. If wealth and income gains are concentrated among a relatively small part of the population, many households may continue to experience economic hardship despite improvements in national economic indicators. The government's proposal comes amid continued debate over the effects of its reforms. Supporters argue that the changes have improved fiscal stability, reduced some distortions and created conditions for stronger investment. Critics have argued that the adjustment has imposed heavy costs on households and that the benefits have not yet been widely distributed. The proposed scorecard could provide a basis for evaluating both arguments through measurable indicators. The government has also emphasised the need for stronger revenue collection and more efficient public spending. Higher government revenue can provide resources for infrastructure, healthcare, education and social protection. However, increased revenue must be translated into effective public services if citizens are to experience meaningful improvements. Social protection programmes are another component of the reform debate. Vulnerable households can require assistance during periods of economic adjustment, particularly when food and transportation costs rise rapidly. Well-targeted programmes can help families cope while longer-term reforms take effect. The challenge is ensuring that support reaches the people who need it most. Nigeria's large population makes measuring economic welfare particularly important. National averages can conceal major differences between regions, urban and rural communities and different income groups. A useful scorecard would therefore need reliable data collected regularly and analysed across different parts of the country. Data quality will be critical to the success of the initiative. If measurements are inconsistent or incomplete, the scorecard may not provide an accurate picture of living conditions. Independent assessment and transparent publication of the results could help build public confidence. The initiative also reflects a broader shift toward measuring government performance through outcomes rather than policy announcements alone. Economic reforms can be judged not only by whether they are implemented but by whether they ultimately improve employment, income and access to basic services. For households struggling with high prices, these outcomes are more tangible than financial-market statistics. The proposed scorecard could therefore become an important tool for assessing Nigeria's economic direction. If poverty falls, real incomes rise and inequality declines, the government would have stronger evidence that its reforms are producing broader benefits. If the indicators fail to improve, policymakers would have clearer evidence that additional measures are needed. The success of the initiative will depend on credible data, regular reporting and a willingness to respond to the results. For Nigeria's citizens, the most important question remains whether economic growth and reform will eventually translate into improved living standards. The proposed scorecard is an attempt to answer that question with measurable evidence.
