headline: Nigeria Brings Home 1,490 Citizens From South Africa After Xenophobic Attacks
summary: Nigeria completed the voluntary evacuation of 1,490 citizens from South Africa following a series of xenophobic attacks against foreign nationals. The government said the evacuation was carried out after discussions with South African authorities over the safety of Nigerians living in the country.
fullStory: ABUJA — Nigeria has completed the voluntary evacuation of 1,490 of its citizens from South Africa following a series of xenophobic attacks against foreign nationals. The Nigerian government said the evacuation was undertaken after discussions with South African authorities over security concerns affecting Nigerians and other African migrants. The final evacuation flight brought 305 Nigerians home from Johannesburg, bringing the total number of returnees to 1,490. The evacuation followed growing concerns over attacks and threats against foreign nationals in South Africa. Nigerian officials have repeatedly condemned xenophobia and violence against Nigerians, stressing that the safety of citizens abroad remains a priority for the government. The development has renewed attention on the long-running problem of xenophobia in South Africa and its implications for relations between African countries. South Africa hosts large migrant communities from across the continent, including Nigerians, Zimbabweans, Mozambicans, Malawians, Ghanaians and other nationalities. Many migrants move to South Africa for employment, business, education and other opportunities. Some establish small businesses and become part of local communities. However, foreign nationals have periodically faced hostility, particularly during periods of economic hardship and high unemployment. Migrants are sometimes accused of taking jobs, competing with local businesses or contributing to crime. Government officials and rights organisations have repeatedly rejected collective blame and argued that criminal behaviour should be dealt with through the justice system rather than directed at entire nationalities. Xenophobic attacks can have serious consequences for both individuals and diplomatic relations. Businesses can be destroyed, families can be displaced and migrants can lose their livelihoods. Governments may then be forced to organise evacuations or emergency assistance for citizens who no longer feel safe. Nigeria and South Africa maintain important political and economic ties and are two of the continent's most influential countries. Their relationship includes trade, investment, diplomacy and cooperation through African institutions. Incidents involving the mistreatment of Nigerians in South Africa can therefore generate significant public and political reactions in Nigeria. The evacuation also highlights the vulnerability of migrants who may have lived in a country for many years but suddenly become targets because of their nationality. Returning home can provide immediate safety, but it can also create economic difficulties for people who lose businesses, employment or property. Some returnees may have to rebuild their lives after arriving in Nigeria. The Nigerian government has continued to call for peaceful coexistence and stronger protection for foreign nationals in South Africa. South African authorities have also condemned xenophobic violence and have a responsibility to prevent attacks and prosecute those responsible. Effective law enforcement is essential because failure to hold perpetrators accountable can encourage further violence. The underlying economic causes of xenophobia are more complicated. High unemployment, inequality and pressure on public services can create frustration within communities. Migrants can become convenient targets for grievances that are actually linked to deeper economic and social problems. Addressing those problems requires employment opportunities, effective public services and stronger community relations. The issue also has wider implications for African integration. The African Continental Free Trade Area and other regional initiatives seek to increase economic cooperation and movement across borders. Such ambitions depend partly on people being able to move safely between African countries. Persistent xenophobia can undermine confidence in those objectives and discourage trade, investment and migration. Nigeria's evacuation of its citizens therefore carries significance beyond the immediate security situation. It demonstrates the consequences that xenophobic violence can have for families, businesses and diplomatic relations. It also places pressure on African governments to strengthen mechanisms for protecting citizens living and working outside their home countries. For Nigerians who returned home, the immediate priority was safety. For those who remained in South Africa, the government will continue to face pressure to ensure that foreign nationals are protected from violence. The episode is another reminder that African solidarity requires more than diplomatic statements. It requires effective institutions capable of protecting people regardless of nationality and addressing the social and economic pressures that can fuel hostility toward migrants.
img: Nigerians returning home from South Africa after a government-assisted evacuation following xenophobic attacks.
source: Reuters; Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs

headline: Nigeria Launches $552 Million Education Programme to Reach 29 Million Children
summary: Nigeria launched a $552 million basic education programme backed by the World Bank and Global Partnership for Education. The HOPE-EDU initiative is expected to benefit about 29 million children, more than 500,000 teachers and thousands of schools and learning centres nationwide.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Federal Government has launched a $552 million basic education programme designed to improve learning outcomes, widen access to schooling and strengthen Nigeria's education system. The initiative, known as HOPE-EDU, is being co-financed by the World Bank and the Global Partnership for Education and is expected to reach millions of children across the country. President Bola Tinubu announced the programme during its launch in Abuja, describing education as an important part of the government's wider effort to improve human capital and reduce poverty. According to the government, HOPE-EDU is expected to directly benefit about 29 million children, more than 500,000 teachers, 65,000 public schools and 10,000 non-formal learning centres. The scale of the programme reflects the size of Nigeria's education challenge. The country has one of the world's largest populations of children and young people, creating enormous demand for classrooms, qualified teachers, learning materials and other educational resources. Improving access alone, however, is not enough. Education authorities also face the challenge of ensuring that children acquire foundational literacy, numeracy and other skills that will prepare them for further education and employment. Teacher development is therefore an important component of efforts to improve learning outcomes. More than half a million teachers are expected to benefit from the new programme, giving the initiative a potentially significant effect on classroom instruction. Teachers require continuous professional development to adapt to changing curricula, technology and teaching methods. Better training can also help teachers identify students who are struggling and provide appropriate support. Public schools across Nigeria face different challenges depending on their location. Schools in urban areas may have better access to facilities and teachers, while rural and remote communities can face shortages of classrooms, learning materials and qualified staff. A national programme must therefore address geographical disparities to ensure that investment reaches communities with the greatest needs. Non-formal learning centres are also included in the programme. These centres can provide educational opportunities to children and young people who are outside the conventional school system. Reaching such learners is important because exclusion from formal education can have long-term consequences for employment and economic participation. The programme forms part of a wider government strategy that also includes initiatives relating to poverty reduction, human capital development, community development, healthcare and social protection. The government has argued that these programmes are interconnected because education, health and household economic conditions influence one another. Children who experience poverty, poor nutrition or inadequate healthcare can face greater difficulty remaining in school and achieving strong learning outcomes. Financing is one of the major challenges facing Nigeria's education system. Public education budgets must compete with other national priorities, including healthcare, infrastructure and security. International development partners can provide additional funding and technical support, but long-term improvements will require sustained domestic commitment. Effective management of the funds will also be important. Large education programmes must have strong monitoring systems to ensure that resources reach schools, teachers and students as intended. Transparency and accountability can help build public confidence and allow policymakers to identify programmes that produce measurable improvements. Technology could also play a role in the programme's implementation. Digital learning tools can provide teachers and students with additional resources, although access to electricity, internet connectivity and appropriate devices remains uneven across Nigeria. Digital programmes must therefore be designed with the realities of rural and underserved communities in mind. The programme comes at a time when Nigeria is seeking to strengthen the skills of its young population. A better educated workforce could support economic growth, technological development and entrepreneurship. Education is particularly important as businesses increasingly demand digital, technical and problem-solving skills. For Nigeria's large youth population, access to quality education can determine future employment opportunities and economic mobility. The HOPE-EDU programme therefore represents a major investment in the country's human capital. Its success will depend on implementation, teacher participation, infrastructure and the government's ability to ensure that resources reach children across all regions. The launch marks an important step, but the real test will come in classrooms, where improved funding and policy must eventually translate into better teaching and stronger learning outcomes. With millions of children and hundreds of thousands of teachers targeted, the programme has the potential to become one of the country's most significant education interventions if it is implemented effectively and sustained over time.
source: Reuters; World Bank; Global Partnership for Education

headline: Global Oil Price Surge Threatens Hopes for Cheaper Petrol in Nigeria
summary: Renewed tensions around the Strait of Hormuz pushed global crude prices higher, reducing expectations that Nigerian motorists would see significant petrol price reductions. Rising international oil prices also created fresh challenges for households and businesses already facing high transportation and living costs.
fullStory: ABUJA — Hopes that petrol prices could fall significantly in Nigeria came under renewed pressure as international crude prices climbed amid heightened tensions around the Strait of Hormuz. The development created fresh uncertainty for Nigerian consumers and businesses, many of whom continue to face high transportation and operating costs. Global oil prices rose after renewed confrontation involving Iran and the United States increased concerns about the security of one of the world's most important oil-shipping routes. The Strait of Hormuz is a major channel through which large quantities of crude oil and petroleum products move to international markets. Any prolonged disruption in the area can therefore affect global supplies and push prices higher. For Nigeria, movements in international oil prices have a complicated effect. As a major crude-oil producer, the country can benefit from higher export prices because increased oil revenue can strengthen government finances and foreign-exchange earnings. However, Nigerians also remain exposed to higher global energy prices through the cost of imported products, transportation and other goods and services. The country's downstream petroleum market has changed significantly since the removal of the petrol subsidy. Fuel prices are now more closely connected to market conditions, crude prices, exchange rates and the cost of importing or producing refined petroleum products. This means international developments can eventually affect motorists and businesses even when the events occur thousands of kilometres away. Nigeria has also increased domestic refining capacity, most notably through the Dangote Petroleum Refinery. Greater domestic refining could reduce dependence on imported petrol and provide more control over local supply. However, the price of crude oil and other production costs remain important factors in determining the final price of petroleum products. Higher transportation costs can have a particularly wide impact because petrol and diesel are used throughout the Nigerian economy. Commercial transport operators spend more on fuel when prices rise, and those costs can be transferred to passengers through higher fares. Businesses also face increased expenses when transporting raw materials and finished products. Food prices can be affected because farmers, wholesalers and retailers all depend on transportation to move agricultural products from production areas to markets. The renewed increase in global crude prices therefore comes at a sensitive time for Nigeria. Households have already been dealing with elevated food and transportation expenses, while businesses are trying to manage operating costs and maintain demand. Lower petrol prices could provide relief by reducing transportation expenses, but international developments can make such reductions more difficult. The naira's exchange rate is another factor affecting petroleum pricing. Even when crude prices decline, movements in the currency can influence the local cost of petroleum products and other imported inputs. Greater exchange-rate stability could make domestic pricing more predictable for businesses and consumers. The government has continued to encourage investment in domestic refining and energy infrastructure as part of efforts to reduce Nigeria's vulnerability to international supply disruptions. More domestic refining could also create opportunities for the country to export refined products to other African markets. However, the benefits will depend on reliable crude supply, efficient infrastructure and competitive pricing. For ordinary Nigerians, the immediate concern remains the cost of living. Fuel prices affect not only motorists but almost every part of the economy because transportation is required to move people, food and goods. A sustained increase in fuel costs could therefore place additional pressure on inflation and household incomes. Policymakers will need to monitor global oil prices closely while balancing the benefits of stronger crude export earnings against the domestic impact of higher energy costs. The developments around the Strait of Hormuz demonstrate how vulnerable energy markets remain to geopolitical tensions. Nigeria's position as both an oil producer and a large energy-consuming economy means the country can experience both gains and pressures when global prices change. As international markets respond to the evolving situation in the Middle East, Nigerian consumers and businesses will continue to watch petrol prices closely. The prospect of cheaper fuel will depend not only on domestic refining and market reforms but also on developments in global crude markets and the stability of international energy supplies.

headline: Lagos Approves Harmonised 2026/2027 Academic Calendar for Public and Private Schools
summary: The Lagos State Government has approved a harmonised academic calendar for public and private primary and secondary schools for the 2026/2027 session. Schools are scheduled to resume on September 14, 2026, under a unified timetable covering terms, breaks and examinations.
fullStory: LAGOS — The Lagos State Government has approved and released a harmonised academic calendar for all public and private primary and secondary schools for the 2026/2027 academic session. The new timetable brings both public and private schools under a common academic schedule and is intended to improve coordination across the state's basic and secondary education system. The Commissioner for Basic and Secondary Education, Jamiu Tolani Alli-Balogun, announced the approved calendar following consultations with education stakeholders coordinated by the Office of Education Quality Assurance. The consultations provided an opportunity for stakeholders to review the proposed timetable and agree on the major dates for the coming academic year. Under the approved schedule, schools are expected to resume on Monday, September 14, 2026. The first term will run through December, followed by the Christmas and New Year break. A mid-term break is also included in the calendar to provide students and teachers with a period of rest during the term. The second term is scheduled to begin in January 2027, while the third term will run from May until the end of July. The government said the harmonised calendar would provide parents, teachers and students with a predictable timetable for the academic year. Having public and private schools follow a common schedule can also make it easier for parents with children attending different types of schools to plan family activities, holidays and other commitments. The policy is particularly relevant in Lagos because of the large number of public and private schools operating across the state. Private schools have traditionally had some flexibility in setting their academic calendars, although they remain subject to education regulations and quality-assurance requirements. A unified timetable is expected to improve consistency and make coordination between schools and government authorities easier. The calendar also provides dates for examinations and other important academic activities. Schools will be expected to organise their programmes within the approved framework while maintaining the instructional requirements established by the education authorities. The government stressed the importance of proper planning as schools prepare for the new academic session. Teachers and school administrators can use the timetable to organise lesson plans, assessments, staff activities and other academic responsibilities ahead of resumption. Parents can similarly prepare for school fees, uniforms, books, transportation and other requirements before the beginning of the session. The decision comes as education authorities across Nigeria continue to focus on improving learning outcomes and strengthening school administration. A predictable academic calendar is one part of effective education management because it helps schools plan instructional time and ensures that students receive adequate teaching throughout the year. The number of instructional days is also important. Schools need sufficient classroom time to cover the curriculum while allowing reasonable periods for holidays and teacher development. The Lagos calendar allocates a defined number of school days across the three terms, providing a framework for schools to organise their academic programmes. Stakeholder consultation was also an important part of the process. Education policies are more likely to be implemented effectively when school owners, teachers, parents and government officials understand the reasons behind them and have an opportunity to contribute to the planning process. The Office of Education Quality Assurance played a coordinating role in the consultations that preceded the approval of the calendar. The harmonisation also reflects the government's broader effort to strengthen oversight of private schools. Lagos has one of Nigeria's largest private-school sectors, serving a substantial number of pupils and students. Ensuring that private institutions meet minimum standards in teaching, facilities and administration remains an important responsibility for education authorities. A common calendar can support that oversight by providing a clear reference point for academic activities. For teachers, the new session will also bring opportunities and responsibilities associated with professional development. Schools are expected to prepare staff before students return, ensuring that teachers understand curriculum requirements and administrative procedures. Effective teacher preparation can contribute to smoother resumption and stronger classroom performance. For students, the new academic year will provide another opportunity to improve learning outcomes and prepare for examinations and further education. The success of the calendar will ultimately depend on compliance by schools and effective monitoring by the state government. Education officials will need to ensure that institutions follow the approved timetable while allowing appropriate consideration for exceptional circumstances where necessary. The harmonised calendar therefore represents an administrative step toward greater consistency in Lagos schools. By establishing a common timetable for public and private institutions, the state government aims to make academic planning easier for schools, teachers, students and parents. With September 14 set as the resumption date, schools and families now have a clear schedule around which to prepare for the 2026/2027 academic year.

headline: Wildfires, Drought and Storms Ravage Parts of Europe as Extreme Weather Intensifies
summary: Wildfires, drought and severe storms continued to affect parts of Europe as authorities battled the consequences of extreme weather. Spain recorded some of the most serious fires, with thousands of hectares burned and more than 1,000 people evacuated.
fullStory: MADRID — Several European countries continued to battle wildfires, drought and severe storms on July 17 as extreme weather created fresh challenges for emergency services, communities and infrastructure. Northeastern Spain was among the worst-affected areas, where a major wildfire had burned more than 12,000 hectares and forced more than 1,000 people to evacuate their homes. Military firefighters were deployed to assist local emergency services as authorities worked to contain the flames. Additional fires were reported near Madrid and Guadalajara, increasing pressure on firefighters and emergency personnel. Authorities remained particularly concerned about the combination of dry vegetation, high temperatures and strong winds, which can allow wildfires to spread rapidly. Spain has experienced increasingly difficult wildfire seasons in recent years, with prolonged periods of heat and drought leaving vegetation highly vulnerable to ignition. The situation was not limited to Spain. Greece remained on high alert for potential wildfires, while other parts of Europe dealt with the effects of drought and severe storms. France experienced significant drought conditions, while low water levels on Germany's Rhine River raised concerns for transport and other economic activities. Severe storms also caused deaths in parts of France and Germany, demonstrating the range of weather-related risks facing the continent. The simultaneous occurrence of heat, drought, fires and storms illustrated the increasingly complex nature of Europe's extreme-weather environment. Scientists have linked the growing frequency and intensity of some heat extremes to human-caused climate change, although individual weather events are influenced by several atmospheric and environmental factors. A warmer climate can increase the likelihood of extreme heat by raising the baseline temperatures from which heatwaves develop. Extreme heat also creates conditions that can worsen drought and increase wildfire risk. When rainfall remains below normal for extended periods, soil and vegetation lose moisture. Dry vegetation then becomes highly combustible, allowing fires to spread quickly once they begin. Emergency services must therefore prepare for the possibility of several fires occurring simultaneously across wide areas. The human cost of wildfires can be significant. Residents may be forced to leave their homes with little warning, while firefighters face dangerous conditions as they attempt to protect communities and infrastructure. Evacuations also place pressure on local authorities, which must provide temporary accommodation and essential services for displaced residents. Agriculture is another sector affected by drought and extreme heat. Farmers can experience reduced crop yields when water supplies decline or temperatures remain unusually high. Livestock can also suffer from heat stress, while reduced water availability can increase production costs. These effects can eventually influence food prices and agricultural supply chains. Transport systems can also be disrupted by extreme weather. Fires can close roads and rail lines, while storms can damage infrastructure and interrupt travel. Low water levels on major rivers can affect the movement of commercial vessels and increase transportation costs. The economic consequences can extend beyond the immediately affected areas. Businesses may face losses when employees cannot reach workplaces or when supply chains are disrupted. Insurance companies can also face increased claims following major fires and storms. European authorities have increasingly invested in early-warning systems and emergency preparedness to reduce the impact of extreme weather. Satellite monitoring, weather forecasting and rapid communication can help authorities identify dangerous conditions before disasters escalate. Public warnings are particularly important because residents may need to evacuate quickly when fires approach populated areas. Urban planning is also becoming an important part of climate adaptation. Cities can reduce heat exposure by expanding green spaces, planting trees and improving access to shaded areas. Buildings can be designed or renovated to remain cooler during extreme temperatures. Rural areas require measures to manage vegetation and reduce the risk of uncontrolled fires. The European experience also carries lessons for African countries, many of which face increasing heat, drought and flooding but have fewer resources for disaster response. Strengthening early-warning systems, emergency services and climate-resilient infrastructure can help reduce the impact of future disasters. International cooperation is important because climate-related risks can affect food supplies, energy markets and migration across borders. The events of July 17 demonstrated that extreme weather can produce several simultaneous emergencies. While temperatures were beginning to decline in some parts of Europe, the effects of the preceding heatwave remained visible through wildfires, drought and stressed infrastructure. Authorities continued monitoring conditions closely as forecasts indicated that some areas could experience renewed high temperatures. The continuing crisis reinforced the importance of both immediate disaster preparedness and long-term climate adaptation. Communities need effective emergency systems to respond when extreme events occur, while governments must invest in infrastructure and environmental management capable of coping with a changing climate. For the people affected by the fires and storms, however, the immediate priority remained safety, evacuation and the protection of homes and livelihoods.

headline: Nigeria, Ghana Move to Deepen Economic Cooperation as West Africa Seeks Stronger Trade Links
summary: Nigeria and Ghana continued discussions on strengthening economic cooperation and trade as West African countries seek to improve regional integration. The two countries are among the region's largest economies and have significant commercial ties.
fullStory: FREETOWN — Nigeria and Ghana continued discussions on strengthening economic cooperation and regional trade as West African countries seek to deepen integration and improve commercial links between their economies. The discussions took place on the sidelines of the ECOWAS Mid-Year Summit in Freetown, Sierra Leone, where regional leaders considered issues affecting economic development and cooperation. Nigeria and Ghana maintain extensive commercial relationships, with businesses from both countries operating across sectors including banking, telecommunications, manufacturing, retail and services. Their economic relationship makes cooperation between Abuja and Accra important to the wider West African market. Regional integration has remained a major objective of ECOWAS, which seeks to facilitate the movement of people, goods and services among member states. Removing unnecessary barriers to trade can help businesses reach larger markets and reduce the cost of moving products across borders. However, traders and companies operating in West Africa continue to face challenges involving customs procedures, border delays, infrastructure and differences in national regulations. These difficulties can increase the cost of doing business and reduce the competitiveness of regional companies. Nigeria and Ghana have both supported efforts to improve trade within Africa through the African Continental Free Trade Area. The agreement seeks to create a larger single market for goods and services by reducing tariffs and addressing other barriers to trade. A successful continental market could provide African businesses with access to hundreds of millions of consumers and encourage investment in manufacturing and other productive sectors. Nigeria's large population makes it one of the most important markets in Africa, while Ghana has developed a significant commercial and financial sector. Greater cooperation between the two countries could therefore create opportunities for companies seeking to expand across West Africa. Financial services are one area where Nigerian and Ghanaian companies already have strong links. Banks and other financial institutions from both countries operate across the region, supporting trade and investment. Cross-border payments and financial technology could also help make regional commerce easier by reducing the difficulties associated with transferring money between countries. Infrastructure remains another major requirement for stronger regional trade. Good roads, railways, ports and border facilities are necessary for businesses to move goods efficiently. Poor transport infrastructure can make locally produced goods more expensive and discourage companies from expanding into neighbouring markets. Investment in regional infrastructure could therefore provide long-term economic benefits. Energy cooperation is also important. West African economies require reliable electricity to support manufacturing, commerce and digital services. Regional electricity markets and cross-border energy projects can help countries manage supply shortages and improve reliability. Businesses benefit when they can plan production without frequent disruptions. Agriculture provides another opportunity for cooperation. Nigeria and Ghana both have large agricultural sectors and significant food markets. Better trade links could allow agricultural products to move more efficiently between countries and help producers access larger consumer markets. At the same time, governments need to ensure that trade policies support domestic production and do not create unnecessary distortions. Small businesses are particularly important to regional commerce. Many traders and entrepreneurs operate across borders, buying and selling goods in neighbouring countries. Simplifying customs procedures and improving border facilities could reduce the costs faced by these businesses. Digital platforms can also help small companies reach customers outside their home markets. Regional economic cooperation has become increasingly important as African countries seek to reduce dependence on overseas markets. Expanding trade within Africa can help countries diversify their economies and create stronger regional supply chains. Manufacturing companies, for example, can source raw materials from one African country, produce goods in another and sell them across the continent. Such supply chains can create employment and support industrial development. Nevertheless, regional integration requires political commitment. Governments must agree on common standards and ensure that national policies do not undermine regional agreements. Sudden border restrictions or changes in trade regulations can create uncertainty for businesses and disrupt supply chains. Consistent policies are therefore important for building investor confidence. Nigeria and Ghana have historically played important roles in ECOWAS and have often supported regional initiatives. Their cooperation can influence the direction of economic integration across West Africa. Stronger bilateral ties could also encourage other countries to deepen their commercial relationships. For businesses, the potential benefits of greater regional integration include larger markets, lower trade costs and more opportunities for investment. For consumers, increased competition can provide greater choice and potentially lower prices. However, governments must also address concerns about local industries and ensure that integration produces broad-based benefits. The discussions in Freetown therefore form part of a wider effort to strengthen West African economic cooperation. Nigeria and Ghana will remain important partners in that process because of their economic size and regional influence. Continued work on trade facilitation, infrastructure, finance and investment could help transform political commitments to integration into practical opportunities for businesses and citizens. As African countries pursue the goals of the African Continental Free Trade Area, stronger cooperation between major economies such as Nigeria and Ghana will remain essential. The success of regional integration will ultimately depend on whether businesses can move goods, services and capital more easily across borders and whether ordinary citizens can benefit from the economic opportunities created by a larger African market.

headline: Nigeria, Ghana Seek Stronger African Response to Afrophobic Attacks
summary: Nigeria and Ghana agreed to work together to address rising Afrophobic attacks against African nationals and seek greater continental action through the African Union. The two countries condemned xenophobia and called for stronger measures to protect migrants and promote peaceful coexistence.
fullStory: FREETOWN — Nigeria and Ghana have agreed to strengthen cooperation in responding to attacks and protests targeting African nationals, as concerns over xenophobia and Afrophobia continue to affect relations among countries on the continent. The agreement followed a bilateral meeting between Nigeria's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Sola Enikanolaiye, and Ghana's Foreign Affairs Minister, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, on the sidelines of the ECOWAS Mid-Year Summit in Freetown, Sierra Leone. The two ministers expressed concern over recent protests and attacks directed at African nationals in South Africa. They condemned xenophobia, Afrophobia, intolerance and violence, warning that such actions undermine African unity, regional integration and the free movement of people across the continent. Nigeria and Ghana agreed to seek the inclusion of the issue on the agenda of the next African Union Summit. The two countries also said they would work with other African states to promote stronger continental mechanisms for monitoring, early warning and preventive diplomacy. The initiative comes amid renewed concern about the safety of foreign nationals in South Africa. African migrants have faced attacks and threats in different parts of the country, with some incidents involving the destruction of businesses and the displacement of families. The developments have attracted attention from governments whose citizens live and work in South Africa. Nigeria has been particularly vocal about the protection of its nationals. Thousands of Nigerians live and operate businesses in South Africa, making the safety of Nigerian citizens an important issue in relations between Abuja and Pretoria. Previous episodes of xenophobic violence have led to diplomatic protests and, in some cases, voluntary evacuations of Nigerians who feared for their safety. Ghana also has citizens living and working in South Africa and has expressed concern over attacks against African migrants. The two countries argued that criminal activity by individuals should be dealt with through the justice system rather than used as a justification for collective punishment of entire nationalities. They stressed that innocent and law-abiding migrants should not be subjected to mob attacks because of the actions of individuals. The ministers linked the issue to the broader objectives of Pan-Africanism and the African Continental Free Trade Area. Greater movement of people, goods and services is central to Africa's plans for deeper economic integration. Persistent hostility toward migrants could undermine those ambitions by creating fear among people who travel across borders for employment, trade and investment. Nigeria and Ghana therefore called for coordinated action that addresses both immediate security concerns and the underlying causes of hostility toward migrants. Economic hardship and unemployment can contribute to resentment against foreigners, particularly when communities believe migrants are competing for jobs or business opportunities. The ministers' position was that such concerns should be addressed through lawful policies and economic development rather than violence. Stronger regional diplomacy could help governments respond more quickly when tensions begin to develop. Early-warning systems could identify emerging threats, while preventive diplomacy could allow governments to engage communities before disputes escalate into violence. Better communication between countries could also help protect citizens when incidents occur. The issue is particularly significant for West Africa, where regional integration has encouraged citizens to move between countries for work, education and business. Nigeria and Ghana have long maintained close political, economic and cultural relations, and their cooperation on the issue reflects a shared interest in protecting African citizens across borders. The countries also reaffirmed their commitment to working through ECOWAS, the African Union and other multilateral institutions. Their cooperation comes at a time when African regional organisations are facing several challenges, including security threats, political transitions and economic pressures. Maintaining solidarity on issues affecting African citizens remains an important part of the continent's integration agenda. South Africa, for its part, has repeatedly condemned xenophobic violence and said that criminals should be prosecuted under the law. The challenge for its authorities is to ensure that those commitments translate into effective protection for foreign nationals and accountability for perpetrators. Preventing attacks will also require addressing misinformation and inflammatory rhetoric that can encourage hostility toward migrant communities. For Nigeria and Ghana, the next step will be turning their diplomatic agreement into concrete action at the continental level. Placing Afrophobia on the African Union agenda could create an opportunity for governments to develop common responses and strengthen existing mechanisms for protecting migrants. The issue also presents an opportunity for African countries to reaffirm the principle that citizens should be able to move and pursue legitimate economic opportunities without fear of violence because of their nationality. The agreement between Nigeria and Ghana therefore carries significance beyond their bilateral relationship. It reflects a wider debate about the future of African integration and the treatment of Africans living outside their countries of origin. As the continent seeks greater economic cooperation and freer movement, governments will face increasing pressure to ensure that migration does not become a source of violence or division. Nigeria and Ghana's call for continental action represents an effort to confront that challenge through diplomacy, cooperation and stronger regional institutions.

headline: Oyo Makes Birth Certificates, NIN Requirements for School Enrolment
summary: Oyo State has made birth certificates and National Identification Numbers requirements for school enrolment as the state expands the digital management of education records. The Ministry of Education said the initiative is being implemented with NIMC to improve student identification and record keeping.
fullStory: IBADAN — The Oyo State Ministry of Education has made birth certificates and National Identification Numbers requirements for school enrolment as the state continues efforts to digitise education records and strengthen the identification of pupils and students. The Permanent Secretary of the ministry, Oyinloye Bamidele, disclosed the policy while discussing school enrolment and digital identity in Ibadan. She said the initiative was being implemented in collaboration with the National Identity Management Commission and was aligned with the Federal Government's broader digital identity programme. According to the ministry, enrolment records in Oyo schools are now being digitised and stored in a central database, replacing a largely paper-based system. The move is expected to make it easier for education authorities to maintain accurate records and manage information about pupils and students across the state. Bamidele said the digitisation of education records was necessary because schools were operating in an increasingly digital environment. Once a pupil or student is registered, the information can be entered into the central education database, allowing authorities to maintain records more efficiently. The policy also links school enrolment more closely with Nigeria's national identity system. Birth registration provides evidence of a child's identity and age, while the NIN provides a unique identification number. Connecting these records with education databases can help authorities improve planning and reduce problems associated with incomplete or duplicated student records. However, the ministry identified the lack of birth certificates among some children as one of the major challenges facing implementation. Some parents have not registered their children's births, while others may be unable to provide the documents during school admission. The situation can be particularly difficult for children whose parents are unavailable or who live in communities where access to registration services is limited. To address the problem, the ministry has been working with NIMC to conduct registration exercises in schools with large numbers of pupils and students who do not have the required identity documents. NIMC officials can visit schools with registration equipment and enrol eligible students in batches after arrangements have been made with school authorities. The ministry has also provided some flexibility concerning NIN registration. While the identification requirements are part of the enrolment process, students who do not yet have a NIN can be given time to obtain one before reaching terminal classes, when the number becomes particularly important for national examinations. The approach is intended to prevent children from being excluded from education simply because they have not completed the identity-registration process. The policy has reportedly been in place across Oyo State for about two years, with the government encouraging parents to obtain birth certificates and NINs for their children. Officials believe early registration will reduce difficulties later in a child's educational journey and improve the accuracy of government records. Digital education records can also provide benefits beyond enrolment. Accurate information about the number and distribution of pupils can help authorities plan for classrooms, teachers, learning materials and other resources. It can also improve monitoring of school attendance and student movement between institutions. However, the collection and storage of children's personal information raises important data-protection responsibilities. The Oyo State Ministry of Education said its education database was not open to the general public and that access was restricted to authorised education officials. Researchers can only obtain approved information for specified purposes, while sensitive student information remains protected. The issue of data security is becoming increasingly important as governments digitise public services. Education databases can contain names, dates of birth, identification numbers and other personal information about children. Strong safeguards are therefore necessary to prevent unauthorised access or misuse. The Oyo initiative reflects a broader effort in Nigeria to connect public services through digital identity systems. If properly implemented, integrated records could reduce the amount of paperwork required from parents and improve the ability of government agencies to plan services. But the success of the system will depend on ensuring that children in rural and underserved communities are not left behind. Parents who lack access to birth registration or NIN services may require assistance from government agencies. School-based registration programmes can help bridge that gap by bringing the services closer to families. The policy also highlights the connection between legal identity and access to public services. A birth certificate can be important for school admission, examinations and other official processes, while a NIN is increasingly used to establish identity across government and financial services. Ensuring that children are properly registered from an early age can therefore have long-term benefits. For Oyo State, the immediate objective is to create a more reliable and efficient education-record system while ensuring that students are not denied access because of documentation difficulties. Continued cooperation between the Ministry of Education, NIMC and other relevant agencies will be necessary to achieve that balance. The initiative represents another step toward the digitalisation of education administration in Nigeria. Its success will ultimately depend on how effectively the state combines improved record management with privacy protection and practical support for families who face difficulties obtaining identity documents.

headline: Nigerian Film Industry Expands International Reach as African Cinema Gains Wider Audience
summary: Nigeria's film industry continued to strengthen its international presence as African films reached wider audiences through cinemas and digital streaming platforms. The expansion is creating new opportunities for filmmakers while increasing global interest in African stories and culture.
fullStory: LAGOS — Nigeria's film industry continued to expand its international reach as African cinema attracted growing attention from audiences beyond the continent. Nigerian filmmakers have increasingly used cinemas, streaming platforms and international film festivals to distribute stories to viewers across Africa and other parts of the world. Nollywood remains one of Nigeria's most important creative industries, employing actors, directors, producers, writers, cinematographers and thousands of other professionals. Its growth has also created opportunities for businesses involved in production, distribution, marketing, fashion, music and event management. Digital streaming has changed the way Nigerian films reach audiences. Filmmakers are no longer dependent entirely on cinema releases or television broadcasters to reach viewers. Online platforms can make films available to audiences in different countries soon after release, allowing Nigerian productions to compete for international attention. The expansion of digital distribution has also increased the importance of production quality. International audiences have access to films from many countries, making competition for viewers stronger. Nigerian filmmakers have responded by investing in better cinematography, sound, visual effects and storytelling while continuing to draw on local culture and experiences. African stories have become increasingly attractive to global audiences because they offer perspectives that are often underrepresented in international entertainment. Nigerian films frequently explore family relationships, social change, ambition, traditional values and contemporary urban life. These themes can appeal to local audiences while also providing international viewers with an introduction to Nigerian society. The industry continues to face challenges, however. Financing remains difficult for many filmmakers, particularly independent producers who lack access to major investors. Producing a high-quality feature film can require substantial resources for locations, equipment, actors, post-production and marketing. Limited access to affordable financing can restrict the ability of emerging filmmakers to compete with larger productions. Piracy is another long-standing problem. Unauthorised distribution can reduce the revenue available to filmmakers and discourage investment in new productions. Strengthening copyright enforcement and improving legitimate access to films are therefore important for the industry's long-term growth. Professional development is also necessary. Film production requires specialised skills in directing, editing, sound engineering, visual effects and production management. Training institutions and industry organisations can help young professionals develop those skills and create a stronger workforce. International partnerships can provide additional opportunities for Nigerian filmmakers. Co-productions with foreign studios and participation in international festivals can expose Nigerian professionals to new production techniques and markets. Such partnerships can also provide access to financing and distribution networks that may otherwise be difficult to obtain. Nigerian cinema is also closely connected to the country's music and fashion industries. Musicians frequently appear in films or contribute soundtracks, while actors and entertainers influence fashion trends. Successful productions can therefore create commercial opportunities across several parts of the creative economy. The wider economic importance of Nollywood is significant because the industry generates employment for people both on and off screen. Production crews, makeup artists, costume designers, transport providers, caterers and other service providers benefit from film projects. As production increases, these indirect economic opportunities can also expand. International recognition can further support Nigeria's cultural influence. Films provide a way for audiences around the world to learn about Nigerian languages, traditions and contemporary life. Cultural visibility can strengthen Nigeria's soft power and contribute to tourism and international interest in the country. Nigerian filmmakers are increasingly conscious of the need to tell authentic stories while meeting international production standards. Balancing local identity with global appeal can be challenging, but successful productions demonstrate that the two objectives can coexist. The industry also continues to diversify its storytelling, with filmmakers exploring genres ranging from drama and comedy to crime, historical stories and social commentary. Women are playing an increasingly visible role in the industry as directors, producers, writers and executives. Their participation has expanded the range of stories being produced and created new opportunities for female professionals. Young filmmakers are also using digital tools to produce independent projects with smaller budgets. Social media has provided additional channels for promoting films and building audiences. As Nigeria's film industry grows, stakeholders continue to call for stronger infrastructure, better financing and effective intellectual-property protection. Government policies can support the industry by improving the business environment and ensuring that copyright laws are effectively enforced. Private investors and international partners can also contribute capital and technical expertise. The future of Nigerian cinema will depend on whether the industry can convert its growing global audience into sustainable revenue for filmmakers and other creative professionals. Greater international visibility is valuable, but long-term success requires strong business structures that allow creators to continue producing high-quality work. Nigeria's film industry remains an important part of the country's cultural identity and creative economy. Its continuing international expansion demonstrates the ability of African filmmakers to tell stories that resonate both at home and abroad. As distribution channels continue to evolve, Nigerian cinema is positioned to remain a significant contributor to Africa's growing influence in global entertainment.

headline: Nigeria's Political Parties Intensify Preparations Ahead of 2027 General Elections
summary: Political parties across Nigeria continued preparations for the 2027 general elections as the political environment became increasingly active. Parties and prospective candidates began strengthening structures, mobilising supporters and positioning themselves ahead of the electoral cycle.
fullStory: ABUJA — Political activity across Nigeria continued to intensify as political parties and prospective candidates strengthened their preparations ahead of the 2027 general elections. Parties have increasingly focused on building grassroots structures, mobilising supporters and positioning themselves for the next electoral cycle. The 2027 elections are expected to generate significant political activity across the country as parties begin identifying candidates and developing strategies for federal and state contests. Nigeria's political system is dominated by several parties, with the ruling All Progressives Congress and major opposition parties competing for influence at national and state levels. The period leading to an election is typically marked by consultations, defections, coalition discussions and internal party negotiations. Political actors have increasingly engaged with party leaders, traditional institutions, community organisations and other groups as they seek support ahead of the elections. Internal party organisation is particularly important because candidates must secure the backing of party structures before appearing on the ballot. The process can involve primaries, consultations and negotiations among competing interests. Disagreements over nominations have historically produced disputes within Nigerian political parties, sometimes resulting in litigation or defections. Electoral reforms and preparations by the Independent National Electoral Commission are also important to the political process. INEC is responsible for organising federal and state elections and maintaining the voters' register. The commission has continued to emphasise the importance of early preparation, accurate voter registration and compliance with electoral rules. Political parties and candidates are expected to meet deadlines established by the electoral authorities. Voter registration remains a key part of preparations because only eligible voters who are properly registered can participate in elections. Expanding access to registration and ensuring that voter information is accurate can help improve participation and reduce disputes. Political parties have also been encouraged to promote peaceful campaigns and discourage violence. Nigerian elections have historically been affected by political violence, hate speech and disputes over results. The conduct of political actors and their supporters will therefore be closely watched as the 2027 cycle approaches. Security agencies also have a role in protecting voters, candidates and electoral officials. The political environment is developing against the backdrop of Nigeria's economic challenges. Inflation and the high cost of living remain important concerns for voters, and economic performance is likely to influence political debates. Parties are expected to present policies addressing employment, food prices, infrastructure, healthcare and education. The credibility of those policy proposals will depend partly on whether voters believe they can realistically be implemented. Youth participation is another major issue. Nigeria has a large young population, making young voters an important constituency. Political parties face pressure to provide greater opportunities for young people to participate in decision-making and political leadership. Social media is also playing an increasingly important role in political communication. Candidates and parties can reach large audiences directly through digital platforms, but online campaigns also create risks involving misinformation and inflammatory content. Political organisations will need to balance effective communication with responsible use of social media. Women remain another important constituency, although their representation in elected political positions has historically been lower than their population share. Civil society groups have continued to call for greater participation of women in political parties and government. Increasing representation could broaden the range of perspectives involved in policy-making. Nigeria's electoral system also requires substantial financial resources. Campaigns, rallies, advertising and mobilisation can be expensive, raising concerns about the influence of money in politics. Electoral laws place limits on campaign spending and require parties and candidates to follow financial rules. Enforcement of those rules remains an important part of ensuring a level playing field. Political parties will also face the challenge of managing internal disagreements. Leadership disputes and disagreements over nominations can weaken party structures if they are not resolved through established mechanisms. Strong internal institutions can help parties manage competition without damaging their broader electoral prospects. For voters, the most important consideration will ultimately be the quality of candidates and policies presented during the campaign. Political competition can strengthen democracy when parties offer credible alternatives and respect electoral rules. It can become damaging when campaigns are dominated by personal attacks, misinformation or violence. The coming electoral cycle will therefore place responsibilities on both political parties and voters. Parties must present realistic programmes and encourage peaceful participation, while voters have the responsibility to evaluate candidates and participate in the electoral process. Nigeria's preparations for the 2027 elections are still developing, but political activity is already increasing. The months ahead are likely to bring further consultations, party realignments and candidate announcements. Maintaining a peaceful and credible electoral process will remain a central responsibility for political leaders, election officials, security agencies and citizens.
