headline: Education Stakeholders Call for Greater Private Investment to Strengthen Nigerian Schools
summary: Education stakeholders at the Nigeria Educational Supplies Summit 2026 in Lagos called for stronger public-private partnerships and increased investment to address challenges facing Nigeria's education sector. Participants also stressed teacher development, technology and practical reforms to build a more effective education system.
fullStory: LAGOS — Education stakeholders have called for stronger collaboration between government and the private sector to address the financial, infrastructural and operational challenges facing Nigeria's education system. The call was made at the Nigeria Educational Supplies Summit 2026 in Lagos, where policymakers, education administrators, development partners and private-sector representatives discussed ways to improve the quality and sustainability of education in the country. Participants argued that government alone cannot meet the growing demands of Nigeria's education sector. With a large and rapidly expanding school-age population, the country requires sustained investment in classrooms, learning materials, technology, teacher training and other educational infrastructure. Greater participation by private organisations could help provide additional resources while supporting innovation within the sector. Teacher development was identified as another important priority. Teachers remain central to educational outcomes, and improvements in infrastructure or technology cannot produce lasting results without a sufficiently trained and supported workforce. Continuous professional development can help teachers improve their classroom methods and adapt to changes in technology and curriculum requirements. Technology was also highlighted as an important tool for improving access to education. Digital learning platforms can provide students and teachers with additional educational materials while helping schools overcome some geographical limitations. However, stakeholders noted that technology must be supported by reliable electricity, internet connectivity, appropriate devices and training. Without these basic requirements, digital education programmes may not reach the communities that need them most. Nigeria's education sector continues to face substantial infrastructure challenges. Some schools lack adequate classrooms, laboratories, libraries, sanitation facilities and other basic resources. In rural communities, the problems can be more severe because schools may also struggle to attract and retain qualified teachers. Addressing these disparities is important for ensuring that children have comparable opportunities regardless of where they live. Private-sector involvement could support government efforts in several areas, including the supply of educational materials, construction and rehabilitation of facilities, technology deployment and vocational training. Businesses can also contribute through partnerships with schools and universities that provide students with practical skills relevant to the labour market. Such partnerships can help reduce the gap between education and employment. The summit also highlighted the importance of innovation. Nigeria's education system must prepare students for an economy increasingly influenced by technology and changing workplace requirements. Digital literacy, technical skills, problem-solving and entrepreneurship are becoming increasingly important alongside traditional academic knowledge. Technical and vocational education can provide alternative pathways for young people who want to develop practical skills. Strengthening vocational education could also help address unemployment by equipping students with skills that are directly applicable to different industries. Funding remains one of the biggest obstacles. Public education budgets must compete with other government priorities, including healthcare, infrastructure and security. Private investment can supplement public funding, but stakeholders stressed the need for transparent and sustainable partnerships. Investors need clear regulations and accountability, while government must ensure that partnerships serve public educational objectives rather than creating additional inequalities. Access and affordability are particularly important concerns. Education reforms should benefit children from low-income households as well as those in more prosperous communities. If new technologies and high-quality learning opportunities are concentrated in private schools or wealthy urban areas, existing inequalities could become wider. Public policy must therefore ensure that disadvantaged students remain a central part of education planning. The summit's emphasis on collaboration reflects the scale of the challenge facing Nigeria. Improving education requires cooperation between federal and state governments, school administrators, teachers, parents, development organisations and businesses. Each group has a role to play in providing resources, improving teaching and ensuring that reforms are implemented effectively. Accountability will also be necessary. Education investments need to produce measurable improvements in learning outcomes, attendance, teacher performance and school infrastructure. Regular monitoring can help identify programmes that are working and areas that require additional support. For Nigeria's young population, the quality of education will have long-term consequences for employment, economic growth and national development. A stronger education system can help young people acquire the knowledge and skills required to participate productively in the economy. It can also support innovation and entrepreneurship by giving students the foundation needed to develop new ideas and businesses. The discussions at NESS 2026 therefore placed education investment within the broader context of Nigeria's development. Stakeholders called for a sustained approach rather than short-term interventions, arguing that improvements in education require consistent funding, effective policy and long-term commitment. Stronger public-private partnerships could provide additional resources, but they must be carefully designed and monitored to ensure that the benefits reach schools and students. As Nigeria continues to confront educational challenges, investment in teachers, infrastructure, technology and practical skills will remain essential. The summit's message was clear: improving the country's education system will require government leadership, private-sector participation and sustained cooperation across the education community.

headline: FG, UNESCO Launch Mobile Learning Initiative to Strengthen Teachers Across Africa
summary: The Federal Government, UNESCO and the African Union launched a mobile-learning initiative designed to strengthen the professional development of teachers and school leaders, with particular attention to women educators. The programme seeks to use mobile technology to expand access to teacher training across Nigeria and other African countries.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Federal Government has partnered with UNESCO and the African Union to launch a mobile-learning initiative aimed at strengthening the professional development of teachers and school leaders across Africa. The programme, which was unveiled in Abuja on July 20, is designed to use mobile technology to make teacher training more accessible, particularly for women educators who may face barriers to conventional professional-development opportunities. The initiative is being implemented through the UNESCO International Institute for Capacity Building in Africa and the Pan African University under the Pan-African Virtual and Electronic University initiative. A three-day master training programme is scheduled to run from July 21 to July 23, bringing together education professionals to develop skills in the use of mobile-based learning tools. The programme is intended to support teachers in improving their classroom practice and adapting to the growing role of digital technology in education. Mobile learning has become increasingly important across Africa because mobile phones are often more accessible than computers and conventional learning facilities. In communities where schools have limited infrastructure or internet access, mobile technology can provide teachers with educational materials and opportunities for professional development without requiring them to travel long distances. The initiative's emphasis on female teachers is also significant because women make up a large proportion of the teaching workforce in many African countries. Providing them with flexible learning opportunities can help educators participate in training while managing professional and personal responsibilities. Organisers said the programme would expose teachers and school leaders to innovative approaches that can improve the quality of education. Digital learning can support teachers with lesson materials, professional resources and opportunities to exchange knowledge with colleagues. It can also help education authorities provide consistent training to teachers working in different locations. Nigeria faces major challenges in providing quality education to its large and rapidly growing population. The country has millions of pupils and students spread across urban and rural communities, creating significant demand for qualified teachers and adequate learning facilities. Teacher development is therefore an important part of efforts to improve educational outcomes. Technology alone, however, cannot solve the challenges facing schools. Reliable electricity, connectivity and access to appropriate devices remain necessary for digital learning to work effectively. Many schools, particularly in rural communities, continue to face infrastructure shortages. The mobile-learning initiative therefore forms part of a broader need to improve the digital foundations of African education systems. Another important issue is affordability. Teachers and students may have access to mobile phones but still struggle with the cost of data. Education programmes that rely on digital platforms must therefore consider how participants can access learning materials without facing prohibitive expenses. Public institutions and development partners can help address some of these barriers through subsidised access and targeted support. The programme also reflects a wider shift toward digital professional development. Traditional teacher-training programmes often require educators to travel to central locations and attend scheduled sessions. Mobile learning can provide greater flexibility by allowing participants to access materials from their schools or homes. This can reduce travel costs and make it easier for teachers in remote communities to participate. The involvement of UNESCO and the African Union gives the initiative a broader continental dimension. Education systems across Africa face different challenges, but many share concerns about teacher shortages, professional development, infrastructure and unequal access to educational resources. Regional cooperation can allow countries to exchange successful approaches and develop training programmes that can be adapted to local circumstances. The programme is also expected to contribute to the broader goals of improving digital literacy among educators. Teachers increasingly need to understand how to use technology not only for their own professional development but also in classroom instruction. Digital skills can help educators introduce students to online resources, research tools and other technologies that are becoming increasingly important in higher education and employment. For Nigeria, strengthening teachers is particularly important as the country seeks to improve learning outcomes and prepare young people for a changing economy. A well-trained teaching workforce can have an impact far beyond the classroom because teachers influence students' academic performance, digital skills and future career opportunities. The mobile-learning initiative therefore represents an investment in both teachers and the wider education system. Its long-term success will depend on sustained implementation, adequate funding and the ability to reach educators outside major urban centres. If those conditions are met, mobile technology could provide an effective way to expand professional development while reducing some of the geographical and logistical barriers that have traditionally limited teacher training. The launch in Abuja marks another step in efforts to modernise education through technology. By combining international cooperation with locally relevant teacher development, the programme aims to strengthen the capacity of educators and ultimately improve the quality of learning available to students across Nigeria and other African countries.
source: Federal Ministry of Education; UNESCO; African Union

headline: Nigeria's Economy Remains Under Pressure as Businesses Adjust to Reform Measures
summary: Nigerian businesses continued adjusting to economic reforms as companies faced high operating costs, currency pressures and changing market conditions. Businesses and policymakers remained focused on improving investment, production and economic stability.
fullStory: ABUJA — Nigerian businesses continued to adjust to the country's economic reforms as companies faced high operating costs, currency pressures and changing market conditions. The adjustments have affected businesses of different sizes, with companies reviewing their prices, supply chains and investment plans in response to changes in the wider economy. Nigeria has been implementing reforms intended to strengthen public finances, improve the foreign-exchange market and encourage private-sector investment. The changes have also produced significant short-term pressures for households and businesses. Companies that depend on imported machinery, raw materials or finished goods have been particularly affected by movements in the naira and higher import costs. Manufacturers have had to reassess production costs while retailers have adjusted prices to reflect changes in wholesale and transportation expenses. Small and medium-sized businesses face additional difficulties because they often have less access to affordable financing. Higher interest rates can increase the cost of working capital and make it harder for businesses to expand. Some companies have responded by reducing expenses, changing suppliers or postponing investment decisions. Others have sought to increase local sourcing in order to reduce exposure to foreign-exchange movements. The government has continued to argue that reforms are necessary to create a more sustainable economic environment. Before the reforms, Nigeria relied heavily on fuel subsidies and maintained a managed foreign-exchange system that created distortions and contributed to shortages of foreign currency. Removing the petrol subsidy reduced the government's direct fiscal burden but also increased transportation and living costs. The foreign-exchange reforms similarly aimed to create a more transparent market, although the transition produced substantial volatility. Inflation has remained one of the main concerns for Nigerian households. Higher food, transportation and housing costs have reduced purchasing power and increased pressure on family budgets. Businesses have also faced higher energy and logistics expenses, making it more expensive to produce and distribute goods. Improving domestic production is therefore important for reducing some of the pressures created by imported inputs and exchange-rate movements. Agriculture remains central to this effort. Nigeria has significant agricultural potential, but farmers continue to face challenges involving security, transportation, storage and access to finance. Increasing food production and improving supply chains could help reduce food-price pressures while creating employment in rural areas. Infrastructure is another important factor. Unreliable electricity and high energy costs have historically forced many Nigerian businesses to rely on diesel generators. This increases operating expenses and can make locally produced goods less competitive. Investment in electricity generation and distribution is therefore important for improving productivity. The government has also continued to encourage private investment in infrastructure and industry. Investors generally require predictable policies, access to foreign exchange and confidence that they can operate in a stable environment. Improving the regulatory system and reducing administrative barriers can help attract investment. Nigeria's large population provides a significant potential market, but businesses need sufficient purchasing power among consumers to take advantage of it. Economic growth must therefore translate into employment and income opportunities. The government has sought to support vulnerable households through social programmes and other interventions while continuing with its reform agenda. The effectiveness of these measures depends on their reach and implementation. Businesses are also watching government efforts to improve revenue collection and public spending. Stronger revenue could allow the government to invest more in infrastructure and public services without relying excessively on borrowing. However, businesses are concerned that poorly designed tax measures could increase costs at a time when many companies are already under pressure. Policymakers therefore face the challenge of expanding the tax base without discouraging investment or placing excessive burdens on productive activity. The banking sector remains another important part of the adjustment process. Banks provide financing to businesses and households, but high interest rates can limit demand for loans. Financial institutions must balance the need to support economic activity with the need to manage credit risks. Greater access to affordable finance would help smaller companies invest in equipment, technology and expansion. Digital finance is also becoming increasingly important. Mobile payments and online banking services are expanding access to financial services and making it easier for businesses to receive payments and manage transactions. Technology companies are creating new opportunities in payments, logistics and commerce, although the sector also faces regulatory and infrastructure challenges. Nigeria's economic outlook will depend partly on whether reforms succeed in improving productivity and investment over time. Short-term adjustment costs can be significant, but policymakers argue that a more stable fiscal and monetary environment can create stronger foundations for long-term growth. Businesses, however, need conditions that allow them to survive the adjustment period and continue employing workers. The July 20 economic environment therefore remained one of transition. Companies continued to adapt their strategies while policymakers monitored inflation, exchange rates, investment and growth. The challenge for government is to maintain the reforms while reducing the pressures on households and businesses. For the private sector, the focus remains on finding ways to control costs, improve efficiency and take advantage of opportunities created by Nigeria's large domestic market. The success of the adjustment will ultimately be measured by whether it produces stronger economic growth, more employment and improved living standards.

source: Central Bank of Nigeria; National Bureau of Statistics

headline: Uganda Repatriates Citizens Fleeing Xenophobic Attacks in South Africa
summary: Uganda repatriated citizens who had fled South Africa amid a wave of xenophobic attacks against foreign nationals. The development renewed concerns about the safety of African migrants and the wider impact of xenophobic violence on relations between African countries.
fullStory: KAMPALA — Uganda repatriated citizens who had fled South Africa amid a wave of xenophobic attacks, highlighting renewed concerns over violence against foreign nationals and the safety of African migrants living and working outside their home countries. Ugandan nationals were received in Kampala after leaving South Africa, where reports of attacks had prompted some migrants to seek assistance and return home. The repatriation brought renewed attention to a longstanding problem that has periodically strained South Africa's relationships with other African countries. Xenophobic violence in South Africa has frequently targeted migrants from other African nations, with attacks sometimes involving assaults, destruction of businesses and threats that force foreign nationals to leave affected communities. The latest developments were particularly significant because migration within Africa is common. People move across borders for employment, education, trade and other economic opportunities, and South Africa has attracted migrants from several countries because of the size of its economy and its comparatively developed commercial infrastructure. Uganda's decision to assist affected citizens reflected the responsibility governments face when nationals become vulnerable abroad. Repatriation can provide an immediate escape for people who no longer feel safe, although it does not address the underlying causes of xenophobic violence. South African authorities have repeatedly condemned attacks on foreign nationals and have said that crimes should be dealt with through the country's justice system rather than through collective punishment based on nationality. However, migrant communities and rights groups have continued to call for stronger preventive measures and faster action against perpetrators. Xenophobia in South Africa is often linked to economic frustration, particularly high unemployment and competition for jobs and business opportunities. Migrants can become convenient targets for anger over problems that have deeper structural causes. Rights organisations and researchers have warned against blaming foreigners for unemployment, crime or pressure on public services, arguing that such claims can fuel hostility and violence. The issue has implications for Nigeria as well. Nigerians form one of the larger African migrant communities in South Africa, with citizens involved in businesses and professional activities across the country. Previous incidents of xenophobic violence have generated strong reactions from Nigerian authorities and public concern over the safety of Nigerians living in South Africa. Abuja and Pretoria have generally sought to manage such disputes through diplomatic channels, but serious attacks can quickly create tension between the two countries. South Africa and Nigeria are among Africa's most influential economies and political powers. Their relationship extends to trade, investment, diplomacy and continental affairs, making stability between them important beyond bilateral concerns. Violence against migrants can damage that relationship when affected governments are forced to demand stronger protection for their citizens. The economic consequences of xenophobia can also be significant. Foreign-owned shops and other businesses may be attacked or forced to close, disrupting local commerce. Migrants who leave suddenly can lose their livelihoods, while communities can experience shortages of goods and services when businesses disappear. Rebuilding trust after attacks can also take considerable time. South Africa's government faces the difficult task of addressing legitimate concerns about unemployment, crime and public services without allowing those concerns to become justification for attacks on foreigners. Effective policing, prosecution and community engagement are essential to preventing violence. Authorities also need to counter misinformation and inflammatory claims that portray entire migrant communities as responsible for social problems. For Uganda, the immediate priority was helping its citizens return safely. The repatriation also demonstrated the wider regional consequences of xenophobic violence. When migrants are attacked, neighbouring governments may be forced to organise evacuations, provide emergency assistance and respond diplomatically. Such incidents can therefore affect relations between countries even when the violence occurs entirely within one state's territory. African governments and regional organisations have repeatedly promoted the principles of free movement, integration and African solidarity. Xenophobic attacks run against those objectives by creating fear among people who move between African countries in search of opportunities. Long-term solutions require both stronger law enforcement and attention to the economic and social conditions that allow anti-migrant sentiment to grow. For migrants already living in South Africa, however, the immediate concern is personal safety. The repatriation of Ugandan citizens underscored the seriousness of those fears and placed renewed pressure on South African authorities to protect foreign nationals and prevent further violence. The episode is also a reminder that xenophobia is not simply a domestic South African issue. It has consequences for the wider African community, bilateral relations and the continent's efforts to promote greater economic and social integration.

headline: Spain Crowned World Cup Champions After Narrow Victory Over Argentina
summary: Spain were crowned 2026 FIFA World Cup champions after defeating Argentina 1-0 in the final in New Jersey. The victory gave Spain another major international title and ended Argentina's campaign as defending champions.
fullStory: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY — Spain were crowned champions of the 2026 FIFA World Cup after defeating Argentina 1-0 in the final at the New York/New Jersey Stadium on July 19. The result gave Spain the tournament title after a closely contested final and brought the month-long competition to an end. Spain entered the final with an impressive tournament record and faced an Argentina side that had arrived as defending champions. Argentina had won the previous World Cup in Qatar in 2022 and were seeking to retain the trophy. The final brought together two of international football's strongest teams and attracted worldwide attention. Spain's victory was secured by a single goal in a match in which both teams had opportunities to influence the result. The Spanish side managed the game effectively and held on to its advantage through the closing stages. Argentina pushed for an equaliser but could not find a way through Spain's defence before the final whistle. The championship was another significant achievement for Spanish football, which has continued to develop a strong national-team structure built around technically gifted players and possession-based football. The victory also added another major international honour to Spain's football history. Argentina's defeat ended its attempt to become back-to-back World Cup champions. The Argentine team had carried the confidence of its 2022 triumph into the tournament, but ultimately fell short in the final. The match also marked the conclusion of a competition that had generated enormous interest across Africa, Europe, Asia, the Americas and other regions. The 2026 tournament was hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico, making it the first World Cup staged across three countries. The expanded tournament brought together 48 national teams, increasing the number of matches and giving more countries an opportunity to compete on football's biggest international stage. African teams were also closely followed throughout the competition. Supporters across the continent watched the performances of their national teams and followed the progress of African players representing both their countries and major clubs around the world. Nigeria's absence from the tournament was particularly significant for Nigerian football fans, who followed the competition despite the Super Eagles failing to qualify. The World Cup final therefore provided a major international sporting story for Nigerian audiences as well as football supporters worldwide. Beyond the result itself, the tournament generated substantial commercial activity. Host cities received visitors from different countries, while broadcasters, sponsors, hotels, restaurants and transportation businesses benefited from the influx of supporters. Football tournaments of this scale can create significant economic activity for host regions, although governments and organisers must also manage the costs associated with stadiums, security and transportation. The final in New Jersey brought together supporters from both countries and neutral fans who had travelled to watch the conclusion of the tournament. Celebrations followed the final whistle as Spanish supporters celebrated their country's latest world title. Argentina's players and supporters were left to reflect on a campaign that ended one step short of retaining the trophy. The conclusion of the World Cup also shifted attention toward the next cycle of international football. Players will return to their clubs, while national teams will begin preparing for future competitions and qualification campaigns. For Spain, the immediate period will be dominated by celebrations and recognition of a team that successfully completed the final stage of the tournament. For Argentina, the focus will turn toward rebuilding and maintaining competitiveness after another appearance on football's biggest stage. The 2026 World Cup final will remain one of the defining sporting events of the year. Spain's victory over Argentina provided a dramatic conclusion to a tournament watched by millions of people around the world and reinforced football's continuing ability to generate global attention. For supporters, the final marked the end of another World Cup chapter, while for the champions it began a period of celebration that will place the achievement among the most important moments in Spanish football history.
img: Spain's players celebrate with the FIFA World Cup trophy after defeating Argentina in the 2026 final at the New York/New Jersey Stadium.

headline: Extreme Heat Pushes European Cities to Strengthen Public Health Measures
summary: Several European countries continued to face dangerous heat as temperatures placed pressure on health services, transport systems and energy networks. Authorities urged residents to take precautions as extreme weather conditions persisted across parts of the continent.
fullStory: PARIS — Authorities in several European countries continued to strengthen public-health measures as an intense period of summer heat placed pressure on communities, infrastructure and energy systems across parts of the continent. High temperatures can pose serious risks to elderly people, children and individuals working outdoors, while prolonged heat can also increase the likelihood of wildfires and place additional demand on electricity networks. European governments have increasingly developed heat-warning systems as extreme temperatures become a recurring summer hazard. Weather services monitor temperatures and issue alerts when conditions reach levels considered dangerous to public health. Local authorities can respond by opening cooling centres, adjusting outdoor work arrangements and providing advice to vulnerable residents. Cities are particularly exposed to heat because buildings, roads and other surfaces absorb and retain solar energy. This can create an urban heat-island effect in which temperatures remain higher than in surrounding rural areas, especially overnight. Residents without access to air conditioning can therefore face prolonged exposure to high temperatures. Public-health officials advise people to remain hydrated, avoid strenuous activity during the hottest part of the day and check on elderly or vulnerable relatives and neighbours. Heat can contribute to dehydration, heat exhaustion and potentially fatal heatstroke. People with certain existing health conditions can also face increased risks during prolonged periods of extreme temperatures. Hospitals and emergency services may experience increased demand when heatwaves continue for several days. The economic effects can also be significant. Outdoor workers may need shorter shifts or additional breaks, reducing productivity in construction, agriculture and other sectors. Heat can also damage roads and rail infrastructure and cause equipment to operate less efficiently. Transport authorities in some countries have introduced speed restrictions or other measures when high temperatures threaten railway tracks. Electricity demand can rise sharply when households and businesses use air-conditioning and cooling systems. Power networks must therefore maintain sufficient capacity to meet peak demand. At the same time, high temperatures can reduce the efficiency of some electricity-generation technologies and affect water availability for power plants. The combination can increase pressure on national energy systems. Agriculture is another vulnerable sector. Heat and drought can reduce crop yields and increase the need for irrigation. Farmers may face higher production costs when water becomes scarce, while livestock can suffer from heat stress. Reduced agricultural output can eventually affect food prices, particularly when extreme weather affects several producing regions simultaneously. Wildfire risks also rise during hot and dry conditions. Vegetation becomes easier to ignite, while strong winds can cause fires to spread rapidly. Southern European countries have invested heavily in wildfire monitoring and emergency response after repeated destructive fires in recent years. Authorities use satellite imagery, aircraft, ground patrols and other technologies to identify and contain fires. Climate scientists have linked the increasing frequency and intensity of some heat extremes to human-caused climate change, although individual weather events are influenced by several factors. A warmer global climate increases the likelihood of record-breaking temperatures because the baseline from which heatwaves develop is higher. Governments are therefore facing both immediate emergency-response needs and longer-term adaptation challenges. Cities are exploring measures such as planting trees, creating shaded public spaces and improving building design to reduce heat exposure. Green spaces can help lower local temperatures while providing residents with areas where they can escape intense heat. Building standards can also be adjusted to improve ventilation and insulation. International cooperation is increasingly important because extreme heat is not limited to one country. Weather systems cross borders, while food, energy and financial markets are interconnected. A severe drought or heatwave in one region can affect commodity prices and supply chains elsewhere. European countries have therefore continued to share information and develop common approaches to disaster preparedness. For African countries, developments in Europe also offer lessons about preparing for extreme heat. Many African cities face rising temperatures but often have fewer resources for cooling, emergency services and resilient infrastructure. Expanding early-warning systems and public-health planning can help reduce the impact of future heat events. The continuing European heat emergency highlights the importance of preparation as extreme weather becomes a more prominent policy concern. Governments must protect vulnerable populations during immediate crises while investing in infrastructure and urban planning capable of coping with higher temperatures. Public awareness remains equally important because individual precautions can reduce health risks. As temperatures remain elevated across parts of Europe, authorities continue to monitor conditions closely and adjust their response according to the latest forecasts.

headline: Nigeria's Federal Government Steps Up Talks With States on Security and Economic Reforms
summary: The Federal Government continued consultations with state governments on security, economic reforms and development priorities. The discussions focused on closer coordination between Abuja and the states as authorities seek to address challenges affecting communities and businesses.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Federal Government continued consultations with state governments on security and economic priorities as authorities sought stronger coordination in addressing challenges affecting communities and businesses across Nigeria. Cooperation between the federal and state governments remains important because many of the country's major challenges require action at both levels of government. Security, infrastructure, economic development and social services are among the areas where responsibilities overlap. State governors have continued to call for closer cooperation with federal security agencies as communities in different parts of Nigeria face kidnapping, banditry and other forms of criminal activity. The federal government has maintained that security agencies are working to improve intelligence gathering and strengthen operations against armed groups. State authorities have also supported local security initiatives and provided logistical assistance to security personnel in some areas. Economic policy has been another major focus of federal-state discussions. Nigeria has been implementing significant reforms aimed at improving public finances, strengthening the foreign-exchange market and increasing domestic revenue. These measures have affected households and businesses, creating pressure on governments to provide targeted support while maintaining the broader reform programme. State governments are particularly important to economic development because they oversee many public services and infrastructure projects. Roads, schools, hospitals and local economic programmes are largely implemented at the state and local levels. Better coordination with Abuja can help ensure that federal programmes complement state initiatives rather than duplicating them. The discussions also come as governments face pressure to improve internally generated revenue. Many states have historically depended heavily on allocations from the federal government, limiting their ability to finance major development projects independently. Improving tax administration and expanding local economic activity could provide states with additional resources. However, higher revenue collection must be balanced against the need to avoid placing excessive burdens on households and businesses. Security remains closely connected to economic performance. In areas affected by violence, farmers may be unable to reach their fields, traders can lose access to markets and businesses may reduce operations. Improving security can therefore create conditions for greater economic activity and investment. The federal and state governments have also recognised the importance of protecting agricultural communities. Nigeria's food prices remain a major concern, and disruptions to farming can reduce supplies and increase costs. Security operations in rural areas are consequently important not only for public safety but also for food production. Infrastructure development is another area requiring cooperation. Federal and state governments frequently share responsibility for roads, transport systems and other public facilities. Poor infrastructure can increase the cost of moving goods and people, reducing economic opportunities. Investment in transport and energy infrastructure can therefore support businesses and improve access to markets. The government has also continued to encourage private-sector investment. Investors generally require predictable regulations, reliable infrastructure and a stable security environment. Cooperation between different levels of government can help create those conditions by reducing administrative uncertainty and improving project implementation. Public accountability remains important as well. Governments at both federal and state levels manage substantial public resources, making transparent budgeting and effective oversight essential. Citizens expect governments to demonstrate how funds are being used and whether promised projects are being completed. Stronger coordination should therefore be accompanied by clear responsibilities and measurable outcomes. Nigeria's federal structure means that disagreements between levels of government can sometimes slow policy implementation. Regular consultations can provide an avenue for resolving such disagreements and identifying areas where joint action is possible. Governors and federal officials can use these discussions to share information about local conditions and coordinate responses to national challenges. For communities, the value of federal-state cooperation ultimately depends on whether it produces tangible improvements. Better security, more reliable infrastructure, improved public services and stronger local economies are among the outcomes citizens expect from government. Discussions and agreements therefore need to be followed by implementation and monitoring. The continued engagement between Abuja and the states reflects the importance of collaboration in managing Nigeria's complex economic and security environment. No single level of government has all the resources or responsibilities required to address the country's challenges. Coordinated action can help make better use of available resources and ensure that national policies take account of conditions on the ground. As Nigeria continues its reform programme, cooperation between federal and state authorities will remain important to maintaining stability and supporting development.

source: Federal Government of Nigeria; Nigeria Governors' Forum

headline: CBN Keeps Interest Rate at 26.5% as Global Tensions Raise Inflation Risks
summary: The Central Bank of Nigeria retained its benchmark interest rate at 26.5% as policymakers assessed inflation and the potential economic effects of renewed conflict between the United States and Iran. The decision reflects the CBN's cautious approach as Nigeria continues efforts to stabilise prices and the wider economy.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Central Bank of Nigeria has retained its benchmark interest rate at 26.5%, maintaining a cautious monetary policy stance as policymakers assess inflationary pressures and the potential effects of renewed geopolitical tensions on the Nigerian economy. The decision was announced on July 21 following the CBN's monetary policy meeting. The central bank's decision comes at a time when Nigeria is continuing to manage the effects of economic reforms introduced over the past several years. Inflation, exchange-rate stability and the cost of imported goods remain important concerns for households and businesses. The renewed conflict between the United States and Iran has added another layer of uncertainty because developments in the Middle East can affect global oil prices, shipping costs and broader financial markets. Nigeria is particularly sensitive to movements in international oil prices because crude exports remain a major source of foreign-exchange earnings. Higher oil prices can increase government and export revenues when production is maintained, but they can also contribute to higher energy and transportation costs in the global economy. The CBN's decision to leave the policy rate unchanged indicates that policymakers considered the existing level appropriate for the current economic conditions. Interest rates influence borrowing costs across the economy. When rates remain high, loans can become more expensive for households and businesses, potentially reducing demand and investment. At the same time, tighter monetary conditions can help moderate inflationary pressures and support confidence in the currency. Nigerian businesses have faced significant increases in financing costs since the central bank began tightening monetary conditions. Companies that depend on bank credit may have to pay more to finance expansion, purchase equipment or maintain working capital. Small and medium-sized enterprises can be particularly affected because they often have fewer financing alternatives. The CBN must therefore balance the need to contain inflation with the need to support economic growth. The decision also comes amid efforts to improve the stability of the naira. Nigeria's foreign-exchange market has undergone major reforms, including the move toward a more market-determined exchange rate. The reforms have produced periods of significant volatility, but authorities have continued to seek greater stability through monetary measures and improved foreign-exchange liquidity. Exchange-rate movements are closely linked to inflation because Nigeria imports a large range of goods and industrial inputs. A weaker naira can increase the local cost of imported products, while greater currency stability can help businesses plan their expenses more accurately. The central bank has also continued to monitor external developments that could affect Nigeria's balance of payments. Oil exports, remittances, foreign investment and other sources of foreign exchange all influence the country's external position. Disruptions in international energy markets can therefore have both positive and negative consequences depending on their effect on oil prices and global demand. For Nigerian households, the most immediate economic concern remains the cost of living. Food, transportation, housing and other essential expenses have risen significantly in recent years. Monetary policy can influence inflation, but it cannot directly resolve supply-side problems such as inadequate transport infrastructure, high energy costs or disruptions to agricultural production. Government policies aimed at improving food supply and reducing production costs are therefore important complements to the CBN's monetary measures. The central bank's decision to hold the rate also provides financial institutions and businesses with some certainty about the immediate direction of monetary policy. Investors will continue to watch subsequent inflation data, exchange-rate movements and economic growth figures for indications of whether the policy stance will change at future meetings. The CBN will need to assess whether inflation is moving sufficiently toward its desired path before considering any significant reduction in interest rates. Global developments will remain another important factor. The conflict involving the United States and Iran has created uncertainty in energy markets and raised concerns about possible disruptions to major oil-shipping routes. A prolonged escalation could increase global energy prices and create additional inflationary pressure for countries that import fuel and other commodities. Nigeria's position as an oil producer could provide some protection through stronger export earnings, provided domestic production remains stable. The July 21 decision therefore reflects the CBN's effort to maintain monetary stability while the economy continues to adjust to domestic reforms and external shocks. Keeping the policy rate at 26.5% leaves the central bank with room to reassess conditions as new economic data becomes available. For businesses and consumers, the decision means borrowing conditions are likely to remain tight in the immediate term. For policymakers, the priority remains controlling inflation, supporting currency stability and ensuring that monetary conditions do not undermine the country's broader economic recovery.

headline: African Music Continues Its Global Rise as Nigerian Artists Expand International Reach
summary: Nigerian and other African musicians continued to strengthen their presence in international music markets, with Afrobeats remaining one of the continent's most visible cultural exports. The growth is creating new opportunities for artists, producers and businesses across Africa's entertainment industry.
fullStory: LAGOS — African music, led by Nigeria's increasingly influential Afrobeats scene, continues to expand its international reach as artists from the continent attract audiences beyond Africa and strengthen the commercial profile of the region's entertainment industry. Nigerian musicians have played a central role in the global growth of Afrobeats, with the genre increasingly appearing on international streaming platforms, concert stages, radio stations and major music charts. The development has created new opportunities not only for performers but also for producers, songwriters, managers, promoters and other professionals working within the entertainment sector. Nigeria's music industry has developed into an important cultural and economic export. Artists increasingly collaborate with musicians from Europe, North America and other parts of Africa, allowing African sounds to reach new audiences while creating opportunities for cross-border projects. International collaborations have also helped expose African artists to different markets and professional networks. Streaming services have played an important role in this expansion. Digital platforms allow musicians to distribute their work to listeners around the world without relying entirely on traditional record-label structures. A song released in Lagos can reach listeners in London, New York, Johannesburg or Paris almost immediately. This has lowered some of the barriers that previously limited African artists' international exposure. Social media has further accelerated the process. Short videos and fan-created content can introduce songs to audiences who may not previously have been familiar with African music. Successful online trends can translate into streams, concert bookings and commercial partnerships. Artists and record companies increasingly use digital platforms as part of their marketing strategies. Live performances have also become an important part of the global expansion of African music. Nigerian artists have performed at major festivals and venues outside Africa, while African music festivals have attracted international audiences. Touring provides artists with additional revenue while allowing them to build stronger relationships with fans in different countries. The industry's growth has also encouraged investment. Record labels, entertainment companies and technology businesses have increased their interest in African music because of the continent's large and youthful population. Nigeria alone has a huge domestic audience, while the Nigerian diaspora provides an additional international market. The combination of local demand and global interest has made the country's music industry increasingly attractive to investors. However, the expansion has not eliminated challenges. Artists and other creative professionals continue to face concerns about copyright protection, royalty collection, piracy and access to professional infrastructure. Ensuring that musicians receive appropriate compensation when their work is streamed or used commercially remains an important issue. Stronger intellectual-property systems can help creators benefit more directly from the growth of the industry. Access to finance is another challenge. Producing high-quality music videos, recording projects and international tours can require substantial investment. Established artists may have access to major sponsors and record companies, while emerging musicians often struggle to finance projects that could help them reach larger audiences. Developing stronger support systems for young creative professionals could therefore help broaden participation in the industry. African music's international success has also contributed to wider interest in African culture. Music can introduce international audiences to African languages, fashion, dance and visual arts. Nigerian artists in particular have helped make elements of local culture more visible in global entertainment markets. This cultural influence can support other creative industries, including film, fashion and digital content production. The Nigerian film industry has similarly developed a large international audience, creating opportunities for collaboration between musicians and filmmakers. Music can also contribute to tourism and the wider creative economy. International visitors attending concerts and festivals spend money on accommodation, transportation, food and other services. Cities that successfully develop entertainment hubs can therefore generate economic activity beyond ticket sales. Lagos has become one of the continent's major entertainment centres, attracting performers, audiences and industry professionals from different countries. The continued growth of African music nevertheless depends on the ability of the industry to build sustainable business structures. Artists need professional management, transparent contracts and effective royalty systems, while investors require confidence that intellectual property can be protected. Governments can contribute by improving infrastructure and creating regulatory environments that support creative businesses. For Nigerian musicians, the international rise of Afrobeats represents both an opportunity and a responsibility. Global audiences are becoming increasingly familiar with African sounds, but sustained success will require continued creativity and professional development. As artists explore new sounds and collaborate across borders, African music is likely to remain an important part of the global entertainment landscape. The industry's growth demonstrates the ability of African creative talent to compete internationally while maintaining strong connections to local culture.
