headline: Nigeria Targets Higher Gas Production as Government Seeks More Investment
summary: Nigeria is stepping up efforts to attract investment into its natural gas industry as authorities seek to increase production and expand the sector's contribution to the economy. The government says stronger gas development can improve energy supply, industrial activity and export earnings.
fullStory: ABUJA — Nigeria is intensifying efforts to attract investment into its natural gas industry as the government seeks to increase production, strengthen domestic energy supply and expand the sector's contribution to economic growth. Natural gas has become a central part of Nigeria's strategy to improve its energy security while generating additional revenue from one of the country's largest natural resources. Nigeria possesses some of Africa's largest proven natural gas reserves, but production and utilisation have historically been constrained by inadequate infrastructure, financing difficulties, pipeline vandalism and other operational challenges. The government has increasingly described gas as a transition fuel and an important component of the country's industrial development strategy. Greater availability of gas could support electricity generation and provide fuel for industries that currently face high energy costs. Manufacturing companies in Nigeria have long struggled with unreliable power supplies and expensive alternative energy sources. Expanding domestic gas production and improving distribution infrastructure could help power producers and industrial users obtain more reliable supplies. The development of gas-processing facilities and pipelines is therefore important to the government's wider economic agenda. Nigeria also sees opportunities to increase exports of liquefied natural gas and other gas-related products. The country's existing LNG industry has established Nigeria as an important supplier to international markets, but additional investment could increase the volume and range of products available for export. Higher gas exports would provide another source of foreign exchange at a time when the country continues to seek greater stability in its external finances. Investment remains a major requirement for achieving these objectives. Gas projects often require large amounts of capital and long development periods, while investors need confidence that regulations, taxes and commercial arrangements will remain predictable. Nigeria has introduced reforms intended to improve the investment environment in the petroleum sector, including changes under the Petroleum Industry Act. The government has also sought to encourage greater participation by indigenous companies and private investors. Security remains another important consideration. Gas and oil infrastructure in the Niger Delta has faced vandalism and theft, while operational disruptions can reduce production and increase costs. Protecting pipelines, processing facilities and other infrastructure is therefore essential to ensuring that new investments produce sustainable output. Government agencies and security forces have continued to work with operators to address these risks. Domestic gas consumption is also expected to grow as Nigeria expands electricity generation and industrial activity. Gas-fired power stations account for a substantial share of the country's electricity generation capacity, making dependable gas supplies important to the performance of the national grid. Shortages of gas can contribute to reduced power generation, while disruptions in electricity supply can affect businesses and households. Improving the reliability of the gas-to-power chain is consequently a major economic priority. The government has also promoted the development of compressed and liquefied natural gas as alternatives for transportation and other uses. Wider adoption of gas-powered vehicles could reduce dependence on petrol and provide consumers with additional fuel options, although infrastructure and affordability remain challenges. The expansion of gas use must also be balanced with environmental considerations. While natural gas generally produces fewer carbon emissions than coal and some other fossil fuels when burned, methane leaks during production and transportation can have significant climate impacts. Investors and regulators are therefore under increasing pressure to improve monitoring and reduce emissions across the gas value chain. For Nigeria, the immediate challenge is to convert its substantial reserves into reliable economic value. This requires investment in exploration, production, processing and transportation while ensuring that projects are commercially viable and environmentally responsible. If these conditions are achieved, increased gas production could support electricity generation, manufacturing, exports and government revenue. The government's renewed focus on gas reflects the sector's potential to contribute to Nigeria's economic diversification. Although crude oil remains the dominant part of the country's petroleum industry, gas could become an increasingly important source of industrial energy and export income. Continued reforms, infrastructure investment and stronger security will determine whether Nigeria can fully realise that potential.

headline: Nigeria and South Africa Move to Ease Tensions Over Attacks on Nigerians
summary: Nigeria and South Africa have agreed to reduce tensions following xenophobic attacks targeting Nigerian nationals in South Africa. Both countries said they would pursue legal action against perpetrators while working to strengthen protections for Nigerians and preserve bilateral relations.
fullStory: ABUJA — Nigeria and South Africa have agreed to take steps to ease diplomatic tensions following a series of attacks against Nigerian nationals in South Africa, with both governments pledging to pursue justice for victims and protect their longstanding bilateral relationship. The agreement followed talks in Abuja between Nigeria's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Sola Enikanolaiye, and South African International Relations Minister Ronald Lamola. The discussions focused on violence against foreign nationals, particularly Nigerians, and the resulting strain on relations between two of Africa's largest economies. Nigerian authorities said South Africa had assured them that people responsible for attacks on Nigerian nationals would be prosecuted. Nigeria is also compiling claims relating to property losses suffered by its citizens during the unrest, which could form the basis for future compensation discussions. The diplomatic engagement comes after months of anti-immigrant protests and attacks in several South African cities. Vigilante groups have targeted foreign nationals and, in some cases, looted migrant-owned businesses. Nigerian citizens have been among those affected, prompting calls from Abuja for stronger protection and accountability. Nigeria said approximately 1,490 of its citizens had been repatriated following the unrest. The number reflects the scale of concern among Nigerians living and working in South Africa and the willingness of some affected residents to return home rather than remain in areas where they felt unsafe. Nigerian officials have called for stronger preventive measures, including an early-warning system for attacks and increased police protection in areas considered vulnerable to violence. Such measures are intended to give authorities more time to respond when tensions rise and to reduce the risk of attacks against foreign-owned businesses and communities. South Africa, for its part, said it condemned xenophobia and rejected any suggestion that the recent violence was sponsored by the government. Lamola stressed that individuals accused of criminal activity should be dealt with through the legal system rather than through vigilante action. South African authorities have previously faced concerns over violence linked to anti-immigrant groups, which often accuse foreign nationals of contributing to unemployment, crime and pressure on public services. Nigerian officials have argued that criminal allegations against individual citizens should not be used to justify attacks against an entire nationality. The disagreement has been particularly sensitive because Nigeria and South Africa maintain extensive economic, political and people-to-people ties. Nigerian businesses operate in South Africa, while South African companies have significant investments in Nigeria. Both countries also play influential roles in continental diplomacy and regional economic affairs. A prolonged diplomatic dispute could therefore have consequences beyond the immediate issue of attacks on migrants. The latest talks were aimed at preventing the tensions from damaging those broader relations. Nigerian officials said both sides had agreed to lower the temperature of public statements and preserve the relationship built through decades of diplomatic cooperation. That commitment could help create room for further discussions on compensation, policing and the protection of foreign nationals. The talks also underline the importance of cooperation between governments when citizens are affected by violence outside their home countries. Consular authorities can help document cases, assist victims and coordinate repatriation, but long-term protection ultimately depends on effective law enforcement in the country where incidents occur. For Nigerians living in South Africa, the immediate concern remains safety and protection from further attacks. For South African authorities, demonstrating that perpetrators will face prosecution will be important to rebuilding confidence among affected communities. The latest diplomatic engagement does not resolve all of the disagreements between Abuja and Pretoria, but it provides a framework for addressing them through official channels rather than escalating public confrontation. Both governments now face the task of turning their commitments into practical measures that protect foreign nationals, address property losses and prevent further violence. The outcome will be closely watched because the relationship between Nigeria and South Africa remains important to wider African political and economic cooperation.
img: Nigerian and South African foreign ministers meeting in Abuja for diplomatic talks aimed at easing tensions between the two countries.

headline: Nigeria Destroys 2,819 Illicit Weapons in Security Crackdown
summary: Nigeria's arms control agency has destroyed 2,819 illicit, obsolete and decommissioned weapons as part of a government effort to reduce the proliferation of firearms linked to insecurity. The exercise comes as authorities intensify efforts to tackle armed violence and criminal activity across the country.
fullStory: ABUJA — Nigeria's arms control agency has destroyed 2,819 illicit, obsolete and decommissioned weapons in a renewed effort to reduce the proliferation of firearms and address the security challenges facing communities across the country. The destruction exercise was announced on July 30 as the Federal Government continued its broader campaign against illegal weapons and the criminal networks that use them. The government has identified the widespread availability of illicit firearms as one of the factors contributing to insecurity in several parts of Nigeria. Armed groups involved in banditry, kidnapping, communal violence and other forms of criminal activity frequently rely on illegally acquired weapons. Removing such firearms from circulation is therefore regarded by authorities as an important part of efforts to improve public safety. The weapons destroyed included firearms that had been seized by security and law-enforcement agencies, as well as obsolete and decommissioned weapons. Their destruction prevents them from returning to circulation through theft, illegal resale or other means. The exercise also demonstrates the importance of maintaining effective systems for the registration, storage and disposal of weapons recovered during security operations. Nigeria has struggled with the proliferation of small arms and light weapons for years. The problem is particularly serious in regions affected by armed banditry and insurgency, where criminal groups have accumulated firearms through trafficking, theft and other illicit channels. Weapons have also been used in kidnapping operations and attacks on rural communities. The government has consequently sought to strengthen control over firearms while improving cooperation among security and regulatory agencies. The National Centre for the Control of Small Arms and Light Weapons has a central role in coordinating efforts to address the problem. Its work includes supporting measures to identify illicit weapons, improve information sharing and strengthen national controls over firearms. Destroying recovered weapons is one component of that broader process. Security agencies continue to conduct operations aimed at recovering firearms from criminal groups and disrupting supply networks. However, officials face the difficult task of preventing new weapons from entering the country or reaching criminal organisations. Nigeria's long borders and extensive informal trading routes create challenges for monitoring the movement of arms. Regional instability in parts of West Africa has also increased concerns about weapons moving across national boundaries. Cooperation with neighbouring countries and regional security organisations is therefore important. The destruction of seized weapons also has symbolic significance for communities affected by violence. Residents in areas experiencing repeated attacks have frequently called for stronger action to prevent armed groups from obtaining firearms. Reducing the number of weapons available to criminal organisations can help limit their ability to carry out attacks, although security experts generally regard weapons control as only one part of a much wider strategy. Intelligence gathering, effective policing, border management and economic measures are also necessary to address the conditions that allow armed groups to operate. The Federal Government has continued to emphasise a combination of military and non-military approaches to insecurity. Security operations have been accompanied by efforts to improve intelligence, strengthen cooperation among agencies and address the movement of illegal weapons. State governments have also been encouraged to work more closely with federal security agencies because much of the intelligence required to identify criminal networks comes from local communities. The latest destruction exercise therefore forms part of a continuing national campaign rather than a standalone response. Authorities will need to maintain effective systems for recovering illicit weapons and ensuring that seized firearms are securely stored until they can be destroyed or otherwise lawfully disposed of. They will also need to pursue the networks responsible for supplying firearms to criminal groups. For communities affected by violence, the ultimate measure of success will be whether fewer weapons translate into fewer attacks, kidnappings and other crimes. Nigeria's destruction of 2,819 weapons represents a concrete step in removing illicit firearms from circulation, while highlighting the wider challenge of controlling the flow of arms in a country facing persistent security threats.
img: Nigerian security and arms-control officials overseeing the destruction of seized illicit and obsolete firearms during a national weapons-disposal exercise.

headline: Nigeria Says Subsidy Savings Absorbed by Debt Costs and Higher Spending
summary: Nigeria's finance minister said savings from the removal of fuel subsidies and foreign-exchange reforms had largely been absorbed by higher debt-servicing costs and increased government spending. The explanation comes amid continued public debate over the economic impact of President Bola Tinubu's reforms.
fullStory: ABUJA — Nigeria's Finance Minister said on July 30 that financial savings generated by the removal of fuel subsidies and reforms to the foreign-exchange market had largely been absorbed by higher debt-servicing costs and increased government spending. The explanation came as the Federal Government continued to defend economic reforms that have significantly changed the country's fiscal and monetary environment while also placing pressure on households and businesses. President Bola Tinubu introduced the fuel subsidy removal and major foreign-exchange reforms after taking office in 2023. The measures received support from investors and international financial institutions, which had long argued that Nigeria's subsidy system placed a heavy burden on public finances and that the foreign-exchange market required substantial reform. The removal of the subsidy immediately changed the economics of petrol consumption in Nigeria. The government no longer bore the same direct cost of maintaining artificially low fuel prices, but motorists and businesses faced significantly higher pump prices. The increase in transportation and operating costs subsequently contributed to broader pressure on household budgets. The foreign-exchange reforms also resulted in a major adjustment in the value of the naira. While the reforms were intended to create a more market-driven system and attract investment, the weaker currency increased the local cost of many imported goods and inputs. Businesses that depend on imported machinery, raw materials and other products faced higher expenses, while consumers experienced increases in the prices of numerous goods. According to the Finance Minister, the financial benefits expected from the reforms have therefore been offset to a significant extent by other government costs. Debt servicing has become a particularly important component of Nigeria's expenditure because the government must meet obligations on both domestic and external borrowing. Higher interest costs can reduce the amount of public revenue available for infrastructure, social programmes and other government priorities. Increased government expenditure has also absorbed part of the savings generated by the reforms. The government's position reflects a central challenge facing Nigeria's economic policy: reforms that improve fiscal sustainability in one area can create significant adjustment costs elsewhere. The subsidy removal reduced one major government expense, but the resulting increase in fuel prices affected transportation, food distribution and household spending. Similarly, foreign-exchange reforms were designed to improve market efficiency, but the adjustment in the naira increased the cost of imports and contributed to inflationary pressure. The government has argued that the reforms are necessary to create a more sustainable economic foundation and attract investment. Supporters say that maintaining the previous subsidy system would have continued to consume public resources that could otherwise have been invested in infrastructure and development. Critics, however, have questioned how effectively the savings are being redirected and whether ordinary Nigerians are receiving enough benefit from the changes. The debate has become particularly important as households continue to deal with elevated living costs. Food, transportation and energy expenses remain major concerns for many Nigerians, while businesses continue to face high operating costs. The government has introduced various measures intended to cushion the effects of the reforms, including social investment programmes and initiatives aimed at supporting businesses and vulnerable households. The effectiveness of those measures remains an important part of the wider economic debate. Nigeria's fiscal position is also closely linked to oil revenue. Although the government has sought to diversify the economy, crude oil remains an important source of foreign exchange and public income. Higher oil production and improved revenue collection could therefore provide additional resources for government programmes and help reduce dependence on borrowing. The Finance Minister's comments highlight the difficult balance facing policymakers as Nigeria continues its economic adjustment. The government wants to preserve the gains associated with subsidy and foreign-exchange reforms while addressing the cost-of-living pressures they have generated. For households and businesses, the key question remains whether the reforms will eventually produce stronger growth, more stable prices and improved living standards. For policymakers, the challenge is ensuring that public finances become more sustainable without allowing the adjustment process to impose excessive burdens on citizens.
img: Nigeria's Finance Minister speaking during an economic briefing on government revenue, debt servicing and ongoing economic reforms in Abuja.

headline: Nigeria's SEC Approves New Rules to Strengthen Digital Asset Market
summary: Nigeria's Securities and Exchange Commission has approved new regulatory measures for the country's digital-asset market, strengthening the framework governing virtual-asset service providers. The move is part of efforts to improve investor protection and bring more transparency to Nigeria's rapidly developing digital-finance sector.
fullStory: ABUJA — Nigeria's Securities and Exchange Commission has approved new measures aimed at strengthening regulation of the country's digital-asset market, as authorities seek to improve investor protection and create clearer operating standards for businesses involved in virtual-asset activities. The regulatory development comes as digital assets and blockchain-based financial services continue to attract users and businesses in Nigeria. The SEC has increasingly moved toward establishing a formal framework for companies operating in the sector rather than leaving digital-asset activities outside the country's financial regulatory system. The objective is to provide clearer rules for businesses while protecting investors from fraud, market abuse and other risks associated with rapidly developing financial technologies. Digital-asset regulation has become an important issue for Nigeria because the country has one of Africa's most active cryptocurrency user communities. Nigerians have used digital assets for payments, investment, remittances and other financial activities, although the market has also experienced volatility and regulatory uncertainty. Establishing clearer rules could make it easier for legitimate businesses to operate while giving regulators greater ability to monitor the sector. Under the regulatory framework, companies providing virtual-asset services are expected to meet registration and compliance requirements. These requirements are intended to establish greater transparency around the businesses handling customers' digital assets and to reduce the risks associated with unregulated operators. The SEC has also emphasised the importance of consumer protection as part of its approach to regulating the sector. Digital-asset markets can expose investors to significant risks because prices can change rapidly and some projects may lack strong governance or reliable financial backing. Investors can also face risks from cybercrime, fraudulent schemes and platforms that operate without effective oversight. Regulation cannot eliminate those risks, but authorities can require businesses to meet minimum standards and provide clearer information to customers. The development of Nigeria's digital-asset market is also connected to the country's broader push toward financial technology. Nigerian technology companies have developed payment platforms and financial services that have attracted both domestic and international investment. Blockchain technology and digital assets form another part of this expanding financial ecosystem. Regulators therefore face the challenge of supporting innovation without allowing new technologies to become channels for financial crime or consumer abuse. The SEC has worked with other government institutions to develop a coordinated approach to digital assets. Financial regulation in Nigeria involves several agencies with different responsibilities, making cooperation important when activities cross traditional boundaries. Digital assets can also create challenges for law-enforcement authorities because transactions may move across borders and involve online platforms outside Nigeria. Stronger regulatory requirements can help authorities identify legitimate businesses and improve monitoring of suspicious activity. For financial institutions and investors, clearer regulation could also improve confidence in the sector. Businesses are more likely to invest in regulated markets when they understand the rules governing their activities. At the same time, excessive restrictions could discourage innovation or push users toward informal markets. Regulators therefore need to balance investor protection with the need to allow legitimate technological development. Nigeria's approach reflects a broader international trend toward bringing digital assets within established financial regulatory systems. Governments and regulators around the world have been developing rules covering cryptocurrency exchanges, digital-asset service providers, stablecoins and other blockchain-based products. The rapid development of the sector has made regulation increasingly important as more consumers and businesses participate in digital finance. For Nigeria, the latest SEC measures represent another step toward establishing a more structured digital-asset market. The success of the framework will depend on enforcement, transparency and the ability of regulators to respond as technology evolves. Businesses will also need to understand and comply with the new requirements if they want to operate legitimately in the Nigerian market. Investors, meanwhile, will continue to face the need to assess risks carefully despite stronger oversight. The new measures therefore mark an important development in Nigeria's financial regulatory environment and could help create a clearer distinction between legitimate digital-asset businesses and unregulated operators. As digital finance continues to expand, regulators are likely to face continuing pressure to update the rules while ensuring that innovation remains possible within a safer and more transparent market.
img: Securities and Exchange Commission officials reviewing Nigeria's digital-asset regulatory framework during a financial-sector briefing in Abuja.

headline: Trump Says US Will Hold Off Fresh Iran Attack in Hope of Quick Deal
summary: US President Donald Trump said Washington would pause plans for a fresh attack on Iran to allow time for a possible agreement aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz and addressing concerns over Iran's nuclear programme. The announcement came amid continuing tensions that have disrupted a major global energy route.
fullStory: WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump said on August 1 that the United States would hold off on a fresh attack against Iran if a deal could be reached quickly to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and address Washington's concerns over Iran's nuclear programme. Trump announced the decision in a post on Truth Social following a telephone conversation with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. The announcement came amid heightened tensions in the Middle East and continuing disruption to one of the world's most important maritime routes. The Strait of Hormuz is a vital passage for global energy supplies, with large volumes of crude oil and other petroleum products moving through the waterway each day. Prolonged disruption has therefore raised concerns about higher energy prices, inflation and pressure on economies that depend heavily on imported fuel. Trump said Iran and other countries had requested additional time to reach an agreement. He said the proposed arrangement would involve the immediate reopening of the strait and measures addressing what Washington describes as Iran's nuclear threat. The US president did not identify all the countries involved in the request. The announcement followed months of escalating confrontation between the United States, Israel and Iran. The conflict has affected regional security and created uncertainty for shipping companies and energy markets. Iran has continued to defend its position on its nuclear programme, while the United States and Israel have demanded restrictions on activities they say could enable Tehran to develop nuclear weapons. Iran has repeatedly maintained that its nuclear programme is intended for peaceful purposes. The Strait of Hormuz has become one of the most sensitive points in the confrontation because of its importance to global energy trade. Any prolonged closure or disruption could affect oil and gas supplies and increase costs for importers around the world. Countries in Asia, Europe and other regions closely monitor developments in the waterway because of their dependence on Middle Eastern energy exports. Saudi Arabia has also been closely involved in diplomatic efforts to reduce tensions. The kingdom has sought to protect regional stability and ensure that disruptions to energy supplies do not produce wider economic consequences. Trump's conversation with the Saudi crown prince therefore came as Washington considered diplomatic options alongside its military posture. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that negotiations between Tehran and Oman concerning alternative arrangements for the Strait of Hormuz were in their final stages, according to Iran's official news agency IRNA. Iran's position indicated that diplomatic contacts were continuing even as tensions remained high. Israel, meanwhile, said it supported Trump's decision to give diplomacy an opportunity but maintained that it would act independently if Iran resumed nuclear or missile programmes that Israel considered a threat. The competing positions leave considerable uncertainty over whether the diplomatic opening can produce a lasting agreement. For global energy markets, the immediate concern is whether shipping through the strait can return to normal. Traders have already responded to the disruption by monitoring crude prices and assessing alternative routes. Any sustained reduction in energy shipments could raise costs for consumers and businesses and place additional pressure on inflation. The situation also has implications for countries outside the Middle East. Higher oil prices can increase transportation and production costs, particularly in economies that rely heavily on imported petroleum products. Developing countries could face additional pressure on foreign-exchange reserves and household incomes if fuel prices remain elevated. Trump's decision to delay further military action therefore represents both a diplomatic opening and a temporary pause in a wider confrontation. Whether the pause develops into a lasting agreement will depend on negotiations involving Iran, the United States and other regional actors. For now, international attention remains focused on the Strait of Hormuz and on whether the latest diplomatic efforts can prevent another escalation in the Middle East.
img: US President Donald Trump speaking during a diplomatic and security engagement concerning tensions with Iran and the Strait of Hormuz.

headline: Nollywood Filmmakers Push for Stronger Support for Nigeria's Creative Industry
summary: Nigerian filmmakers and other creative-industry stakeholders have renewed calls for stronger investment, better infrastructure and policies that can help the country's film sector compete internationally. The discussion comes as Nollywood continues to expand its audience across Africa and global streaming platforms.
fullStory: LAGOS — Stakeholders in Nigeria's film industry have renewed calls for stronger support for Nollywood as filmmakers, producers and other creative professionals seek better conditions for producing and distributing Nigerian films. The sector has grown into one of the country's most recognisable cultural industries, reaching audiences across Africa and gaining increasing international attention through cinemas and digital streaming platforms. Industry participants have continued to identify financing, production infrastructure, distribution and skills development as areas requiring greater attention. Producing films at a competitive standard can require substantial investment in equipment, locations, post-production and marketing. Independent filmmakers in particular can face difficulties securing the capital required to complete projects and bring them to audiences. Stakeholders have therefore argued that policies supporting access to finance could help more Nigerian filmmakers develop commercially viable productions. Distribution has also changed significantly as streaming services have created new opportunities for Nigerian films to reach viewers outside the country. Nollywood productions are now available to audiences in many parts of the world, allowing filmmakers to build international recognition without relying exclusively on traditional cinema distribution. The expansion of digital platforms has also created new questions about how producers and performers are compensated when films generate revenue through streaming. Industry representatives have continued to call for clearer commercial arrangements and stronger protection of intellectual-property rights. Piracy remains another major concern. Unauthorised distribution of films can reduce revenue for producers and discourage investment in new productions. The availability of legitimate digital platforms has helped provide audiences with more legal ways to watch Nigerian films, but enforcement of copyright protections remains important to protecting creators. The industry's development is also linked to employment. Film production supports actors, directors, writers, editors, camera operators, costume designers, set workers and many other professionals. A stronger film sector can therefore create opportunities for young Nigerians entering creative careers. Training and professional development remain important as productions become more technically demanding and compete for international audiences. Nigerian filmmakers have also increasingly explored stories that reflect local experiences while appealing to viewers abroad. The global interest in Nigerian culture has created opportunities for the industry to present different aspects of the country's history, society and contemporary life. However, industry participants have stressed that international success should be matched by sustainable domestic production structures. Investment in studios, equipment, post-production facilities and distribution networks could reduce production costs and improve the quality and competitiveness of local films. Government agencies have introduced various programmes aimed at supporting the creative economy, while private investors and international partners have also increased their involvement. The challenge is ensuring that support reaches a broad range of filmmakers rather than being concentrated among a small number of established companies. Transparent funding systems and professional industry standards can help create a more sustainable environment. The Nigerian film industry has demonstrated considerable resilience despite economic pressures and production challenges. Filmmakers continue to release new projects and experiment with different genres and distribution models. The growth of streaming has particularly expanded the potential market for Nigerian productions, while international collaborations have created additional opportunities for local talent. For the industry to maintain this momentum, stakeholders say Nigeria must continue improving the business environment surrounding film production. Better access to finance, stronger copyright enforcement, reliable infrastructure and skills development could help more creative businesses grow. With a large domestic audience and increasing international interest, Nollywood remains an important part of Nigeria's cultural and creative economy. The latest calls from industry stakeholders therefore reflect a broader effort to ensure that the sector's growth produces sustainable careers, stronger businesses and more globally competitive Nigerian productions.
img: Nigerian filmmakers and actors working on a Nollywood film production on location in Lagos.

headline: Russia Pounds Kyiv With Missiles, Killing at Least Nine
summary: A major Russian missile attack struck Kyiv on August 1, killing at least nine people and injuring dozens more, according to Ukrainian officials. The overnight strikes damaged residential buildings and other civilian infrastructure as the war entered another period of intensified attacks.
fullStory: KYIV — A major Russian missile attack struck Kyiv in the early hours of August 1, killing at least nine people and injuring 28 others, including four children, according to Ukrainian authorities. The attack sent residents into shelters as explosions were reported across the Ukrainian capital and surrounding areas. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said emergency services were working at several locations affected by the strikes. Residential buildings and other civilian infrastructure were damaged, while rescue workers searched affected areas for victims and survivors. The attack was among the latest in a continuing series of Russian strikes against Ukrainian cities as the war between Russia and Ukraine enters another prolonged phase. Kyiv has frequently been targeted by missiles and drones, forcing residents to rely on air-raid warnings and underground shelters for protection. Ukrainian authorities have repeatedly called on international partners to strengthen the country's air-defence capabilities, arguing that improved systems are essential to protecting cities and critical infrastructure. The latest attack also came amid continuing diplomatic efforts to find a path toward ending the war. Despite negotiations and international pressure, fighting has continued along the front lines while both sides have carried out long-range strikes. Civilian areas remain particularly vulnerable when missiles and drones reach major population centres. Ukraine's emergency services have developed extensive response procedures for missile attacks, including rapid deployment of rescue teams, firefighters and medical personnel. However, the scale and frequency of attacks can place considerable pressure on emergency workers and local authorities. Residents in Kyiv have also become accustomed to receiving air-raid alerts, although repeated attacks continue to create fear and disruption. Schools, businesses and public services can be affected when strikes damage infrastructure or when authorities impose temporary restrictions for safety reasons. The human cost of the war extends beyond those killed or injured during individual attacks. Millions of Ukrainians have been displaced since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, while communities across the country continue to deal with damaged homes, disrupted electricity supplies and other infrastructure losses. Kyiv has generally remained under Ukrainian control but has repeatedly come under long-range attack. The capital's air-defence systems have intercepted many incoming missiles and drones, according to Ukrainian officials, although some weapons continue to reach their targets. The effectiveness of air defence has become a central part of Ukraine's efforts to protect its population and maintain essential services. Russia has not immediately provided a detailed public account of the specific attack. Moscow has repeatedly said that its military operations are directed at military and strategic targets, while Ukrainian officials have accused Russian forces of striking civilian areas. Independent verification of individual damage assessments can be difficult during ongoing attacks. The latest casualties nevertheless demonstrate the continuing danger faced by civilians in major Ukrainian cities. International governments have continued to call for an end to the fighting and a negotiated settlement. Diplomatic efforts have involved Ukraine, Russia and external partners, but disagreements over territory, security guarantees and the future political relationship between the two countries remain major obstacles. For residents of Kyiv, the immediate priority after the August 1 attack was rescue and medical assistance for those affected. Emergency crews continued working at damaged sites while authorities assessed the extent of destruction. The attack serves as another reminder that, despite diplomatic efforts, the conflict continues to impose a heavy cost on civilians and communities across Ukraine.

headline: Nigeria's Oil Industry Records Stronger Production as Government Targets Higher Output
summary: Nigeria's oil sector continued its gradual production recovery in 2026 as government agencies and producers intensified efforts to curb crude theft and improve output. Higher production remains central to efforts to strengthen foreign-exchange earnings and government revenue.
fullStory: ABUJA — Nigeria's petroleum industry continued to focus on increasing crude oil production in 2026 as the government and oil producers intensified efforts to address theft, pipeline vandalism and other operational challenges affecting output. The drive to restore production remains central to Nigeria's efforts to strengthen foreign-exchange earnings and improve government revenue. Crude oil has historically been one of the country's largest sources of export income, making production levels an important indicator for the wider economy. Nigeria has faced several years of lower-than-potential output as crude theft, damaged infrastructure, ageing facilities and investment constraints affected operations in oil-producing areas. The government has consequently placed greater emphasis on securing production facilities and creating conditions that can attract new investment. Security agencies and oil companies have expanded surveillance around pipelines and production facilities, while new measures have been introduced to tackle illegal crude-oil activities. These efforts are intended to reduce losses and ensure that a greater share of Nigeria's production reaches legitimate export and refining channels. Higher production could provide several benefits for the Nigerian economy. Increased crude exports generate foreign exchange that can support imports and help strengthen the country's external position. Additional oil revenue can also improve government finances, although the effect depends on international crude prices, production costs and the amount of oil actually reaching the market. The government has also encouraged greater participation by indigenous oil companies. Nigerian producers have acquired assets previously operated by international oil companies, increasing the role of local firms in exploration and production. The shift has created opportunities for indigenous operators but also placed greater responsibility on them to maintain production, invest in infrastructure and meet environmental and regulatory requirements. Domestic refining is another major part of Nigeria's petroleum strategy. Increased refining capacity means more crude can potentially be processed inside the country rather than exported as raw material and later imported as refined products. The growth of large-scale refining capacity has changed the structure of the downstream petroleum market and could gradually reduce Nigeria's dependence on imported fuels. However, the benefits of higher crude production and domestic refining depend on reliable infrastructure and stable operating conditions. Producers need access to finance, equipment and secure production environments, while refiners require dependable crude supplies. The government has therefore continued to pursue reforms intended to improve the overall petroleum investment climate. The Petroleum Industry Act remains the main legislative framework for the sector and provides new rules for upstream operations, regulation and investment. Authorities have said the reforms are intended to create greater certainty for investors and improve the efficiency of the industry. Nigeria also faces pressure to reduce its dependence on crude oil over the longer term. The government's economic diversification agenda places greater emphasis on agriculture, manufacturing, technology and other non-oil sectors. Nevertheless, oil is expected to remain an important source of foreign exchange and public revenue for the foreseeable future. The challenge is therefore to use petroleum income to support broader economic development while gradually reducing vulnerability to oil-price fluctuations. For communities in the Niger Delta, increased production also raises questions about environmental protection and local development. Oil-producing communities have long called for greater investment in infrastructure and stronger action against pollution. The success of the sector will therefore be measured not only by production figures but also by the benefits delivered to communities and the wider economy. Nigeria's production recovery remains a work in progress. Sustaining higher output will require continued action against theft, investment in infrastructure and a stable regulatory environment. If those conditions are maintained, stronger production could provide useful support for the country's foreign-exchange position and government finances while the broader economy continues its transition toward greater diversification.

headline: UEFA and CONCACAF Withdraw Confidence in FIFA President Infantino
summary: UEFA and CONCACAF said they had lost confidence in FIFA President Gianni Infantino following the collapse of a controversial proposal to sell a stake in the commercial rights of the World Cup and other FIFA competitions. The dispute has intensified calls for greater transparency and consultation within world football's governing body.
fullStory: ZURICH — FIFA President Gianni Infantino faced mounting pressure on August 1 after UEFA and CONCACAF said they had lost confidence in his leadership following the withdrawal of a controversial plan to sell a stake in the commercial rights of the World Cup and other FIFA competitions. The dispute has triggered an unusually public confrontation between FIFA's president and several of the organisation's regional confederations. FIFA had proposed creating a commercial subsidiary that would manage the World Cup and other competitions and raise about $4.2 billion by selling a 20% stake to outside investors. The proposal was presented to FIFA's 211 member associations, but several regional confederations complained that they had not been adequately consulted before the plan was advanced. The proposal was subsequently abandoned after strong opposition from football officials. UEFA welcomed the withdrawal but said the episode had exposed deeper concerns about FIFA's governance. Europe's governing body said it had lost confidence in Infantino and called for greater accountability over decisions affecting the future of world football. CONCACAF, which governs football in North America, Central America and the Caribbean, also criticised the process and said the proposal had been advanced outside established governance procedures. The criticism represents a significant challenge for Infantino, who has been one of the most influential figures in international football since becoming FIFA president in 2016. He has been re-elected twice without facing opposition and had appeared to be in a strong position ahead of the next presidential election. The dispute could nevertheless complicate his political position as FIFA prepares for another leadership contest. The controversy centres not only on the commercial proposal but also on the way it was developed. Regional confederations argued that a decision with potentially far-reaching consequences for the finances and governance of global football should have involved consultation with FIFA's confederations, council and member associations before being presented as a formal initiative. Critics have described the process as lacking transparency and said FIFA's leadership needs stronger checks and balances. Infantino and FIFA have defended their approach to developing commercial opportunities and have argued that additional revenues could support football development around the world. The abandoned proposal was expected to generate substantial funds that could have been used for football development programmes, although critics questioned whether the benefits justified changing the structure through which FIFA manages its commercial assets. The dispute has also highlighted tensions over FIFA's financial resources. UEFA argued that FIFA already holds substantial reserves and questioned the need to sell a stake in future World Cup commercial income. The disagreement therefore involves both governance and the distribution of football revenues. Several national football associations have joined the debate, with some expressing concern about the lack of consultation while others continuing to support Infantino. The division could become more significant as the next FIFA presidential election approaches. Infantino has said he intends to seek another term, and his previous electoral dominance had made his re-election appear relatively secure. The latest dispute, however, has demonstrated that influential football organisations are prepared to challenge his leadership publicly. The episode has also renewed broader discussions about how FIFA makes major commercial decisions. Regional confederations have called for future initiatives to be discussed through established governance structures and for member associations to have sufficient time to assess their implications. For FIFA, restoring trust among its regional partners could now become a major priority. The organisation will need to rebuild relationships with confederations that have questioned the transparency of its decision-making while continuing to manage the commercial and sporting demands of global football. The collapse of the proposal therefore marks more than the end of a single commercial initiative. It has exposed a serious governance dispute within international football and placed additional scrutiny on Infantino's leadership ahead of the next FIFA presidential election.

headline: Fire Breaks Out at FMBN Headquarters in Abuja, No Injuries Reported
summary: A fire incident occurred at the headquarters of the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria in Abuja, with emergency responders containing the flames before they spread further. The bank said no injuries were recorded and that investigations had begun to determine the cause of the incident.
fullStory: ABUJA — A fire incident occurred at parts of the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria headquarters in Abuja, prompting a rapid response from emergency services and raising concerns over the safety of public buildings in the Federal Capital Territory. The incident occurred shortly after 8pm on Saturday, August 1, at the bank's head office in the Central Business District of Abuja, according to a statement issued by the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria on August 2. The fire affected parts of the second floor of the building. The bank said combined teams from the Federal Fire Service and the Federal Capital Territory Fire Service responded quickly after the outbreak was reported. Their intervention brought the flames under control and prevented the incident from developing into a larger emergency. No injuries were recorded, according to the bank. The absence of casualties provided some relief following an incident that occurred in a busy part of the capital where public and commercial buildings are located. The bank did not immediately give a full assessment of the material damage caused by the fire. It said investigations were underway to establish the cause of the incident and determine the extent of the damage. A detailed statement was expected after the assessment had been completed. The Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria is a government-owned financial institution established to support the development of Nigeria's housing and mortgage sector. Its headquarters is located in Abuja's Central Business District, an area that hosts several government institutions and commercial establishments. A fire at a major public institution can create operational and safety concerns even when casualties are avoided. Emergency responders must first contain the immediate threat while authorities subsequently determine whether affected areas remain safe for staff and visitors. The FMBN said the quick response by the fire services helped to bring the situation under control. The bank also acknowledged the support of the Nigeria Police Force and other stakeholders involved in the emergency response. The incident highlights the importance of effective fire prevention and emergency-response systems in public buildings. Abuja has experienced fires in commercial and government facilities in the past, making fire safety an ongoing concern for building managers and emergency agencies. Regular inspection of electrical systems, fire alarms, extinguishers, emergency exits and other safety equipment can help reduce the risk of serious incidents and improve evacuation procedures when fires occur. The cause of the FMBN fire had not been established at the time of the bank's statement. Investigators are expected to examine the affected section of the building and assess possible electrical, mechanical or other sources. Determining the cause will also help authorities establish whether additional safety measures are necessary. The bank's decision to wait for the outcome of the investigation before announcing the extent of the damage reflects the need for a proper technical assessment. Premature estimates could be inaccurate while parts of an affected building are still being inspected. For staff members and stakeholders who use the headquarters, the immediate concern is likely to be the safety of the premises and the continuity of the bank's operations. Government institutions generally have contingency arrangements for maintaining essential services during emergencies, although the extent to which those arrangements are needed will depend on the damage assessment. The incident ended without reported loss of life, but it nevertheless underscores the need for public institutions to maintain strong fire-safety procedures. The Federal Mortgage Bank said it appreciated the concern expressed by stakeholders and members of the public following the incident. Further information on the cause and extent of the damage is expected after the investigation is completed. Until then, the successful containment of the fire and the absence of reported injuries remain the key developments from the incident.

headline: African Leaders Renew Push for Stronger Continental Trade Cooperation
summary: African leaders and regional officials renewed calls for stronger implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area as countries seek to increase trade within the continent. The discussions focused on reducing trade barriers, improving infrastructure and helping African businesses access regional markets.
fullStory: ADDIS ABABA — African leaders and regional officials have renewed calls for stronger implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area as countries across the continent seek to increase trade among themselves and reduce dependence on external markets. The discussions have focused on removing barriers that continue to make cross-border commerce difficult and creating conditions that allow businesses to take greater advantage of Africa's combined market. The African Continental Free Trade Area is intended to create one of the world's largest single markets by bringing together economies across the continent. Its long-term objective is to increase trade among African countries, encourage investment and support industrial development. Supporters argue that stronger intra-African trade could help countries diversify their economies and reduce dependence on the export of raw commodities. Despite the potential benefits, trade between African countries remains constrained by several practical challenges. Differences in customs procedures, regulations and standards can make it difficult for businesses to move goods across borders. Poor transport infrastructure and high logistics costs can also make regional trade more expensive than importing goods from outside the continent. Small and medium-sized businesses are particularly affected because they often have fewer resources to navigate complex cross-border procedures. African governments have therefore continued to discuss ways of simplifying customs processes and improving trade infrastructure. Digital systems are also increasingly being used to reduce paperwork and improve the movement of goods. Faster customs clearance can lower costs for businesses and make regional markets more attractive to producers. Improved roads, railways, ports and border facilities are equally important to achieving the objectives of the continental trade agreement. Manufacturing is another major area of focus. African economies have historically relied heavily on exports of oil, minerals and agricultural commodities, leaving many countries vulnerable to fluctuations in global commodity prices. Expanding manufacturing and processing capacity could allow countries to capture more value from their natural resources and create additional employment. Regional trade can support this process by giving manufacturers access to a larger customer base. For Nigeria and other large African economies, the continental market offers opportunities to expand exports of locally produced goods. Nigerian businesses already trade across West Africa, but regulatory and logistical challenges can limit the scale of cross-border commerce. Stronger implementation of the trade agreement could provide opportunities for Nigerian manufacturers, agricultural processors and service providers to reach customers in other African markets. However, businesses will require competitive production costs and reliable infrastructure to take advantage of those opportunities. The agreement also places emphasis on reducing restrictions on services and investment. Expanding trade in financial services, technology, telecommunications and professional services could create additional opportunities for African companies. Digital businesses in particular can reach customers across borders without the same physical infrastructure requirements as traditional manufacturers, although differences in national regulations remain a challenge. The renewed focus on implementation comes as African governments face pressure to create jobs and strengthen economic resilience. Africa's growing population provides a potentially large consumer market, but governments must ensure that businesses can produce goods and services competitively enough to meet that demand. Greater regional integration could contribute to this objective by encouraging investment and creating larger markets for African companies. The success of the continental trade project will ultimately depend on implementation at national and regional levels. Governments need to align policies, improve border procedures and invest in infrastructure while businesses need to develop products and services that can compete across different markets. Continued political commitment will also be necessary to overcome disagreements that may arise during implementation. The renewed calls from African leaders therefore underline the importance of turning the principles of continental free trade into practical benefits for businesses and consumers. If trade barriers are gradually reduced and infrastructure improves, stronger intra-African commerce could support industrialisation, investment and job creation across the continent. For Nigeria and other major African economies, the expanding regional market presents an opportunity to strengthen domestic production while building stronger economic links with neighbouring countries.

headline: Nigeria's Oil Output Rises as Production Reaches New 2026 High
summary: Nigeria's crude oil production increased in July, providing a boost to the country's export earnings and government revenue outlook. The improvement came as authorities and oil producers continued efforts to curb theft and restore production capacity.
fullStory: ABUJA — Nigeria's crude oil production recorded an improvement in July, providing a boost to the country's petroleum sector as authorities continued efforts to restore output and reduce losses caused by theft and operational disruptions. The increase comes at a time when the Federal Government is seeking stronger oil production to improve foreign-exchange earnings and government revenue. Crude oil remains one of Nigeria's most important sources of foreign exchange, despite years of efforts to diversify the economy. Higher production can therefore strengthen the country's external position and provide additional resources for government spending. Nigeria's oil industry has faced significant challenges in recent years. Crude theft, pipeline vandalism, ageing infrastructure and operational difficulties have reduced production from levels the country could potentially achieve. Security operations and investments in production infrastructure have consequently become central to efforts to reverse the decline. The July improvement suggests that some of these measures are beginning to support higher output. However, maintaining the increase will require continued investment and effective protection of oil-producing facilities. The government has encouraged oil companies to increase production and has introduced measures aimed at improving the investment environment. The Petroleum Industry Act has also provided a new regulatory framework intended to encourage investment and improve efficiency in the sector. International oil companies and indigenous producers are expected to play an important role in increasing output as new investments come on stream. Higher production could have several benefits for the Nigerian economy. Increased exports would provide additional foreign exchange, while stronger government revenue could improve the ability of federal and state authorities to finance public programmes. Oil production also supports employment and activity across transportation, engineering, logistics and other supporting industries. However, increased output does not automatically translate into improved living conditions. The wider economy continues to face inflation and high operating costs, while government finances remain under pressure from substantial expenditure commitments. The benefits of higher oil revenue will therefore depend partly on how effectively the additional income is managed. Nigeria has also sought to increase the contribution of its refining sector and reduce dependence on imported petroleum products. Increased domestic refining capacity could allow more of the country's crude to be processed locally, reducing some of the foreign-exchange requirements associated with importing refined products. The growth of domestic refining and improved crude production could therefore strengthen the petroleum value chain. Security remains one of the most important factors affecting production. Oil-producing areas have experienced theft and attacks on infrastructure, while illegal tapping of pipelines can result in substantial losses and environmental damage. The government and security agencies have increased efforts to protect production facilities and disrupt criminal networks involved in crude theft. Oil companies have also adopted additional monitoring and surveillance measures. Sustained production growth will depend on whether these interventions remain effective. Producers also need stable regulations and access to financing to maintain and expand their operations. The government has therefore continued to encourage investment in both existing fields and new developments. For international investors, Nigeria's large reserves remain attractive, but security, regulatory and infrastructure concerns continue to influence investment decisions. The July production improvement nevertheless provides a positive signal for the petroleum sector. If sustained, higher output could strengthen export earnings and improve the government's revenue position. The immediate challenge will be maintaining production while addressing the structural problems that have constrained Nigeria's oil industry for years. Authorities and producers will need to continue investing in infrastructure, improving security and creating a stable environment for new projects. For Nigeria's economy, the return of stronger crude production could provide important support at a time when the country is seeking greater foreign-exchange stability and stronger economic growth.

headline: Gunmen Kill 12, Abduct Women and Children in Sokoto Village
summary: At least 12 people were killed and several women and children abducted during a night attack on Lajinge village in Sokoto State. Witnesses said the attackers also stole livestock and burned a family to death after setting fire to a house where residents had taken shelter.
fullStory: SOKOTO — At least 12 people were killed and women and children were abducted during a night attack on Lajinge village in Sabon Birni Local Government Area of Sokoto State, according to witnesses and police authorities. The attack was carried out by armed men who entered the community late on Saturday and remained in the area for several hours, residents told Reuters. The attackers reportedly arrived at about 11pm and continued their assault until approximately 3am on Sunday. Witnesses said the gunmen moved through the community, attacking residents, stealing livestock and setting fire to houses. Six members of one family were among those who died after the attackers set fire to a house where they had taken shelter. A resident told Reuters that the attack left at least 12 people dead and four others injured, while women and children were taken away by the assailants. The incident adds to continuing security concerns in parts of north-western Nigeria, where armed criminal groups have carried out attacks on rural communities, kidnapped residents for ransom and stolen livestock. Sokoto and neighbouring Zamfara states have experienced repeated attacks in recent years, placing considerable pressure on rural communities and security agencies. Residents of affected areas have frequently called for stronger protection, particularly in communities located far from major towns and security formations. The latest attack also illustrates the wider consequences of insecurity for rural livelihoods. Livestock theft can deprive families of an important source of income, while fear of attacks can discourage farmers from travelling to their fields. When communities become insecure, commercial activity and movement can also be disrupted, affecting food production and local markets. Police in Sokoto said they were investigating the incident and would provide further information. The authorities' response is expected to include efforts to establish the identity of those responsible and determine the whereabouts of the abducted residents. The attack occurred about a week after bandits reportedly killed at least 24 farmers in neighbouring Zamfara State, underlining the continuing threat facing farming communities in the region. Repeated attacks have also raised concerns about the ability of criminal groups to operate across rural areas and move between communities and state boundaries. Security agencies have increasingly relied on intelligence gathering, local informants and joint operations to track armed groups. However, the size of rural territories and the mobility of criminal gangs continue to make prevention difficult. For residents, the absence of rapid security intervention during attacks can deepen fear and encourage some communities to organise local vigilante groups. Such groups can provide early warnings and limited protection but generally lack the equipment and training required to confront heavily armed attackers. The Federal Government and state authorities therefore face continued pressure to strengthen formal security operations in vulnerable communities. Beyond immediate security measures, the effects of repeated attacks extend to education, agriculture and local development. Families may relocate after attacks, children can lose access to schooling and farmers may abandon fields because of fear. These consequences can worsen economic hardship in communities already facing limited infrastructure and employment opportunities. The Lajinge attack therefore represents more than a single security incident. It reflects the continuing challenge of protecting rural communities in north-western Nigeria from armed groups that combine kidnapping, livestock theft and violent raids. Authorities will now face the task of identifying the attackers, locating the abducted residents and improving security arrangements around vulnerable communities. For the families affected, the immediate priority remains the safe return of those taken and support for those who survived the attack.

headline: NNPC Offers Two Crude Oil Cargoes as Nigeria Seeks Higher Export Output
summary: The Nigerian National Petroleum Company has issued tenders for two crude oil cargoes scheduled for September, including the country's newer Cawthorne grade and Bonny Light. The move comes as Nigeria seeks to increase oil production and diversify its crude export streams.
fullStory: ABUJA — The Nigerian National Petroleum Company has issued tenders for two crude oil cargoes scheduled for September, including a shipment of Nigeria's relatively new Cawthorne crude grade and another cargo of Bonny Light, according to tender documents seen by Reuters. The development comes as Nigeria continues efforts to increase crude production and expand the range of grades available to international buyers. The Cawthorne cargo is scheduled to load on September 21 and 22 and will comprise approximately 950,000 barrels. NNPC is also offering a 950,000-barrel Bonny Light cargo scheduled to load between September 30 and October 1. Both cargoes are being offered on a free-on-board basis, meaning the buyer assumes responsibility for the crude once it is loaded onto the vessel at the designated export terminal. The tenders form part of Nigeria's continuing efforts to strengthen crude oil exports after years of production challenges caused by underinvestment, oil theft and operational disruptions. Crude oil remains one of Nigeria's most important sources of foreign exchange and government revenue, making the performance of the petroleum sector important to the wider economy. Cawthorne is among several newer Nigerian crude grades introduced as the country's oil industry seeks to increase production and offer international refiners additional options. The grade began exports earlier in 2026, joining other newer streams such as Nembe and Utapate. Diversifying Nigeria's crude export streams can help producers respond to different market requirements and potentially attract a broader range of buyers. Bonny Light, meanwhile, remains one of Nigeria's best-known export grades and is regularly traded in international markets. Preliminary loading information indicated that the Bonny Light production stream was expected to account for about 364,000 barrels per day across 12 cargoes. The latest tenders come amid heightened attention to global oil markets. Traders have been monitoring supply disruptions and geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, including developments affecting shipping routes around the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Such disruptions can influence crude prices and the relative attractiveness of different grades. Nigerian crude producers have therefore been operating in a market where international buyers are assessing both supply security and quality. Increasing production remains a major priority for Nigeria because output has been affected for years by theft, pipeline vandalism, ageing infrastructure and insufficient investment. The Federal Government and oil companies have introduced measures aimed at improving security around production facilities and encouraging new investment. Higher output could strengthen export earnings and provide additional foreign exchange for the economy. The government has also sought to improve the operating environment in the petroleum sector through reforms introduced under the Petroleum Industry Act and other policy measures. Greater regulatory certainty is expected to encourage investment in exploration, production and infrastructure. However, sustained production growth will depend on whether these reforms can address the operational and security problems that have constrained the industry. For international buyers, the availability of additional Nigerian cargoes provides another source of Atlantic Basin crude. For Nigeria, successful sales of the September shipments would contribute to export activity and reinforce the country's position as an important crude supplier. The tender process also provides an indication of the production and export volumes NNPC expects to bring to market in the coming months. As the bids are evaluated, market participants will continue watching international crude prices, shipping conditions and Nigeria's production levels. The latest offering therefore reflects both the immediate commercial activity of NNPC and the broader effort to restore Nigeria's oil production capacity and strengthen one of the country's most important sources of export revenue.

headline: Tinubu Meets Governors, Pushes Fresh Action on State Security
summary: President Bola Tinubu met with state governors in Abuja as the Federal Government intensified consultations on security and other national priorities. The meeting came amid continuing concerns over kidnapping, banditry and other forms of insecurity in several parts of the country.
fullStory: ABUJA — President Bola Tinubu held consultations with state governors in Abuja on August 3 as the Federal Government and state governments continued discussions on security and other national priorities. The meeting brought together the President and governors at a time when communities in several parts of Nigeria remain concerned about kidnapping, banditry and other forms of insecurity. Security has remained one of the major issues confronting the administration, with federal and state authorities under pressure to protect communities, improve intelligence gathering and strengthen the capacity of security agencies. The meeting provided an opportunity for the Federal Government and the states to review the challenges facing different parts of the country and consider areas where closer cooperation could improve the response. Nigeria's security situation varies considerably from one region to another. The North-East continues to face threats from insurgent groups, while parts of the North-West and North-Central have experienced attacks by armed bandits and criminal kidnapping networks. Other parts of the country have also faced communal violence and other security concerns. State governors play an important role in the national security architecture because they work directly with communities and state-level institutions. Although the armed forces and police operate under federal authority, state governments provide important local information and support for security operations. Cooperation between federal and state authorities can therefore improve the speed with which threats are identified and addressed. Intelligence sharing is particularly important in dealing with kidnapping networks. Criminal groups can move between communities and state boundaries, making isolated responses less effective. Coordinated intelligence can help security agencies identify movements, locate victims and disrupt criminal operations. The Federal Government has increasingly emphasised intelligence-led operations as part of its response to insecurity. The meeting also comes as the government continues to review the welfare and operational capacity of security personnel. Better equipment, training, communications systems and personnel welfare are considered important to maintaining effective security operations. The administration has approved additional funding for security and has continued to pursue measures aimed at improving the ability of the military and other agencies to respond to threats. For state governments, insecurity also has economic consequences. Attacks can disrupt farming, transportation and local commerce, particularly in rural communities. Farmers who fear attacks may reduce the amount of land they cultivate or avoid travelling to distant farms, while traders and transport operators can face additional costs. Prolonged insecurity can therefore affect food supply and household incomes as well as personal safety. Governors have consequently continued to call for stronger security measures in vulnerable communities. The Federal Government has also encouraged state authorities to strengthen community-level intelligence and cooperation with security agencies. Such cooperation can help authorities identify emerging threats before they develop into major attacks. However, the effectiveness of these measures depends on the reliability of information and the ability of security agencies to respond quickly. The Abuja meeting therefore forms part of a continuing national effort rather than a single solution to Nigeria's security challenges. The government faces the task of combining military and police operations with intelligence gathering, community engagement and measures addressing the economic conditions that allow criminal networks to operate. For affected communities, the immediate priority remains protection from attacks and the safe movement of residents, farmers and businesses. For the Federal Government and governors, sustained cooperation will be necessary to translate security discussions into practical improvements on the ground. The latest consultations underline the continuing importance of a coordinated national response as Nigeria works to reduce kidnapping, banditry and other threats affecting communities across the country.

headline: Canal+ Secures Exclusive UEFA Club Competition Rights Across Sub-Saharan Africa
summary: Canal+ has secured exclusive broadcasting rights for UEFA's three major men's club competitions across more than 40 countries in Sub-Saharan Africa. The agreement covers the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League from mid-2027 through 2031.
fullStory: JOHANNESBURG — French media group Canal+ has secured exclusive broadcasting rights for UEFA's three major men's club competitions across more than 40 countries in Sub-Saharan Africa, in a deal that will expand access to European football competitions across the continent.
